decisions.title: What is Jet's first-party event system semantic model?
decisions.gist: Choose the core event model Jet should standardize for games, web UI, servers, plugins, hooks, Canvas, and debugging.
decisions.explainer: Events touch too many domains to be a Canvas-only affordance. Jet needs one source-visible, type-safe, lifetime-safe event model that beginners can use with one line and experts can tune for dispatch, ordering, cancellation, async, backpressure, and failure policy.
decisions.story: Doris is building a game HUD and a server dashboard in the same Jet codebase. A button click, a collision, a save hook, and a hot-reload notification should all use the same typed event model, so Canvas, source, debugger, and tests agree on what happened.
decisions.detail: Audit pass: C# gives typed delegates/events but weak lifetime/async policy; DOM gives phases, once/passive, and AbortSignal cleanup but stringly/weak typing; Node EventEmitter is tiny but stringly and has special error/async traps; Godot signals fit games/editor UX but can stay dynamically loose; UnityEvent gives designer-persistent callbacks but ties truth to scene/editor data; Unreal dispatchers feel right visually but live in Blueprint assets. Jet should take typed delegates, signal/editor projection, AbortSignal-style lifetime cleanup, explicit phases/options, and structured-concurrency integration while rejecting stringly names, hidden graph assets, untyped payloads, and unhandled async failures.

options.name: Library-only Event and Hook values
options.detail: Ship Event<T>, Hook<T,R>, Subscription, EventScope, and EventPolicy as ordinary Core/runtime types. No special syntax, no compiler-known event diagnostics beyond normal typing. Smallest language surface, but tools/debugger may not get enough semantic facts unless we later make the library magical.

options.name: Language-level event declarations
options.detail: Add first-class user syntax for declaring events and hooks. Excellent readability and toolability, but risks a new mechanism before the semantic model is proven and creates syntax churn across domains.
options.code:
event clicked(Click)
hook before_save(SaveRequest) -> SaveDecision

options.name: Actor/mailbox/channel-first events
options.detail: Treat events as typed messages delivered to actors/tasks. Strong for concurrency and servers, but awkward for UI/game editor workflows where direct owner lifetimes, inspector wiring, and hooks matter.

options.name: Hybrid Event/Hook family: typed values, compiler-known facts, syntax reserved (recommended)
options.detail: Build Event<T>, Hook<T,R>, Subscription, EventScope, and EventPolicy as ordinary source-visible values, but make the family compiler/tooling-known for diagnostics, debugger traces, Canvas projection, ownership cleanup, async/failure checks, and docs. Reserve user syntax only after real examples prove library spelling is too noisy. One semantic model serves beginner clicks, game collisions, web lifecycle, server hooks, plugin interception, and expert async/backpressure policies.

comparisons.note: Typed delegates/events, many subscribers, sync invocation by default; lifetime leaks and async policy are not solved by the event type.
EventTarget has phases, once/passive options, and AbortSignal cleanup, but event names are strings and handlers receive generic Event objects.
Signals are editor-friendly and first-class enough for games, but payload/arity checking can remain a runtime/user responsibility.
Event Dispatchers feel right in visual scripting but are tied to Blueprint assets; Jet needs source-owned semantics.
comparisons.code: Bind Event to StartFire; Call StartFire

decisions.title: Canonical binary interchange format for core.encoding
decisions.gist: Which single binary serialization format Jet ships beside json/toml/yaml/csv.
decisions.explainer: A: standardization plus a specified deterministic form (hashing/signing/content-addressing all want stable bytes) outweighs MessagePack’s ecosystem edge; one format keeps I8.
decisions.story: Marco's game syncs replay state between a Jet server and clients 60 times a second. JSON is the only interchange format Jet has, so he pays text encode/parse on every tick and his packets are 3x larger than needed. He needs one blessed binary format that works through the same @[Codable] derive — not a menu of five.

options.name: CBOR (RFC 8949)
options.detail: IETF standard with a deterministic-encoding profile (stable bytes for hashing/signing — pairs with crypto.seal and content-addressed stores), native binary strings, and a clean extension model. Same parse/to_string/decode<T> verbs as every other codec.
options.code:
use core.encoding.cbor as cbor

bytes :: cbor.to_bytes(tick)              // [U8], ~1/3 the JSON size
back :: cbor.decode<Tick>(bytes)?

// deterministic profile: same value → same bytes, always
hash :: crypto.sha256(cbor.to_bytes_canonical(tick))

options.name: MessagePack
options.detail: The most popular binary format by ecosystem (Redis, Fluentd, many game stacks). Slightly tighter encoding than CBOR in common cases; no IETF standard, no canonical-form spec — deterministic bytes for hashing would be Jet-invented.
options.code:
use core.encoding.msgpack as msgpack

bytes :: msgpack.to_bytes(tick)
back :: msgpack.decode<Tick>(bytes)?

options.name: Ship both
options.detail: Maximum interop, but two mechanisms for one semantic job — exactly what I8 rejects. Every API that accepts one must document why not the other, forever.
options.code:
use core.encoding.cbor as cbor
use core.encoding.msgpack as msgpack   // which one does your team use? both, eventually

options.name: Decline binary interchange for now
options.detail: JSON stays the only interchange. Games, caches, and IPC keep paying text overhead or hand-rolling formats — the gap every systems language fills in year one.
options.code: // status quo: json.to_string(tick) on a 60Hz loop

comparisons.note: stdlib ships encoding/gob (Go-only) — everyone actually uses CBOR or msgpack third-party; shipping neither pushed the ecosystem off-stdlib.
Codable has JSON + plist only; binary interchange is a long-standing community complaint.
comparisons.code: JSONEncoder() // or a third-party CBOR encoder

comparisons.note: CBOR is the substrate for COSE signing/encryption and WebAuthn — standards momentum is behind it.

decisions.title: Filesystem watch surface and home
decisions.gist: Where filesystem change notifications live and what the beginner surface looks like.
decisions.explainer: A: discovery beats taxonomy — the person with a path in hand is already in core.files; normalize per-OS quirks and debounce by default.
decisions.story: Lena writes a static-site tool in Jet and wants rebuild-on-save. Today she loops fs.list_dir + mtimes on a timer — wasteful, laggy, and subtly wrong on renames. jet dev itself watches files internally; users deserve the same primitive.

options.name: files.watch in core.files
options.detail: One more capability on the module that owns paths: watch(path) returns a WatchHandle whose events() iterate typed changes (Created/Modified/Removed/Renamed). Debounced by default (beginner-safe); raw stream behind an option.

options.name: New core.watch module
options.detail: Separate module name for the whole watching domain (files now; maybe processes/ports later). Cleaner if watching grows beyond files, but today it is one function and a new top-level name to learn.

options.name: Decline — polling helper only
options.detail: Ship files.poll_changes(path, interval) sugar over mtime polling. No OS notification backends to maintain, but it bakes the laggy/wasteful pattern in as the blessed answer.
options.code: loop ev in files.poll_changes("site/", time.ms(500)) { rebuild() }

comparisons.note: fsnotify is the de-facto standard everyone pulls in — Go not shipping it in stdlib is a known gap.
fs.watch is stdlib but semantics vary per-OS; chokidar exists to paper over it — the lesson is to normalize events in the library.

decisions.comment: also include processes and ports now, not later

decisions.title: WebSocket module home
decisions.gist: Where WebSocket client/server support lives.
decisions.explainer: A: upgrade-from-a-route is the dominant real-world shape; keeping it inside core.http gives one import and shared types. Every mainstream stdlib that declined WebSockets regretted it.
decisions.story: Tomás builds a collaborative editor backend in Jet. HTTP endpoints come from core.http; for the live channel he needs WebSockets and finds nothing — he would have to hand-roll the upgrade handshake and frame protocol over raw sockets.

options.name: core.http.ws submodule
options.detail: WebSocket is an HTTP upgrade; it lives where the connection starts. Server: a route handler upgrades; client: ws.connect(url). Shares http types (headers, Url, TLS).

options.name: Standalone core.ws module
options.detail: Own top-level name, imports http types underneath. Slightly more discoverable in a module listing; splits the connection story across two imports for the common server case.

options.name: Decline for this epoch
options.detail: Server-sent events (already in the #301 audit scope) cover server→client push; bidirectional realtime waits. Collaborative/game use cases stay unserved or hand-rolled.
options.code:
// SSE only:
router.get("/live", (req) => http.sse(req, events))

comparisons.note: stdlib has no WebSocket — gorilla/websocket then nhooyr filled it; a decade of "why is this not stdlib".
stdlib has none; websockets/aiohttp fill it. Same story.
WebSocket is just there, next to fetch — the modern expectation Jet should match.

decisions.title: Password hashing surface: crypto.password_hash / password_verify
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a misuse-resistant password hashing pair, and what it exposes.
decisions.explainer: A: PHC-string self-description makes upgrades free and misuse hard; matches the ratified misuse-resistant envelope direction (D-CRYPTOENV1) and I1 safe-by-default.
decisions.story: Deb builds her first Jet web app with signup/login. The seal/open envelope (D-CRYPTOENV1) encrypts data but is wrong for passwords; without a blessed surface she will do what beginners do — sha256(password) — which is exactly the breach headline. The stdlib either hands her Argon2id correctly-parameterized, or the footgun is the default.

options.name: Misuse-resistant pair, Argon2id inside
options.detail: crypto.password_hash(pw) -> String encodes algorithm+params+salt in one PHC string (safe defaults, no knobs required); crypto.password_verify(pw, stored) -> Bool re-derives from the stored params — old hashes keep verifying after defaults change. Expert cost overrides via optional args. Backend follows the ratified D-DEP-CRYPTO1 bridge path.

options.name: Expose raw KDF primitives
options.detail: crypto.argon2id(pw, salt, cost…) and friends; users assemble salting/encoding/verification themselves. Full control, but the beginner path is back to holding sharp edges — the opposite of the libsodium lesson.

options.name: Decline — document seal + external services
options.detail: Point auth at hosted identity providers; stdlib ships nothing. Every self-hosted Jet app (the jetos story!) still needs it and will hand-roll worse.
options.code:
// docs: "use an identity provider" — meanwhile:
db.execute("…", [user, crypto.sha256(password)])   // what actually happens

comparisons.note: password_hash/password_verify with self-describing output is the acknowledged best-in-class API shape here — rare praise for PHP.
crypto_pwhash_str/_str_verify — same shape, same reasoning.
both push users to external packages (bcrypt/argon2 crates) — stdlib silence is the common gap, not the standard to copy.

decisions.title: Core filesystem depth surface
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical shape for deep file and path operations.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A keeps one semantic path model: typed Path is the backbone for composition and audit, while core.files keeps beginner-friendly string entrypoints that immediately coerce into Path. This reconciles D-PATHFS1 with today's core.files docs without creating two mechanisms.
decisions.story: Marta writes a static-site publisher. She needs to create nested folders, copy an asset tree, atomically write output, inspect mtimes, skip symlink cycles, and clean a temp directory when the build exits. If Jet gives her only read/write/list_dir, she falls back to brittle string paths and shell commands.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: Path-only purity makes beginner scripts noisy; string-only helpers make expert audit and cycle-safe walking weak. The hybrid is one mechanism because every string entrypoint lowers to Path before sema/codegen effects, docs, and audit facts see it. No aliases: names are stable once ratified.

options.name: Path backbone plus string entrypoints (recommended)
options.detail: Ratify typed Path as the internal and expert surface, and keep core.files string helpers as the beginner facade. Add Stat, FileKind, WalkEntry, TempDir, FileLock, and one canonical operation set: stat, create_dir_all, remove_dir, remove_all, glob, walk, symlink/read_link, hard_link, temp_dir/temp_file, lock, canonicalize, absolute, copy_dir, read_at/write_at/seek, fsync, write_atomic.
options.code:
use core.files as files

p :: Path.from("site").join("posts")
files.create_dir_all(p)?              // Path accepted
files.create_dir_all("site/posts")? // String accepted by same coercion

stat :: files.stat(p)?
if stat.kind == .Dir {
    loop ent in files.walk(p)? { print(ent.path.to_string()) }
}

tmp :: files.temp_dir()?              // RAII cleanup
lock :: files.lock("build.lock")?   // advisory, scoped
files.write_atomic(p.join("index.html"), bytes)?

options.name: String-only core.files
options.detail: All operations are module functions over String paths. Very easy to type, but path composition, relative roots, symlink-cycle handling, and audit output stay stringly typed.

options.name: Path-only methods
options.detail: Every deep operation hangs off Path methods. Strong audit and discoverability from a Path value, but beginner one-file scripts must learn Path before simple tasks like mkdir -p or remove_all.
options.code:
root :: Path.from("site")
root.join("posts").create_dir_all()?
root.walk().filter((e) => e.stat.kind == .File)

options.name: Decline depth for now
options.detail: Keep read/write/list_dir/open and document shell/core.process workarounds. This leaves Jet worse than Python pathlib, Go os, and Rust fs for everyday scripting and build tools.
options.code:
process.run(["mkdir", "-p", out])?
process.run(["cp", "-R", src, out])?

comparisons.note: pathlib gives a pleasant Path object, but many APIs still accept strings. Jet can keep that ergonomics while making audit facts typed.
os and filepath are robust but split path values into strings. Jet can be more discoverable with typed Path plus module helpers.
std::path and std::fs have strong types and broad coverage, but error copy is not beginner-facing. Jet keeps the front-end diagnostic contract.

decisions.title: Unified watch surface for files, processes, and ports
decisions.gist: Choose how watch-style change notifications cover files, processes, and ports.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A honors the owner's D-FSWATCH1 comment now: one Watch/Event model, with constructors in the domain where the thing lives. Beginners find files.watch(path); experts compose typed watchers across files, process exit, and port readiness without polling.
decisions.story: Earl builds a dev runner in Jet. It rebuilds when source files change, restarts a child server, waits until port 3000 is accepting connections, and exits cleanly if the child dies. Today he needs three different polling loops and timing guesses.
decisions.inWild:
use core.files as files
use core.process as process
use core.net as net

watch :: WatchSet.new()
watch.add(files.watch("src")?)
child :: process.spawn(["jet", "run", "server.jet"])?
watch.add(process.watch(child))
watch.add(net.watch_port(3000))

loop ev in watch.events() { handle(ev) }
decisions.detail: Devil pass: a single core.watch module looks clean, but it becomes a taxonomy drawer and steals discovery from the domain APIs. Domain constructors plus one shared WatchSet/Event type preserve one mechanism while keeping entrypoints where users already are.

options.name: Domain constructors plus shared WatchSet (recommended)
options.detail: files.watch(path), process.watch(child_or_pid), and net.watch_port(port_or_addr) return typed Watch handles with one shared WatchEvent enum and WatchSet multiplexer. Debounced file events are the default; raw event streams are explicit options.

options.name: One core.watch module
options.detail: watch.files, watch.process, and watch.port live under one top-level module. Easy to enumerate, but the common beginner case imports a taxonomy module instead of the file/process/net module already in use.
options.code:
use core.watch as watch

w :: watch.set([
    watch.files("src")?,
    watch.process(child),
    watch.port(3000),
])

options.name: Only files in Epoch 3
options.detail: Implement D-FSWATCH1 literally and defer process/port watching. This ignores the owner ratification comment and leaves dev-runner tooling polling process/port state.

options.name: Callback watchers
options.detail: Each watch call takes a lambda callback. Good for tiny examples, but harder to compose, cancel, test, and replay than event values.
options.code:
files.watch("src", (ev) => rebuild())?
process.watch(child, (ev) => stop())?
net.watch_port(3000, (ev) => ready())?

comparisons.note: Node has fs.watch and child process events, but port readiness is hand-rolled. Jet can unify these as typed event values.
comparisons.code: fs.watch('src', cb); child.on('exit', cb); net.createConnection(port).on('connect', cb)

comparisons.note: Go pushes file watching to fsnotify and process/port readiness to ad hoc goroutines/channels. Jet can ship the channel-like composition in Core.
notify plus tokio process/net can compose, but through external crates and async runtime choices. Jet keeps a blocking beginner surface and explicit expert control.

decisions.comment: a & b - instead of putting file watcher in file module/lib, put all watcher methods in a core.watcher lib. ALSO, support callback/event triggers with our new event system

decisions.title: Encoding XML and streaming codecs
decisions.gist: Choose how XML and large-file streaming join core.encoding.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: beginner whole-value APIs and expert bounded-memory streaming share one codec model.
decisions.story: Priya ingests a 20 GB vendor feed. Loading all JSON/XML into Data first is not acceptable; she needs pull parsing, typed decode, and namespace-correct XML without a second serialization model.
decisions.inWild:
use core.encoding.json as json

all :: json.parse(files.read("huge.json")?)?  // memory cliff
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: beginner whole-value APIs and expert bounded-memory streaming share one codec model.

options.name: Hybrid: same codec modules, tree and stream modes (recommended)
options.detail: Every codec module keeps one adapter identity: parse/to_string/decode<T> for whole values and reader/writer event streams for large inputs. XML, JSONL, canonical JSON, and CBOR all flow through Data/DataTree and Codable, so streaming is a mode of the same codec, not a second library.
options.code:
doc :: xml.parse(input)?
item :: xml.decode<Item>(input)?

reader :: json.reader(file)?
loop ev in reader.events() { handle(ev) }
writer :: cbor.writer(out, canonical: true)?

options.name: Separate core.stream_encoding module
options.detail: Streaming codecs live away from normal codecs. Clear boundary, but splits one format into two places.
options.code: use core.stream_encoding.json as jsons

options.name: Tree-only codecs
options.detail: All formats parse to Data/DataTree first. Simpler surface, but fails large files and server streaming.
options.code: data :: xml.parse(input)?

comparisons.note: encoding/json Decoder streams tokens; XML decoder handles namespaces.
serde has one data model with streaming backends; Jet should keep the same one-mechanism shape.

decisions.title: Unicode text completeness
decisions.gist: Choose the Unicode floor for core.text.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: Unicode completeness and beginner discoverability without bloating String with duplicate methods.
decisions.story: Ana builds a terminal UI and search index. Case folding, grapheme clusters, display width, normalization, and segmentation decide whether text works outside ASCII.
decisions.inWild:
use core.text as text

len :: name.length()     // bytes, scalars, clusters, display columns?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: Unicode completeness and beginner discoverability without bloating String with duplicate methods.

options.name: Hybrid: core.text algorithms with String-aware tooling (recommended)
options.detail: core.text owns Unicode algorithms: normalization, case folding, segmentation, width, classification, and UTF-8/scalar helpers. String stays small. LSP/docs expose common text helpers from String contexts but insert core.text calls, preserving one callable surface.

options.name: Methods on String
options.detail: String exposes every Unicode helper directly. Discoverable, but makes the default type feel large and hides the byte/scalar/cluster distinctions.
options.code: cols :: label.display_width()

options.name: ASCII plus UTF-8 validity only
options.detail: Keep text minimal. International users and terminal/editor features keep failing in edge cases.
options.code: if s.bytes_len() > 10 { ... }

comparisons.note: String is grapheme-aware, friendly but sometimes surprising for performance.
Rust keeps algorithms in crates; Jet wants first-party Core breadth.

decisions.title: Socket layer surface
decisions.gist: Choose the socket API beneath HTTP and services.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: Go-like simple networking with explicit expert hooks for readiness/cancellation/performance.
decisions.story: Nora writes a Redis-like protocol and a health checker. She needs TCP/UDP, Unix sockets where available, timeouts, listeners, addresses, DNS, and TLS handoff without inventing raw OS wrappers.
decisions.inWild:
use core.net as net

conn :: net.tcp_connect("example.com", 443)?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: Go-like simple networking with explicit expert hooks for readiness/cancellation/performance.

options.name: Hybrid: blocking-looking sockets over shared runtime handles (recommended)
options.detail: core.net exposes typed blocking-looking Tcp/Udp/Unix/DNS APIs for beginners. Under the hood the handles are compatible with the task runtime, so experts can opt into readiness, deadlines, cancellation, and high-concurrency serving without a second socket model.

options.name: Async-first sockets
options.detail: Every net op returns tasks/futures. Good for servers, but beginner scripts pay async ceremony before they need it.
options.code: conn :: await net.connect(addr)

options.name: HTTP-only networking
options.detail: Push raw protocols out of Core. That blocks servers, DB clients, and tooling that Go owns today.
options.code: http.get("https://...")?

comparisons.note: net gives blocking-looking APIs multiplexed by runtime; Jet can mirror ergonomics while preserving task law.
std::net is blocking; async ecosystems add split APIs.

decisions.title: HTTP client/server depth
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical HTTP API beyond WebSocket placement.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: Go-scale one-module HTTP ergonomics layered on explicit typed URL/MIME/net primitives.
decisions.story: Gwen builds an API server and a client SDK. She needs routing, middleware, typed requests/responses, streaming bodies, forms/multipart, cookies, redirects, timeouts, TLS defaults, SSE, and clean errors.
decisions.inWild:
use core.http as http

http.get("https://api")?  // today too thin for real apps
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: Go-scale one-module HTTP ergonomics layered on explicit typed URL/MIME/net primitives.

options.name: Hybrid: batteries-included core.http on typed foundations (recommended)
options.detail: core.http owns Client, Server, Router, middleware, streaming bodies, forms/multipart, cookies, redirects, timeouts, TLS policy, SSE, and the ratified WebSocket home. It consumes core.url/core.mime/core.net types and lets experts drop lower to those layers without changing the HTTP model.
options.code:
client :: http.Client.new(timeout: time.seconds(5), redirects: .Follow(limit: 5))
res :: client.get(url.parse("https://api")?)?

router.get("/users/:id", (req) => http.json(get_user(req.param("id")?)))
router.ws("/live", (socket) => sync(socket))
http.serve(8080, router)?

options.name: Small http plus web framework later
options.detail: Core ships low-level request/response only; routing/middleware forms become another package. Splits the beginner server path.
options.code: srv :: http.listen(8080, (req) => route(req))

options.name: Client-only Core
options.detail: Core HTTP is requests; server remains external. That fails Go-replacement and flagship server goals.
options.code: body :: http.get(url)?.text()?

comparisons.note: net/http integrates client, server, routing primitives, streaming bodies.
Great ergonomics, but split across third-party packages.

decisions.title: Misuse-resistant crypto suite
decisions.gist: Choose the high-level crypto suite beyond password hashing.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: misuse-resistant default path plus full cryptographic control behind explicit expert surfaces.
decisions.story: Deb encrypts backups and signs release metadata. She should call seal/open and sign/verify with safe envelopes, not assemble nonces, algorithms, and key encodings herself.
decisions.inWild:
use core.crypto as crypto

// Need authenticated encryption, signatures, KDF, constant-time equality
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: misuse-resistant default path plus full cryptographic control behind explicit expert surfaces.

options.name: Hybrid: safe envelopes with audited expert primitives (recommended)
options.detail: Beginner APIs are seal/open, sign/verify, password_hash/verify, key agreement, file envelope, and Secret/Key types that refuse accidental display. Expert primitives live under crypto.expert with explicit algorithm selection, audit docs, and unsafe/effect gates where needed. Algorithm agility and key encoding are part of the envelope.

options.name: Expose primitives directly
options.detail: Ship AES/ChaCha/nonce/KDF/signature primitives as the main API. Experts get control, beginners get nonce/key mistakes.
options.code:
nonce :: crypto.random_bytes(12)
cipher :: crypto.aes_gcm_encrypt(key, nonce, msg)

options.name: Hash/HMAC/password only
options.detail: Avoid encryption/signature scope. Jet users keep reaching for third-party crypto and lose the safe default.
options.code: digest :: crypto.sha256(data)

comparisons.note: Box/secretbox/sign APIs are the misuse-resistant reference.
File encryption envelope hides algorithm choices and enables migration.

decisions.title: Dataframe and table API depth
decisions.gist: Choose how core.data grows into dataframe-class workflows.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: spreadsheet-like beginner flow and Polars-class lazy execution over one table/series model.
decisions.story: Walter explores CSV/JSON data and plots a result. He wants typed columns, joins, group-by, lazy filters, missing values, and deterministic export without dropping into Python.
decisions.inWild:
use core.data as data

table :: data.read_csv("sales.csv")?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: spreadsheet-like beginner flow and Polars-class lazy execution over one table/series model.

options.name: Hybrid: typed tables with lazy plans and eager escape hatches (recommended)
options.detail: core.data exposes Table and Series<T> with schema, typed rows, lazy query plans, joins, windows, missing values, and plotting. Small data can use eager helpers; large data uses the same operations as lazy plans. Bridges remain direct provider roots, not the canonical model.
options.code:
sales :: data.read_csv("sales.csv")?
result :: sales.lazy()
    .filter(col("amount") > 100)
    .group_by("region")
    .sum("amount")
    .collect()?
quick :: sales.filter_eager((r) => r.amount > 100)

options.name: Eager tables only
options.detail: All ops materialize immediately. Easier to reason about, but weak for large data and query optimization.
options.code: result :: sales.filter(...).group_by(...).sum(...)

options.name: Bridge to Python/R only
options.detail: Use external data stacks instead of native Core. Useful escape hatch, not master-of-all.
options.code: py.pandas.read_csv("sales.csv")

comparisons.note: Lazy dataframe plans plus typed columns are the competitive bar.
Huge ecosystem, but runtime errors and weak typing.

decisions.title: Jetpack package overlays and overrides
decisions.gist: Choose how packages, patches, per-host channel swaps, third-party namespaces, and unfree policy are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: reviewed source truth, reusable overlay composition, and beginner-friendly CLI drafting with no hidden override state.
decisions.story: Marta has one host tree and a plasma-beta variant that uses a different provider pin, disables one package default, applies a source patch, and allows one unfree package. Nix overlays can do it, but nobody can explain the fixpoint. Jetpack should make every override typed and explainable.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: reviewed source truth, reusable overlay composition, and beginner-friendly CLI drafting with no hidden override state.

options.name: Hybrid: workspace policy plus reusable overlay modules and CLI drafting (recommended)
options.detail: workspace.jet owns reviewed policy and named overlay sets. Per-package overlay modules can package reusable override logic, but they must materialize as typed workspace policy facts. CLI commands are allowed only as drafting tools that write source patches/policy, not hidden state.

options.name: Per-package overlay modules
options.detail: Each overlay is a Jet module/package exporting override records. Composable for teams, but common one-repo policy becomes more files and less first-run discoverable.

options.name: CLI grants only
options.detail: Users run trust/override commands and lock records the result. Good for experiments, weak for reviewed source and CI reproducibility.
options.code: jetpack override nixpkgs:kdePackages.plasma-desktop --patch patches/x.patch

comparisons.note: Powerful but untyped fixpoint; Jet should preserve reach while making causes explainable.
Reviewable source policy, but narrow: redirects sources only.

decisions.title: Declarative containers and microVMs
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos declares containers and microVMs under one proof model.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one proof-backed workload model with explicit isolation backends.
decisions.story: Walter runs Postgres in a container and a risky service in a microVM. Both need network, storage, secrets, health checks, and rollback proof, but they should not become two unrelated config languages.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one proof-backed workload model with explicit isolation backends.

options.name: Hybrid: workload declarations with container/microVM profiles (recommended)
options.detail: One workload.<name> mechanism declares isolated workloads. The backend enum selects Container or MicroVM; shared fields cover image/package, ports, mounts, secrets, health, resources, proof, and rollback. Backend-specific knobs live under nested profiles. Beginners see one concept; experts control isolation depth.

options.name: Separate `containers` and `microvms` trees
options.detail: Matches ecosystem words and keeps backend specifics obvious, but duplicates policy/proof fields.
options.code:
containers.db { image: image.postgres }
microvms.sandbox { memory: 2048.MiB }

options.name: Packages only
options.detail: Treat containers/VMs as packages launched by services. Reuses service machinery, but hides isolation/proof semantics.
options.code: services.db.exec: package.postgres_container.run

comparisons.note: Powerful but split modules; Jet can unify proof concepts.

decisions.title: Hardware profiles and specialisations
decisions.gist: Choose the surface for hardware scans, reusable device profiles, and boot-selectable variants.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: generated local truth, reusable device knowledge, and boot-selectable variants without duplicating hosts.
decisions.story: Earl installs on a laptop with NVIDIA and a desktop with GPU passthrough. He needs hardware facts generated once, community profiles applied explicitly, and specialisations selectable at boot without duplicating a host.
decisions.inWild:
jet os init halcyon
// emits what? how do variants compose?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: generated local truth, reusable device knowledge, and boot-selectable variants without duplicating hosts.

options.name: Hybrid: scanned hardware modules plus reusable profiles and specialisations (recommended)
options.detail: Hardware scan emits hardware.<host> source. Systems import that source and can apply first-party/community hardware profile packages. Specialisations are named boot variants over the same host and generation, with option-priority/explain output showing what changed.

options.name: Inline hardware in system
options.detail: All facts live in system.<host>. Fewer modules, but generated hardware and authored policy mix noisily.
options.code: system.halcyon { hardware.gpu: .Nvidia }

options.name: Profile packages only
options.detail: Hardware profiles are packages users add. Good sharing, weak for local scan facts and drift reporting.
options.code: packages: [hardware.nixos-hardware.framework-13]

comparisons.note: hardware-configuration.nix + nixos-hardware + specialisations are separate conventions.

decisions.title: Declarative disks and impermanence
decisions.gist: Choose how disk layouts, encryption, filesystems, and persisted paths are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: guided beginner install and expert disko/impermanence power share one storage source truth.
decisions.story: Inez wants btrfs subvolumes, LUKS, an ephemeral root, and a precise persist list. The installer must show exactly what will be destroyed and what survives rollback before touching a disk.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: guided beginner install and expert disko/impermanence power share one storage source truth.

options.name: Hybrid: storage tree consumed by installer and activation (recommended)
options.detail: One storage tree declares disks, partitions, encryption, filesystems, mounts, ephemeral roots, and persistence. The installer uses the same source for destructive actions; activation uses it for mounts and persistence proof. Guided install can draft storage source, never own hidden disk state.

options.name: Separate `disk` and `impermanence` modules
options.detail: Mirrors existing tools. Clear boundaries, but persistence and mount truth can drift.
options.code:
disk.main { ... }
impermanence.persist: ["/var/lib"]

options.name: Installer-generated only
options.detail: Installer records disk facts outside source. Fast first install, but not reproducible or reviewable.
options.code: jet os install --guided

comparisons.note: Community tools solve each half separately; Jet can make one proof-backed source.

decisions.title: Declarative theming
decisions.gist: Choose the source surface for wallpaper, palette, fonts, cursor, and per-app theme projection.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one reusable theme source with exact host/app control and Studio preview over the same facts.
decisions.story: Doris wants one wallpaper and palette to drive GTK, Qt, terminals, editors, and the display manager, with per-app opt-outs and Studio preview. It should be first-party source, not community glue.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one reusable theme source with exact host/app control and Studio preview over the same facts.

options.name: Hybrid: reusable theme profiles with inline host overrides (recommended)
options.detail: theme.<name> modules are reusable theme profiles. A system references one and may override specific targets inline. The theme engine derives/apply palettes across GTK, Qt, terminals, editors, DM, and Studio preview; per-app opt-outs stay explicit.

options.name: Inline system.theme tree
options.detail: Fewer modules, but themes are harder to reuse across hosts/variants.
options.code: system.halcyon { theme.wallpaper: file("forest.png") }

options.name: Per-app theming only
options.detail: Each app module owns colors/fonts. Flexible, but no single source of truth.
options.code:
programs.ghostty.theme: ...
programs.helix.theme: ...

comparisons.note: Community module proves the demand; Jet can make it first-party and proof-backed.

decisions.title: Declarative Flatpak and foreign app ecosystems
decisions.gist: Choose how Flatpak remotes, apps, permissions, and reconcile policy are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one Flatpak authority graph, ergonomic per-user app use, and proof-gated reconciliation.
decisions.story: Sam currently has an activation script that adds Flathub, installs desired apps, removes undeclared apps, and updates them. Jetos should plan that change, prove it, and roll it back like everything else.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one Flatpak authority graph, ergonomic per-user app use, and proof-gated reconciliation.

options.name: Hybrid: central Flatpak policy plus user-app projections (recommended)
options.detail: apps.flatpak declares remotes, refs, pins/tracking, reconcile mode, and permission policy. User environment app modules can reference those Flatpak apps for per-user install intent. Activation computes one plan/diff/proof and rollback path.

options.name: User-env app modules
options.detail: Flatpaks are just per-user program modules. Good integration, but remotes/reconcile/permissions become scattered.
options.code: user.nate.programs.discord.source: flatpak("com.discordapp.Discord")

options.name: Activation script bridge
options.detail: Keep a generated script. Preserves today’s behavior, but diff/proof semantics stay opaque.
options.code: activation.script("flatpak install ...")

comparisons.note: Community module exists because NixOS lacks first-party Flatpak reconciliation.

decisions.title: Kernel and performance tuning surface
decisions.gist: Choose how kernel profiles, sysctl, zram, sched-ext, initrd, and bootloader tuning are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: friendly profiles for the default path, exact typed knobs for experts.
decisions.story: Hank wants a safe laptop default, a CachyOS performance profile for gaming, zram, one sysctl, sched-ext, and a quieter initrd. These knobs affect boot and performance, so they need typed source and proof.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: friendly profiles for the default path, exact typed knobs for experts.

options.name: Hybrid: safe profiles plus typed expert overrides (recommended)
options.detail: Beginners choose profile enums such as safe/lts/performance. Experts override typed boot/performance families for kernel params, sysctl, zram, sched-ext, initrd, and bootloader. Every override carries risk/proof classification and explain output.
options.code:
performance.profile: .Gaming
boot.kernel.profile: .CachyOSLatest
boot.kernel.params += ["quiet"]
performance.zram.memoryPercent: 50
performance.sysctl.vm.swappiness: 10
performance.scheduler: .Scx("scx_lavd")

options.name: Free-form kernel option map
options.detail: One map for all low-level knobs. Flexible, but loses type checks and explainability.
options.code: boot.options["vm.swappiness"] = "10"

options.name: Profiles only
options.detail: Choose safe/lts/performance profiles; no individual knobs. Great beginner path, insufficient expert control.
options.code: performance.profile: .Gaming

comparisons.note: boot/sysctl/zram/scx are powerful but scattered across modules.

decisions.title: jetos fleet target and authority surface
decisions.gist: How fleet hosts name remote machines and authority.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: tiny label defaults for beginners, explicit reusable authority facts for real fleets.
decisions.story: Mara deploys to web1, web2, and db from CI. The fleet already says which system each host runs, but jetos still needs to know the SSH target, user, privilege boundary, and host identity without hiding authority in shell scripts.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: tiny label defaults for beginners, explicit reusable authority facts for real fleets.

options.name: Hybrid: host target fields with label defaults and reusable target refs (recommended)
options.detail: Each fleet host carries typed target/authority fields beside its system. If omitted, the friendly label can be used as a safe SSH default. Reusable deploy.target refs avoid duplication for bastions/CI. Host key policy, privilege boundary, and identity are proof-visible.

options.name: Host label is SSH name
options.detail: Use `web1` as the SSH target by default, with few knobs. Very small for beginners, but weak for CI, non-DNS labels, alternate users, bastions, host-key policy, and audit output.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
# jet push prod uses ssh web1

options.name: Separate deploy.targets map
options.detail: Fleet topology stays pure and a separate map binds labels to SSH details. Explicit, but splits one host's deploy facts across two places and creates ordering/debug friction.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
deploy.targets.web1: ssh("deploy@web1.example.com")

options.name: External inventory file
options.detail: Read SSH targets from YAML/JSON/SSH config. Familiar to ops teams, but Jet cannot type-check or explain the full authority graph from source alone.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
# targets loaded from inventory.yml

comparisons.note: Node deployment facts live in node config fields such as targetHost and targetUser.
Deploy nodes bind host names to SSH user/host details and profiles.

decisions.title: jetos fleet rollout and rollback policy
decisions.gist: How fleet push sequences hosts and rolls back failures.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: safe magic default plus exact rollout choreography for experts and CI.
decisions.story: Olive pushes a config changing OpenSSH and a service port. She needs jetos to stage hosts safely, prove health on each machine, stop on bad health, and roll back the failed host without leaving a mystery half-deploy.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: safe magic default plus exact rollout choreography for experts and CI.

options.name: Hybrid: staged proof-gated rollout with plan/stage controls (recommended)
options.detail: Default push is staged and proof-gated with rollback-and-stop. Experts can choose batch/canary/dependency order, health timeout, and stage-only/continue flows using the same rollout object. All-at-once is an explicit policy, never the default.
options.code:
rollout: .Staged(
    batch: 1,
    canary: [web1],
    health_timeout: 60s,
    on_failure: .RollbackAndStop
)

$ jet push prod --plan
$ jet push prod --stage
$ jet push prod --continue

options.name: All-at-once with rollback
options.detail: Activate every host concurrently, then roll back failures. Fast for homogeneous fleets, but a bad config can hit every machine before proof catches it.
options.code: rollout: .Parallel(on_failure: .RollbackFailed)

options.name: Plan-only until explicit continue
options.detail: Every push computes and uploads generations, then requires a second command to activate. Very cautious, but beginners lose the magic safe default and CI needs extra orchestration.
options.code:
$ jet push prod --stage
$ jet push prod --continue

options.name: Delegate rollout to external orchestrator
options.detail: jetos builds closures and an external deploy tool decides sequencing. This avoids owning rollout semantics but fails the first-party deploy-rs/colmena parity goal.
options.code:
$ jet push prod --emit-plan deploy.json
$ external-rollout deploy.json

comparisons.note: Supports remote activation with rollback-on-failure profile behavior.
Rolling updates default to staged rollout with health gates and stop/rollback controls.
Can deploy to many nodes but the health/proof model is less language-owned.

decisions.title: jet ? help app — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: What jet ? opens: an instant command finder, a full reference book, or a goal-first guide.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — the two-second palette everyone uses, with tasks' goals greeting beginners and browser's full depth one key away, all over a single index. Speed, intent, and depth without three apps.
decisions.story: Ana installed Jet an hour ago and wants "run my file and rebuild on save"; Marco has used Jet for a year and just forgot a flag. Three genuinely different apps serve them: a fuzzy finder that drops over the shell and prefills the command in two seconds, a two-pane reference covering every command, flag, error code and syntax page, or a goal-first explorer that starts from what you want to DO. The axis is speed vs depth vs intent. Browse: file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#help (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
$ jet ?
# what opens? Ana types "watch" or picks a goal —
# either way she should land back at her shell with:
$ jet run --watch src/main.jet▌   ← prefilled, never executed
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid help, modified so the default surface is a command palette categorized like the browser. Remove task-based search/goal home as its own managed surface. Task/outcome phrases can be fuzzy keywords/aliases on explicit command entries, so users can type what they want and still land on concrete commands. Keep explicit command entries, category grouping, command/flag/example/error-code search, Tab inline detail, F1 full two-pane reference, and Enter prefill-never-run.

options.name: Palette — instant overlay, prefill and go
options.detail:
Core loop: summon → type three chars → Enter → back in the shell with the command prefilled. An fzf-style finder drops OVER the shell (no alt-screen takeover; the shell stays dimmed behind). Search spans commands, flags, and examples; Tab peeks flags inline; Enter prefills the shell line and never runs it. The two-second path for someone who roughly knows what they want. Risk: fuzzy ranking quality is the whole UX; prefill-not-run must be unmistakable. NO_COLOR: > selection + [ ] match brackets.
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/help/palette.html
options.code:
web-api ❯ jet ?
┌─ find a command ─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ > run                                        5 shown │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
> jet [run] <file>      run a file, rebuilding if changed
│ jet [run] --watch     rerun on every save            │
│ jet [run] --release   run an optimized build         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ example  jet run examples/features/basics/hello.jet  │
│ ↑↓ move · ⏎ prefill shell · ⇥ flags · Esc close      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
→ Enter closes overlay, shell line:  web-api ❯ jet run _

options.name: Browser — the full reference book
options.detail:
Core loop: explore the whole tool like a reference book — category → command → man-depth detail. Alt-screen two-pane app (lazygit model): category tree + commands left; usage, description, flags table, runnable examples, see-also right. The reference also covers error codes and syntax — each code page renders the verbatim diagnostic (E0112 shown). Enter on an example still prefills the shell after exit. The learn-it-properly surface. Risk: heavier to invoke; large content to author and maintain. NO_COLOR: ▾/▸ tree glyphs + > selection.
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/help/browser.html
options.code:
jet ? reference              Build & run › run › usage
┌─ commands ──────────┬─ jet run ────────────────────────┐
│ ▾ Build & run       │ Usage                            │
│ >  run              │   jet run <file> [flags]         │
│    build            │ Run a file, rebuilding first if  │

decisions.title: jet / jetpack / jetos public ownership boundary
decisions.gist: How public commands and binaries are owned after the code split.
decisions.explainer: Recommend C: clean architecture, low user disruption, one canonical ownership story.
decisions.story: Rita installs Jet and expects `jet run` to stay tiny, `jetpack` to own packages/envs, and `jetos` to own OS workflows without confusing aliases.
decisions.inWild:
jet run app.jet
jetpack env enter
jetos switch halcyon
jet os switch halcyon  # compatibility?
decisions.detail: Recommend C: clean architecture, low user disruption, one canonical ownership story.

options.name: Keep all aliases
options.detail: `jet`, `jetpack`, and `jetos` all keep broad overlapping command aliases.
options.code: jet os switch; jetos switch; jetpack os switch

options.name: Hard product split
options.detail: Each binary owns one domain; old cross-product forms error immediately.
options.code: jet os -> error: use jetos

options.name: Canonical split with teaching shims (recommended)
options.detail: Canonical ownership is split; existing `jet os` and legacy jetpack forms route with clear provenance until deprecation policy says otherwise.
options.code:
jet os switch halcyon
# note: jetos owns this command; running jetos switch halcyon

decisions.title: Variable and function metadata: how editor-facing facts (category, tooltip, exposure) are spelled in Jet source
decisions.gist: Blueprint lets an author tag a variable with a category, tooltip, and 'designers may edit this' flag from the Details panel. Canvas needs a source spelling for the parts Jet doesn't already have.
decisions.explainer: B keeps metadata honest (sema-checked, formatter-stable, diffable) and gives Canvas a trustworthy write target; A rots silently via typos, C forfeits the designer-tunable surface that makes Blueprint usable by non-programmers — the audience Jet's beginner facet exists for. If B feels heavy, ratify it scoped to the two fields Canvas needs now (category, tunable) and grow by future ballot.
decisions.story: Ana builds a game-balance module her designer teammate tunes through Canvas. She wants `speed` grouped under 'Movement' with a hover explanation, editable from the editor; and `debug_seed` visible but locked. In Blueprint this is checkboxes on the variable. Canvas is source-backed, so whatever the checkbox writes must be honest Jet text the designer's git diff shows.

options.name: Doc comments only — structured keys inside ///
options.detail: No new syntax. Canvas parses conventional keys from the doc comment (category:, tunable:). Zero language surface; the convention lives in Canvas docs. Risk: stringly-typed, unchecked by sema, typos silently ignored.

options.name: #Meta attribute with typed fields
options.detail: One attribute, sema-checked fields, formatter-stable. Unknown keys are compile errors (E-code with what/why/fix). Canvas Details checkboxes write exactly this.

options.name: Existing mechanisms only — no metadata this epoch
options.detail: Category = module/file organization; tooltip = doc comment; tunable = a convention (e.g. a config struct with Codable). Defers the decision; Canvas ships M3 without grouping/exposure flags and revisits after real usage.
options.code: // movement.jet groups movement values; docs are tooltips; nothing new.

comparisons.note: UPROPERTY specifiers (Category, EditAnywhere, ExposeOnSpawn, ToolTip) surfaced as Details checkboxes — the mechanism Canvas designers will expect.
Typed attributes with compile-checked contents; serde's #[serde(rename = …)] shows the one-attribute-many-typed-fields pattern of option B.

decisions.title: Desktop option spellings — the one-line swap surface
decisions.gist: The exact user-typeable spellings for choosing a desktop. Everything else derives from these lines, so they are the most-typed jetos options after packages. Under D-JPK-OSNS1=B full-word namespaces.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: B contradicts ratified namespace law (D-JPK-OSNS1=B / D-JOS-SYSTEMTREE1 place desktop under services) and spends an amendment on saved keystrokes; C's record value has undefined merge semantics — does setting the record reset unset fields? — vagueness that bites the option-priority engine; D's combinatorial enum explodes on every new session type and has no home for displayManager. A wins but leaves `.Auto` derivation and invalid-combo diagnostics unstated, which is where implementers diverge. One flag for the ratifier: the environment enum has no value for the D-JOS-DESKTOP1=A JetOS-owned Wayland session — reconcile when that frozen surface (D-JETOS-FREEZE1) ships natively.
decisions.story: One line must swap the whole desktop; a second may pin the session type; a third may override the display manager. Enum values are teaching surfaces: unknown values list the valid set.
decisions.inWild:
services.desktop.environment: .Gnome
services.desktop.environment: .Kde        // entire desktop swapped
services.desktop.session: .X11             // wayland is the default
services.desktop.displayManager: .Greetd   // else auto-derived

options.label: services.desktop.{environment, session, displayManager}
options.detail: Nested under the existing services.desktop.* namespace next to autoLogin/profile; enums .Gnome/.Kde/.Hyprland/.Niri, .Wayland/.X11, .Auto/.Gdm/.Sddm/.Greetd.

options.label: top-level desktop.* namespace
options.detail: desktop.environment / desktop.session / desktop.displayManager as a new top-level namespace — shortest to type, needs a namespace-list amendment to D-JPK-OSNS1.

options.label: single record option
options.detail: services.desktop: Desktop.{ environment: .Kde, session: .Wayland } — one structured value, one line for the common case, record fields for the rest.

options.label: DE value carries session
options.detail: desktop: .KdeWayland / .KdeX11 / .Gnome / .Hyprland — one enum, zero second line; combinatorial values, no invalid combos possible by construction.

options.name: services.desktop.* with lawful .Auto derivation and typed assertions (hybrid)
options.detail: Spellings are Option A's under the ratified full-word tree (D-JPK-OSNS1=B, D-JOS-SYSTEMTREE1): `services.desktop.environment: .Gnome/.Kde/.Hyprland/.Niri`, `session: .Auto/.Wayland/.X11` defaulting `.Auto`, `displayManager: .Auto/.Gdm/.Sddm/.Greetd` defaulting `.Auto` — one line swaps the desktop; the other two exist only as overrides. `.Auto` derivation is law, not vibes: session resolves to the DE's preferred session, displayManager resolves Gnome->.Gdm, Kde->.Sddm, Hyprland/Niri->.Greetd, and `jet os explain services.desktop.displayManager` prints the derivation and winning priority. Invalid combos fail at eval as typed assertions naming both source lines (`.Niri` supports only `.Wayland`/`.Auto`), and an unknown enum value lists the full valid set with a nearest-match suggestion. Combinatorial DE-x-session values (Option D) are rejected forever: every fact keeps exactly one option home, so adding a session type or DM never renames existing configs.
options.code:
services.desktop.environment: .Kde     // one line, whole desktop swaps
services.desktop.session: .X11          // optional; default .Auto -> wayland
// error: .Niri supports only .Wayland — set at services.desktop.session (line 7)
jet os explain services.desktop.displayManager   # .Sddm, derived from .Kde

decisions.title: Baseline profiles — exact visible contents of terminal and graphical installs
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos ships a lean modern terminal and a complete no-command-line desktop while keeping every installed part visible in config.jet.
decisions.explainer: Recommended D treats baselines as source templates, not runtime imports. The installer materializes every package, service, option, policy, and low-level component into config.jet; the realized closure must trace every installed root back to one of those source entries. The terminal template stays small but modern. The graphical template adds one complete GNOME path and hardware support, with Studio handling settings, packages, updates, generations, proof, and rollback without requiring a terminal. No duplicate app for the same job, no second package system by default, and no unexplained background service. Experts may remove or replace any layer; jetos reports broken obligations and proof failures but never silently restores a baseline choice.
decisions.story: Maya installs jetos on a small server and wants a useful modern terminal without a desktop. Her father installs it on a laptop and expects Wi-Fi, headphones, printing, updates, files, documents, media, and system settings to work without opening a terminal. Later Maya replaces the kernel and network stack. Both need config.jet to show the whole system, with no hidden profile contents or defaults silently returning after an edit.

options.name: Named profile imports
options.detail: config.jet imports baseline.terminal or baseline.graphical. This keeps the file short, but the installed package and service graph is hidden behind the import until the user follows it elsewhere. Baseline updates can also change a machine without an obvious local source diff.

options.name: Fully materialized minimal profiles
options.detail: Both terminal and graphical installs write their complete contents into config.jet, but the graphical set adds only GNOME, a browser, audio, fonts, Bluetooth, and printing. Auditability is strong; the desktop still leaves common beginner jobs and system administration dependent on package discovery or the terminal.
options.code:
packages: [packages.fish, packages.helix, packages.git, packages.ripgrep]
services.desktop.environment: .Gnome
services.audio.pipewire.enable: true
// Files, updates, documents, archives, disks, and media need later setup.

options.name: One universal batteries-included profile
options.detail: Every install writes the complete graphical tool and service set into config.jet, including headless machines. This is maximally consistent and visible, but a server receives desktop packages and services with no baseline job to perform.

options.name: Two fully materialized, purpose-built baselines (recommended)
options.detail: Terminal and graphical are two source templates, expanded directly into config.jet by init/installer; there is no baseline import and no hidden installed default. Terminal contains the boot/kernel/init/filesystem/user/logging/time/locale/certificate/network/firewall/package-management substrate; standard compatibility utilities; fish, Helix, Git, OpenSSH client, curl, rsync; and the curated modern interactive set ripgrep, fd, bat, eza, fzf, zoxide, jq, and btop. No remote server is enabled by default. Graphical contains all terminal entries plus GNOME on Wayland/GDM; NetworkManager UI; PipeWire/WirePlumber; Bluetooth; printing/scanning; firmware and power management; portals, polkit, keyring, fonts, input, automount, and notifications; jetos Studio; Firefox; Nautilus; GNOME Console, Text Editor, Papers, Loupe, Showtime, File Roller, Calculator, Calendar, Clocks, Disks, Snapshot, Settings, and a Jetpack-backed Software view. One app per baseline job; Flatpak and alternate app stores remain explicit opt-ins. Studio exposes install/remove, settings, updates, generations, proof, and rollback through the same config.jet transactions. Baseline evolution arrives as a reviewable source diff and never applies silently. Removing or replacing a low-level entry is authoritative: jetos shows unmet typed obligations and failed proof, but does not heal or reinsert the old choice.

comparisons.note: NixOS offers deep declarative control, but imports and module defaults can make the effective system larger than configuration.nix shows. D keeps the declarative graph while materializing the chosen baseline into the user's source and requiring source provenance for every installed root.

Arch makes a minimal system and expert choice straightforward, but the user assembles desktop completeness by hand. D preserves a lean terminal target while giving graphical users a complete, maintained starting source.
comparisons.code:
pacstrap /mnt base linux networkmanager
# User chooses and wires every desktop component afterward.

comparisons.note: Fedora provides a cohesive GNOME experience and modern applications, but image manifests and package layering are not a single user-owned declarative system file. D adopts cohesive desktop curation while keeping the whole machine editable as source.
comparisons.code:
rpm-ostree status
# Strong image provenance; baseline contents are not materialized into one local config.

comparisons.note: Guix can describe a whole system in one program and supports generations, but users still commonly compose imported service sets and package lists. D shares the source-owned system model and adds a no-terminal graphical authoring path over the same source.

decisions.title: Native Nix compatibility engine implementation
decisions.gist: Choose what code Jetpack uses to evaluate Nix inputs without an installed Nix.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A is right on sovereignty, but "implement from official specs" is fiction — Nix behavior is defined by its C++ implementation, and A leaves field-divergence handling unspecified. B and C both need I6 waivers for Tvix, which itself diverges from reference Nix at nixpkgs scale and carries license/upstream-tracking burden. The hybrid keeps A's native ownership, makes oracle use dev/CI-only law consistent with ratified D-JOS-NIXEVAL1 (no nix binary on product paths), and adds drvPath/NarHash self-verification so divergence fails closed instead of silently corrupting cache identity.
decisions.story: Walter moves a production flake to Jetpack. He expects the same derivations and cache hits on a clean machine, while Jet remains the only package language his team must learn.
decisions.inWild:
$ PATH=/usr/bin jetpack fetch nixpkgs:postgresql_16
resolved with Jetpack Nix compatibility engine
no `nix` executable used
decisions.detail: Correctness comes from pinned differential corpora; native ownership best preserves I6 and long-run control.

options.name: Native Jetpack engine
options.detail: Implement from official formats/specs, differential-test against Nix/Tvix, and keep Jetpack sovereign. Amends D-JPK-NONIX1: compatible Nix refs resolve natively; E1272 remains only for explicitly unsupported compatibility cases.
options.code:
$ jetpack fetch nixpkgs:postgresql_16
+ evaluated natively
+ verified cache closure

options.name: Vendor audited Tvix modules
options.detail: Vendor selected evaluator/NAR/derivation code only in an isolated Jetpack runtime binary behind the existing process protocol. Requires a scoped I6 waiver, license approval, and pinned source audit; never enters compiler/driver dependency closure.
options.code:
$ jetpack doctor
Nix engine process: vendored tvix modules
compiler dependency: none

options.name: External Tvix runtime dependency
options.detail: Use Tvix crates only inside an isolated Jetpack runtime binary behind the process protocol. Requires a scoped I6 waiver and locked/audited dependency; never enters compiler/driver dependency closure.
options.code:
$ jetpack doctor
Nix engine process: external tvix, locked
compiler dependency: none

options.name: Native engine, dev-only oracles, self-verifying store paths (hybrid)
options.detail: Implement the engine natively from formats and observed reference behavior; Jetpack ships no Tvix code and needs no I6 waiver. Reference Nix and Tvix run only in a dev/CI differential harness against the D-JPK-NIXBASELINE1-pinned corpus — never on product paths (per D-JOS-NIXEVAL1) — and any divergence is a hard internal compatibility failure, never a silent field difference. Product paths self-verify: computed drvPath/outPath/NarHash must match substituted cache metadata, and mismatch fails closed with one E-code naming the construct plus a `jetpack compat report` bundle. No provider/product path enables an evaluator stage before it passes the pinned corpus bit-exact (JP9/JP10). Amends D-JPK-NONIX1 as in A: compatible refs resolve natively; E1272 covers only named unsupported cases.
options.code:
$ jetpack fetch nixpkgs:postgresql_16
+ evaluated natively (baseline: Nix 2.34)
+ drvPath/NarHash cross-checked against cache metadata
$ jetpack compat diff --oracle nix   # dev/CI harness only
corpus <nixpkgs-pin>: 0 divergences

comparisons.note: Reference evaluator and store formats; compatibility oracle, never user-facing canon.
Own functional package engine and store implementation.

decisions.title: Strong sandbox default and fallback law
decisions.gist: Choose what happens when a machine cannot enforce Jetpack's strong build sandbox.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A keeps ambient-authority execution as the default, an opt-out footgun that violates philosophy and plan Law 4. Option B is sound but leaves the degrade order (substitution/remote before override), non-executing exemption, CI behavior, and error UX unstated; option C denies experts and beginners any path on platforms without a backend. The hybrid keeps B's audited digest-bound grant, adds C's exemption logic inverted (copy/prebuilt always safe), and closes the gaps with substitute-first fallback, deny-by-default CI, and exact fix lines.
decisions.story: Doris opens an unfamiliar repository and runs `jet build`. A dependency's build script tries to read her SSH keys and call localhost. The safe default must decide before that process starts.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build
Error [E12xx]: this package needs executable build steps, but strong sandboxing is unavailable
Fix: enable the platform sandbox or approve an untrusted local-only build
decisions.detail: Safe beginner default; expert override stays explicit, audited, and barred from trusted publication.

options.name: Keep warning fallback
options.detail: Current law: warn, then run executable builds with ambient host authority unless `sandbox require` was configured.
options.code:
warning L0205: build runs unsandboxed
$ jet build   # continues

options.name: Require for third-party execution; audited local-only override
options.detail: Strong sandbox is mandatory for fetched/transitive executable steps. A local-source action may receive an exact trust grant bound to action/source/script digest, declared capabilities, reviewer, and expiry; outputs stay private/untrusted and can never promote. Amends D-JPK-NODAEMON1 fallback default.
options.code:
$ jet build
blocked: strong sandbox unavailable
$ jet trust grant build-action:<digest> --expires 1h
~ output: private/untrusted

options.name: Require universally
options.detail: Any executable build without a strong backend fails, including local first-party work. Copy/prebuilt verification remains allowed because it executes no upstream code.
options.code:
$ jet build
Error: strong sandbox required on this platform

options.name: Sandbox-or-substitute; audited local grant; non-executing steps exempt (hybrid)
options.detail: Non-executing actions (copy, prebuilt verification) always proceed. Fetched or transitive executable steps require the strong sandbox with no warning fallback; when the backend is unavailable, Jetpack first tries substitution from a trusted cache or an approved remote builder (D-BUILDREMOTE1), then fails with an E12xx naming both the backend fix and the override. A local first-party action may run under `jet trust grant build-action:<digest>` bound to action digest, script digest, declared capabilities, reviewer, and expiry (default 1h); its outputs are marked private/untrusted, never promote to shared cache or trusted publication, and every grant lands in `policy.trust` and the audit log. CI defaults to deny; `sandbox require` remains the one-line tightening to option-C behavior. This amends only the D-JPK-NODAEMON1 warning fallback; rootless operation is unchanged.
options.code:
$ jet build
blocked [E12xx]: strong sandbox unavailable for fetched step sharp@0.34
try substitute: trusted cache... miss
Fix 1: jet doctor sandbox
Fix 2: jet trust grant build-action:sha256:9f2a --expires 1h
~ granted: output private/untrusted, never publishable

comparisons.note: Sandbox configuration can be enabled/disabled; multi-user builds add privilege separation.
Sandboxing is an execution strategy and remote-cache correctness boundary.

decisions.title: Secure shared-store architecture
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jetpack supports cross-user store sharing and how privilege separation works.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A abandons the epoch parity claim and gives CI hosts nothing; option C forces a resident privileged daemon on every machine, gutting D-JPK-NODAEMON1 far beyond need. Option B is right in shape but vague where implementers will bleed: no admission law, no builder-identity isolation rule, no fallback semantics, and 'broker' quietly re-introduces a resident daemon. The hybrid states the admission proof, makes the broker transient/socket-activated to preserve NODAEMON1's spirit, defines transparent fallback, and wires status/audit surfaces.
decisions.story: Hank runs a CI host used by thirty developers. They should share identical gigabyte toolchains without letting one user inject bytes another user trusts.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker
root: /var/lib/jet/hangar
builders: isolated identities
user writes: private namespace
decisions.detail: Rootless beginner path stays intact; shared machines gain secure dedup and isolated trust.

options.name: Per-user stores only
options.detail: Preserve D-JPK-NODAEMON1 without exception. Users never share local objects; teams rely on remote caches. Selecting this explicitly drops secure cross-user local-store parity from the epoch claim.
options.code:
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: per-user
parity exception: multi-user local store

options.name: Per-user default plus optional broker
options.detail: Default remains rootless. Admins may install a narrowly-scoped broker that owns the shared store, verifies immutable objects, isolates builders, and never evaluates user package source. Explicit amendment to D-JPK-NODAEMON1 only for shared mode.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker

options.name: Always-installed system daemon
options.detail: All Jetpack operations use one privileged service and shared store, matching classic multi-user Nix architecture. Explicitly amends D-JPK-NODAEMON1.
options.code:
$ jetpack daemon start
all users share /var/lib/jet/hangar

options.name: Per-user default; verifying transient broker opt-in, scoped amendment (hybrid)
options.detail: Default stays rootless per-user per D-JPK-NODAEMON1; every command works identically with no broker present. Admins opt in via `jetpack shared-store install`, which installs a socket-activated transient broker (no resident daemon) owning the shared store; the broker admits objects only after re-verifying canonical output digest, signatures, and provenance inside its own privilege domain — user-supplied bytes are never trusted on assertion — and it never evaluates user package source. Builds it performs run as ephemeral isolated builder identities inside the strong sandbox; user writes land in private namespaces, and promotion to shared follows D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1 writer law. Clients fall back to per-user mode transparently when the broker is absent, and `jetpack hangar status` plus `jet audit` report mode, broker version, and admission policy. This is an explicit audited amendment to D-JPK-NODAEMON1 scoped solely to shared mode.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install   # admin, once
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker (socket-activated, non-resident)
admission: digest+signature+provenance verified
user writes: private namespace
$ jet audit broker
builders: ephemeral isolated identities

comparisons.note: Multi-user mode uses a privileged daemon and isolated build users.
A system daemon owns the store and performs builds.

decisions.title: Dynamic dependency graph law
decisions.gist: Choose whether build results may create later build graph.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A forfeits the plan's Nix-parity exit claim; C is the rejected recursive-resolution anti-pattern that destroys determinism and cache identity. B is directionally right but silent on stage bounds, on how fragments enter action keys and the lock (so staged builds could silently break offline replay per D-JPK-OFFLINE1), and on diagnostics. The hybrid keeps B's architecture and adds the missing law: declared bounded depth, lock-recorded fragment identity, structural impossibility of recursive resolution, and a named diagnostic.
decisions.story: Betty generates bindings from a schema whose imports determine a second set of packages. She needs generated planning without letting arbitrary builds recursively call the package manager.
decisions.detail: Generated graphs work through one typed mechanism; Jet avoids ambient recursive planning while compatibility remains faithful.

options.name: Static graphs only
options.detail: Jet-authored graphs must be complete before execution and imported Nix IFD is unsupported. Selecting this explicitly narrows the Nix parity claim.
options.code:
Error: imported Nix input uses IFD
parity exception: IFD

options.name: Finite typed staging; isolated Nix IFD compatibility
options.detail: Jet-authored builds get one finite typed planning stage. Imported Nix compatibility preserves repeated IFD evaluation/realization semantics only inside the isolated compatibility engine, with the same sandbox, trust, and resource limits; it never becomes Jet syntax.
options.code:
Jet plan: one checked stage
Nix compatibility: isolated IFD trace, every realization verified

options.name: Arbitrary recursive planning
options.detail: Any build/evaluator step may inspect the store and invoke resolution recursively, matching maximum Nix flexibility.
options.code: build step calls jetpack resolve dynamically

options.name: Finite staged planning, locked fragments, isolated Nix IFD (hybrid)
options.detail: Jet-authored builds get finite typed staging: a sandboxed plan action emits a BuildPlan fragment that passes canonical-hash, sema, authority, and acyclicity checks before merging, with stage depth statically declared (default 1) and raised only by an audited manifest field. Fragment digests and their exact inputs enter action identity and the semantic lock, so staged graphs replay deterministically offline; no API exists for a build step to read the store or invoke resolution. Imported Nix IFD replays only inside the isolated compatibility engine under the same sandbox, trust, and resource limits, every realization verified; it never becomes Jet syntax. Stage violations raise one E12xx naming the plan action, the exceeded bound, and the fix.
options.code:
$ jet build
plan stage 1/1: bindings -> fragment sha256:... (sema ok, acyclic, authority ok)
lock: fragment + inputs recorded; offline replay proven
Nix compatibility: isolated IFD trace, every realization verified

comparisons.note: Import-from-derivation interleaves evaluation and realization.
Analysis creates a finite action graph before execution.

decisions.title: Package profile ownership and surface
decisions.gist: Choose how users declare atomic package profiles without duplicating JetOS user environments.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A stands up a second generation engine beside the ratified JetOS one, violating the plan's one-graph law and JP14's no-second-mechanism rule; B drops non-JetOS parity, hostile to the tier-1 three-OS product (D-JPK-PLATFORM1). C picks the right engine but leaves the verb set, generation naming, view drift, and GC rooting unspecified. The hybrid keeps C's shared engine and states the surface as law: verbs mirror ratified `jetos user`, D-JPK-OSGEN1 naming, plan-before-apply, one history, generations as JP4 roots.
decisions.story: Earl wants separate daily, graphics, and incident-response toolsets with offline rollback. His JetOS user config and Jetpack package profiles must not become two generation engines.
decisions.detail: One semantic generation engine serves package-manager and OS views; ownership stays source-backed and explicit.

options.name: Jetpack-only profile namespace
options.detail: `profile.*` and `jet profile` own package generations; JetOS `user.*` remains separate and imports profiles explicitly.
options.code:
module profile.daily { packages: [...] }
$ jet profile switch daily

options.name: JetOS user profiles own everything
options.detail: Package generations exist only through `user.<name>` and `jetos user`; non-JetOS users keep project envs only. Selecting this drops non-JetOS profile parity.

options.name: One generic generation engine, product-specific views
options.detail: A shared source-backed profile engine owns identity, switching, rollback, collision, and GC. Jetpack exposes package profiles; JetOS user environments compose the same objects.
