Cache keys bind source, decision, generator, lock, target, features and toolchain. Dependency errors map through D-HTTP-CORE2 closed errors; backend prose never reaches users.

Epoch-3 deletion gates exist per seam: parser/framing hostile differential corpus and smuggling review; HTTP/2 RFC vectors/flow-control/HPACK review; pooling/redirect/proxy/cookie interop; gzip bombs/truncation/differential; multipart boundary/filename injection; rustls/root bridge inherited native replacement; scheduler/readiness/cancellation; every supported target, independent review, rollback, bridge/lock/SBOM/cache deletion and symbol absence. Beginner: no dependency ceremony. Expert: exact graph, authority, feature, target and audit evidence inspectable. Hybrid: one signed operation-sliced bundle powers shortcuts and expert clients/servers.

options.name: Exact signed pure-Rust bridge, graph amendment required
options.detail: Approve the strict bridge/evidence/deletion model; implementation stays blocked until the exact lock/SBOM amendment is owner-ratified.
options.code:
jet audit dependencies --verify-before-fetch
# exact operation slice only; offline failure if proof absent

options.name: Native std-only HTTP stack now
options.detail: Approve no new dependency. Jet implements and independently validates HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gzip, multipart and all hostile protocol behavior natively before shipping the companion APIs; existing separately ratified TLS bridges remain governed by their own deletion gates.
options.code:
core.http backend: native
new external packages: 0

options.name: Retain current ureq client and std server
options.detail: Approve no expanded graph and decline production HTTP/2/streaming/compression/server-parser completion. This conflicts with the reopened production mandate and therefore is not recommended.
options.code:
client: current ureq bridge
server: current std parser
HTTP/2: unavailable

comparisons.note: Separates protocol engine from runtime/TLS policy; Jet must lock the full chosen composition rather than approve a brand name.
comparisons.code: http + http-body + hyper + h2 + rustls adapter

decisions.title: DNS resolver trust and platform contract
decisions.gist: Choose how ordinary DNS lookups use the host, validate replies, and fall back.
decisions.story: Mira runs the same service on Linux, macOS, Windows, a VPN, and a corporate split-DNS network. A lookup must honor each host's resolver policy, never silently send private names to a public resolver, reject forged packets, and still allow an expert to query a named DNS server.
decisions.inWild:
use core.net as net

addrs :: net.resolve_ip("db.corp.example")?
records :: net.DnsResolver.at("10.20.0.53:53").txt("_policy.corp.example")?
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: the host resolver is automatic. Expert pass: one typed resolver handle controls server, deadline, and audit-visible behavior. Hybrid pass: both return the same record types and NetError law. Security law: unpredictable IDs; source, ID, QR, opcode, question, class, RCODE, bounds, compression-loop, and truncation validation; UDP TC retries over TCP; no invented public fallback. Platform law: native resolver configuration on Linux, macOS, Windows, BSD; search domains and hosts-file behavior belong only to the system path. Dependency law: std/OS APIs or an owner-approved runtime bridge outside compiler seam crates; never a compiler dependency; any bootstrap bridge carries native-ize ownership.

options.name: System default plus strict first-party wire resolver (recommended)
options.detail: Ordinary calls delegate to the platform resolver and preserve VPN, search-domain, hosts-file, and enterprise policy. `DnsResolver.at` is the single expert escape hatch and uses a strict first-party UDP/TCP DNS client. Missing/invalid host configuration is an error, never a public fallback.

options.name: Strict first-party resolver for every lookup
options.detail: Every call parses platform resolver configuration, then sends validated DNS itself. This gives uniform packet behavior but partially reimplements platform policy and can diverge from VPN, mDNS, hosts files, NSS, and Windows resolver behavior.

options.name: Approved resolver bridge for every lookup
options.detail: A vetted runtime resolver bridge owns platform policy and DNS parsing. It may be bootstrapped behind the Core FFI boundary only after separate dependency approval; the compiler remains dependency-free and the bridge must expose Jet's exact errors and deadlines.

comparisons.note: `net.Resolver` uses system or Go resolution depending on platform/config and offers an explicit resolver hook; Jet should keep one typed result/error law.
`ToSocketAddrs` follows the platform but does not expose TXT/SRV; ecosystem DNS clients add explicit wire resolution.

decisions.title: Socket bytes, text helpers, and close law
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical payload and shutdown model for TCP, UDP, and Unix sockets.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a database driver whose frames contain arbitrary bytes and half-closes its request side before reading the reply. He also writes a beginner echo server that should remain pleasant for UTF-8 text.
decisions.inWild:
conn :: net.Tcp.connect("127.0.0.1:5432")?
conn.write_all(frame)?
conn.shutdown(.Write)?
reply :: conn.read(64.kib)?
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: `read_text` and `write_text` make the echo case obvious. Expert pass: bytes preserve every protocol, partial reads/writes, limits, peer EOF, half-close, local close, and UDP truncation metadata. Hybrid pass: text helpers are checked projections over the same byte operations, not a second transport; the same byte operations are the ratified `Reader`/`Writer` stream contract (D-IO2 `FileReader`/`FileWriter`, D-ENCSTREAM1 codec stream modes), so stream sockets and a wrapped TLS stream compose with the same generic middleware as files and codecs. Datagram law: UDP is packet-oriented, never a byte stream, so it keeps `receive` with source, original length, and `truncated`, and does not implement the stream contract. Socket-only facts (half-close, peer address, readiness) stay first-class inherent methods, never trait-probed capabilities. Unix sockets are available on Unix; unsupported targets reject at compile time when target is known, otherwise return `.Unsupported(.UnixSocket)`. Close law: `close` is idempotent; `shutdown(.Read|.Write|.Both)` is explicit and subsequent misuse returns `.Closed`. Option D subtlety: conformance reuses the reserved `Reader`/`Cursor` core names under D-IO2's user-type-wins guard and adds no new trait or transport; a socket read through generic `Reader` middleware and a direct `conn.read` are the identical byte operation, so there is one canonical mechanism, not two.

options.name: Bytes canonical, checked text helpers
options.detail: TCP/Unix `read(limit)` returns bytes and empty bytes means EOF; `write` returns count; `write_all` loops. UDP packets contain bytes, source, original length, and `truncated`. `read_text` validates UTF-8. `close` is idempotent; `shutdown(.Read|.Write|.Both)` is explicit and subsequent misuse returns `.Closed`. Sockets carry these operations as their own methods only, so generic buffering, framing, or codec middleware cannot compose over them without a socket-specific adapter.
options.code:
chunk :: conn.read(64.kib)?
if chunk.is_empty() { print("peer closed") }
conn.write_all(chunk)?
line :: conn.read_text(8.kib)? // invalid UTF-8 => .InvalidText
conn.shutdown(.Write)?
conn.close()?

packet :: udp.receive(64.kib)?
if packet.truncated { return .PacketTooLarge(packet.original_len) }

options.name: Generic readable/writable stream trait
options.detail: Sockets expose bytes through shared `Reader`/`Writer` traits; text uses Core codecs. This unifies files, TLS, and sockets, but makes socket-only facts such as datagram boundaries, peer address, half-close, and readiness additional capability methods.
options.code:
chunk :: io.read(conn, 64.kib)?
io.write_all(conn, frame)?
net.shutdown(conn, .Write)?
packet :: udp.receive(64.kib)?

options.name: Keep String payloads
options.detail: TCP, UDP, and Unix operations remain UTF-8-only. Arbitrary protocols fail with invalid-text errors and UDP cannot safely represent all datagrams, so Core cannot meet the raw-socket mandate.
options.code:
text :: conn.read()?
// binary frame => error: tcp read: invalid UTF-8

options.name: Byte-canonical sockets that also conform to the shared Reader/Writer contract (recommended)
options.detail: Recommended. Keep every byte and close rule of A, and additionally make stream sockets (TCP, Unix) and the wrapped TLS stream implement the ratified `Reader`/`Writer` core contract (D-IO2, D-ENCSTREAM1) so files, codecs, TLS, and sockets all compose with one generic middleware set. `read_text`/`write_text` stay checked UTF-8 projections over the same bytes. Socket-only facts stay first-class inherent methods, so datagram boundaries, peer address, half-close, and readiness are never capability probes. UDP stays datagram-only and does not implement the stream contract. This dominates A by adding generic composition at no cost to socket richness, and dominates B by keeping datagram and half-close facts concrete instead of trait-probed and text a checked projection instead of a separate codec step.

comparisons.note: Connections read/write byte slices and expose half-close on TCP; text is layered above.
`Read`/`Write` are byte-oriented; `shutdown` selects read, write, or both.

decisions.title: Typed network error law
decisions.gist: Choose what callers can reliably inspect when networking fails.
decisions.story: Asha retries timeouts, reports DNS not-found without retrying, and removes a Unix-socket feature on unsupported targets. String matching would make those decisions depend on OS wording.
decisions.detail: All fallible core.net operations return `? NetError`; stable cases include InvalidInput, PermissionDenied, AddressInUse, AddressUnavailable, ConnectionRefused, ConnectionReset, NotConnected, Closed, Timeout, Cancelled, Unsupported, Dns, Tls, Protocol, and Other. Each carries operation plus relevant address/name and a display message; raw OS code is optional expert audit data, never control-flow law. Compiler diagnostics cover statically known target/API misuse; runtime failures remain values.

options.name: One structured NetError family (recommended)
options.detail: One exhaustive top-level network error with nested DNS/TLS/protocol detail. Stable variants drive logic across platforms; `message`, `operation`, `address`, `os_code` support reporting/audit. Deadline and cancellation are distinct.

options.name: Per-operation error enums
options.detail: ConnectError, ReadError, DnsError, and TlsError precisely enumerate each call. Callers gain narrow types but generic middleware must repeatedly translate them and the same OS event can acquire divergent names.
options.code:
conn: TcpStream ? ConnectError :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)
chunk: Bytes ? ReadError :: conn.read(64.kib)

options.name: Keep String errors
options.detail: Every operation preserves human-readable strings only. This is easy to print but unsafe for retry, fallback, metrics, and cross-platform control flow.

comparisons.note: `net.Error` exposes timeout/temporary behavior while concrete errors retain operation and address.
comparisons.code: if ne, ok := err.(net.Error); ok && ne.Timeout() { ... }

comparisons.note: `io::ErrorKind` gives stable categories plus optional raw OS codes.

decisions.title: Socket deadlines, cancellation, and readiness
decisions.gist: Choose how one socket model serves scripts and high-concurrency tasks.
decisions.story: Leo writes a simple health check, then grows it into ten thousand concurrent probes. The same socket calls must honor the surrounding task budget, permit an explicit per-operation deadline, cancel promptly, and expose readiness without creating async-only socket types.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: blocking-looking calls automatically observe current #Context. Expert pass: named `deadline:` override, cancellation token/context, readiness interest, and scheduler integration use the same handle. Hybrid pass: no AsyncTcpStream type. Precedence: earliest of current context deadline and explicit deadline; cancellation returns `.Cancelled`; expiry returns `.Timeout`; manual socket timeout is persistent configuration and cannot extend a context budget.

options.name: Context-aware calls plus readiness on same handles (recommended)
options.detail: Every blocking-looking operation yields through the shared runtime where available, checks cancellation, and obeys the earliest budget. Experts call `ready` or pass named deadlines on the same Tcp/Udp/Unix/DNS handles. Native-thread fallback preserves semantics without claiming multiplexing.

options.name: Context-only blocking calls
options.detail: Operations observe #Context but expose no readiness or per-call override. Simple and coherent, yet expert event loops cannot integrate sockets without a second lower-level API.

options.name: Separate async socket types
options.detail: Blocking sockets remain simple while AsyncTcp/AsyncUdp own cancellation and readiness. This splits semantics and violates the ratified one-handle hybrid direction.
options.code:
conn :: await net.AsyncTcp.connect(host)
chunk :: await conn.read(64.kib)

comparisons.note: Blocking-looking operations are runtime-polled; context is commonly passed to dialing and DNS while connection deadlines interrupt I/O.
Structured cancellation applies through coroutine context while sockets remain resources.

decisions.title: TLS layering over socket streams
decisions.gist: Choose how TLS wraps sockets without creating a second I/O model.
decisions.story: Noor connects through a preconfigured TCP socket, sets SNI and verification policy, reads binary protocol frames, and needs the same deadline, cancellation, close, and audit behavior before and after TLS.
decisions.inWild:
tcp :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)?
tls :: tls.client(tcp, server_name: "api.example.com")?
tls.write_all(frame)?
reply :: tls.read(64.kib)?
decisions.detail: D-TLS1 remains law: safe HTTPS defaults use rustls and system roots; advanced client TLS configuration lives in core.tls. This ballot only fixes stream composition. Default verification cannot be disabled outside the audited expert/unsafe policy already governing TLS. ALPN, roots, client identity, SNI, protocol versions, handshake deadline, peer identity, and close-notify are explicit expert controls. Runtime rustls bridge remains outside compiler seam crates under the existing approved dependency/native-ize law.

options.name: core.tls wraps the canonical byte stream (recommended)
options.detail: `tls.client` consumes a connected TcpStream and returns TlsStream implementing the same byte/readiness/deadline/close law. Safe defaults verify hostname with system roots. `TlsClientConfig` adds roots, ALPN, identity, and version bounds; insecure verification is unavailable here.
options.code:
cfg :: tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_alpn(["h2", "http/1.1"])
tcp :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)?
secure :: tls.client(tcp, server_name: host, config: cfg, deadline: 3.seconds)?
secure.write_all(frame)?
secure.close()? // sends close-notify, then closes transport

options.name: TLS methods remain inside core.net
options.detail: `net.tls_connect` consumes TcpStream and returns a separate TlsStream API. This keeps current placement but mixes transport and security policy, duplicates read/write functions, and conflicts with core.tls ownership of advanced configuration.
options.code:
secure :: net.tls_connect(tcp, host)?
net.tls_write(secure, text)?
net.tls_close(secure)?

options.name: TLS only through core.http
options.detail: Raw TLS is hidden; HTTPS works but database, mail, messaging, and custom protocols cannot securely compose over sockets.
options.code:
response :: http.Client.get("https://api.example.com")?
// no raw TLS stream for another protocol

comparisons.note: A TLS connection wraps transport I/O while configuration owns roots, SNI, ALPN, and protocol versions.
TLS wraps `net.Conn`, preserving deadline and address behavior while adding handshake/peer state.

decisions.title: Place fuzz and LSP in the frequency-ringed CLI
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical homes for the two native commands omitted from D-CLI-SURFACE1's exhaustive rings.
decisions.explainer: Recommend A: fuzzing is part of the test/dev loop and stays flat; LSP is self/tooling infrastructure and moves under `jet self`. The editor integrations change atomically, and bare `jet lsp` becomes the same immediate teaching error required for every moved verb.
decisions.story: Maya fuzzes a parser before release and her editor launches Jet's language server automatically. D-CLI-SURFACE1 precisely names every flat daily verb and every grouped long-tail verb, but today's registry also contains `fuzz` and `lsp`. An implementer cannot remove, group, or retain either spelling without inventing user-facing command law.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet lsp                 # launched by VS Code/Zed, normally not typed

# D-CLI-SURFACE1 currently assigns neither command a destination.
decisions.detail: This ballot only closes D-CLI-SURFACE1=B's two-command omission. It does not reopen its four groups, daily list, or no-alias rule. EngineDispatch front doors (`env`, `push`, `trust`, `bridge`, `services`, `image`, `os`, `config`, `outdated`, `search`, `info`, `logs`, `clean`) remain outside #468's native-verb shrink exactly as the card scoped them; existing product decisions own them. `jet ?`, help, man, completions, shell completion, editor installers, docs, tests and external-command collision checks must all read the same nested registry. A moved spelling is intercepted before external `jet-<name>` discovery, emits E2101 with What/Why/Fix, preserves all following argv verbatim in the printed replacement, exits 2, performs no action, and is never an alias. `--json` emits the existing diagnostic schema with replacement argv. No L2001 deprecation window applies: D-CLI-SURFACE1 explicitly chose teaching errors rather than compatibility aliases. Beginner pass: fuzz remains discoverable beside test; editor setup hides LSP plumbing. Expert pass: `jet self lsp --bench/doctor` retains exact flags and stdio behavior. Hybrid pass: one registry entry owns canonical argv plus migration metadata; generators cannot drift.

options.name: Flat fuzz; self lsp
options.detail: Keep `jet fuzz` in the daily developer ring. Move the machine-facing server to `jet self lsp`; update every first-party editor/installer atomically and teach the old spelling without executing it.
options.code:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
   PASS  100000 cases
$ jet self lsp             # editor argv

$ jet lsp
Error [E2101]: `lsp` moved under `jet self`
 Why: language-server plumbing belongs with Jet's own tooling
 Fix: run `jet self lsp`

options.name: Self group for both
options.detail: Treat fuzzing and LSP as specialist tooling under `jet self`. This makes the flat ring smaller, but separates fuzz from `test` even though both execute test properties and share fixtures.
options.code:
$ jet self fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet self lsp

$ jet fuzz parser.jet
Error [E2101]: `fuzz` moved under `jet self`
 Fix: run `jet self fuzz parser.jet`

options.name: Keep both flat but hide LSP from human help
options.detail: Preserve current argv for integrations and fuzz users. `lsp` is marked machine-facing and omitted from ordinary help/palette unless searched exactly. This avoids a migration but leaves an undocumented top-level exception to the frequency-ring inventory.
options.code:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet lsp
# `jet help` omits lsp; `jet ? lsp` still finds it

comparisons.note: Compiler-adjacent protocol servers are commonly launched by editor configuration rather than taught as daily compiler verbs.
Fuzzing stays adjacent to the test/build developer loop even when implemented by specialist machinery.

decisions.title: Hand-writable Encode/Decode surface (and whether built-in derives re-enter through it)
decisions.gist: Decide the Jet spelling a person writes to give a type its own wire form, and whether the built-in @Codable/@Encode/@Decode derives generate that same spelling (re-entering the front end, R11) or stay compiler-synthesized Rust that skips it.
decisions.explainer: Today @Codable works by having the compiler write Rust `impl` blocks directly (crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Items.rs::emit_struct_serde) over an internal value tree (jet_std::DataTree), using method names (jet_encode/jet_decode) the docs say `the user never types`. That is the one derive in the language that does NOT follow R11 (architecture.md rule: every build-time code-gen step emits Jet source that re-enters lexer/parser/sema like hand-written code). User-authored derives already follow R11 (D-METADERIVE1=A). This decision fixes (1) whether a person can hand-write a codec for a type the automatic field-walk can't express, and in what Jet syntax, and (2) whether the built-in derives become ordinary derives that emit that Jet source, closing the R11 gap. Note: architecture.md line 188 currently claims @Codable `already works this way` (re-enters); that line is stale and will be corrected to match whichever option is ratified. Ratifying this also fixes an adjacent live bug: the compiler-synthesized impls emit unqualified paths, so decode<T> across an imported module file fails today and only works in the entry file (memory: codable-derive-module-gap).
decisions.story: Ada builds a signup service. Most of her types are plain records: she puts @Codable on `Signup` and `json.to_string(signup)` just works, no ceremony. But `email` is not a plain string — it is an `Email` type that must reject a malformed address on the way in, and should appear on the wire as a bare string "ada@lovelace.org", not as a nested object {"value": "..."}. The automatic field-walk cannot express either the flat wire shape or the validation. Ada needs a way to say, in Jet, `here is how an Email turns into data and back` — and she needs that hand-written codec to compose automatically when `Email` is a field of a derived `Signup`.
decisions.detail: Recommend A. It is the only option where there is exactly one mechanism (I8): a derive is just the compiler auto-writing the same `impl Encode`/`impl Decode` a person could write by hand, re-entering the front end exactly like a user derive (R11, matching the already-ratified D-METADERIVE1 shape). Beginner magic is untouched — @Codable stays zero-ceremony. The expert who needs a custom wire form or validation writes ordinary Jet that composes into any derived parent. B keeps R11 but leaves the hand path second-class (an ‘internals’ module you are steered away from), so the custom-codec story is a demotion rather than a feature and the surface splits in two. C permanently forks built-in derives (compiler-synthesized Rust) from user derives (R11 Jet source), records a standing carve-out in a core safety rule, and gives the expert no override at all — Ada would have to abandon the `Email` type. Effort is not a factor in this ranking.

options.name: First-class Encode/Decode protocol; built-in derives emit it as Jet source (R11)
options.detail: Ratify a user-facing `Encode`/`Decode` protocol: methods `encode(self) -> DataTree` and `decode(tree: DataTree) -> Result<T, DecodeError>`, with DataTree constructors (.Text/.Int/.Float/.Bool/.Null/.Array/.Object), the `?`-chaining accessors already listed in the spec (.text()/.int()/.field(name)/.at(i)), and `DecodeError { path, reason }`. A hand-written impl composes into any @Codable parent because both sides speak the same protocol. The built-in @Codable/@Encode/@Decode derives stop synthesizing Rust and instead generate this exact Jet source, which re-enters lexer→parser→sema like hand-written code — closing the R11 gap and, as a side effect, fixing the cross-module path bug (the generated source resolves names the same way user code does). One mechanism: the derive is the auto-written hand impl. This is the shape the spec already reserved for D-SERDE2 (`encode`/`decode` verbs over DataTree) and matches user derives (D-METADERIVE1).

options.name: Blessed-but-internal encoding module; derives re-enter through it, hand-impl is unblessed
options.detail: Ship the DataTree value tree and the Encode/Decode traits as an ordinary readable Jet module (`core.encoding.internals`), so the built-in derives can emit Jet source that re-enters against it (R11 honored). But the hand-impl path is documented as internal plumbing users are steered away from, not a taught first-class feature. A person CAN read the module and, in a pinch, write against it, but there is no blessed `impl Encode for T` ergonomics story — the intended answer to ‘I need a custom wire form’ stays ‘restructure your type so the field-walk fits’. Keeps the surface small by hiding the protocol, at the cost of leaving Ada's Email case awkward: she reaches into internals rather than using a taught mechanism, and the two surfaces (blessed derive vs unblessed internals) mean encode/decode is learned twice.

options.name: Keep built-in derives compiler-synthesized; record an R11 carve-out; fix only the path bug
options.detail: Accept that the built-in @Codable/@Encode/@Decode derives stay compiler-written Rust over the internal DataTree, and record that as a ratified standing exception to R11 (built-in derives are exempt; user derives are not). No user-facing hand-codec surface ships this increment. Scope the work to fixing the cross-module path bug (qualify the emitted paths so decode<T> works outside the entry file). Ada gets no override: `Email` cannot choose its own wire form and cannot validate on decode through the codec — she must drop the `Email` type and use a plain String, validating by hand somewhere else. Permanently forks two derive machineries (built-in Rust-synth vs user-derive R11 source) and carves a hole in a core safety/trust rule.

comparisons.note: Derive and hand-impl are the SAME trait: #[derive(Serialize)] writes exactly the `impl Serialize` a person could write, and a hand impl composes anywhere the derive would. This is the A shape — one mechanism, derive == auto-written hand impl.
Automatic conformance for plain types; override by writing encode(to:) / init(from:) on the same protocol. Custom and automatic are one mechanism and compose — again the A shape.

A type overrides its wire form by implementing MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON; the struct walker calls into it automatically. Composition-by-interface, like A — but Go bolts custom codecs onto []byte rather than a typed value tree, which is the ergonomics A improves on with DataTree + typed accessors.

decisions.title: Task cancellation model at wait points
decisions.gist: When a task is cancelled (race loser, fail-fast sibling, or handle.cancel()), what happens the next time it hits a wait point (channel recv/send, sleep, task join, I/O): does the wait hand a sentinel back to the task body and let it keep running, or does the task stop right there and unwind — running its Drop-backed cleanup — the way a blown deadline (E3003) already does?
decisions.explainer:
Glossary (terms used below):
- wait point / cancellation point: any place a task can park — channel recv()/send(), time.sleep(), task.wait()/join(), select, I/O. Pure CPU code between wait points never parks.
- unwind: the task stops executing forward at the wait point and runs every value's Drop-backed cleanup on the way out (same machinery as a returned error or an E3003 deadline). No further body code runs.
- Drop-backed cleanup: Jet has no `defer`; a value's close/release runs automatically when it leaves scope on ANY exit path (ratified, syntax-decisions.md line 858). Cleanup fires under all three options below — the question is only whether the code BETWEEN the wait point and scope exit runs.
- sentinel: a stand-in return value meaning 'this wait was cancelled' — e.g. recv() returning None, send() returning false, sleep() returning early.

What already shipped and is NOT reopened: the task/channel/taskgroup model (D-ASYNCRT1, D-NURSERY1, D-TASKSCOPE1), select (D-CONCSELECT1), race winner (D-RACEWIN1), combinators g.all/g.race/g.any (D-CONCCOMB1), and deadlines (D-DEADLINE1 / E3003). Cancel already wakes a parked task correctly — a task blocked in sleep or recv unblocks the instant it is cancelled. This ballot decides ONLY what the woken task does next.

Why it needs a decision now: today the two halves disagree. A blown deadline UNWINDS the task at its wait point and prints E3003 (see examples/features/concurrency/deadline_context.jet). But an explicit cancel is COOPERATIVE — the woken recv()/sleep() returns a sentinel and the task body keeps running until it decides to stop (or never does, if it has no wait point and no check). A deadline is just an ambient cancellation, so the same task can behave two different ways depending on WHY it was cancelled. That is observable, and it is cross-tier: interpreter, JIT, and AOT must agree (R12).
decisions.story: Priya writes a price-quote service. A request fans out to three providers with g.race — first quote wins, losers are cancelled. One provider task, before it loses, has already opened a ledger handle and is parked in a 200ms wait. Priya expects: quote wins, the two losers stop and release their ledgers, done. What she must NOT get is a loser that, after being cancelled, wakes up and still commits a transfer to the ledger — a real side effect from a task the runtime told to stop. Whether that stray commit can happen is exactly this decision.
decisions.detail:
Two-facet pass. Beginner: option A makes the footgun the default — every wait silently returns a sentinel, and if the beginner forgets to check it (or the code past the wait has no check), a cancelled task keeps doing work and commits Priya's stray transfer. That is leaked half-done work, which philosophy.md ranks safety above convenience against. Options B and C make cancel behave like the deadline the beginner already met (E3003): the task just stops at the next wait point and Drop closes the ledger — no sentinel to forget, no stray commit. Expert: all three keep an escape hatch — under A cooperative-continue IS the default; under B/C the shielded region (option C) is the explicit 'let this finish' opt-out for a genuine atomic section. Hybrid/I8: B and C use ONE cancellation mechanism (unwind at wait points, identical to deadlines) instead of two rules for two causes; C adds a scoped opt-out rather than a second system. Recommend C: B's safe, ceremony-free default plus the one control experts need for cleanup-critical sections, and it unifies explicit cancel with the already-shipped E3003 deadline unwind.

Honest cost (behavior change to shipped goldens; difficulty is not an argument, disclosure is): B/C change tasks that are cancelled while still doing forward work. Re-bless expected: examples/features/concurrency/all_failfast.jet (the surviving g.all sibling currently runs to completion; under B/C it unwinds at its sleep) and task_controls.jet (t.cancel() after resume becomes an unwind at the next wait rather than a cooperative flag). race_cancel.jet is unaffected — its loser has no post-wait side effect. Touch points: recv/send/sleep/yield/select cancel handling in BOTH scheduler copies (crates/jet-codegen/src/scheduler.rs and Prelude/Scheduler.rs) and the g.all/race/any result path (JetSchedulerResult::Cancelled is already the wiring). New surface only under C: the shielded-region keyword — spelling is the owner's; candidates in the option.

options.name: Cooperative — wait returns a sentinel, the body finishes on its own terms (Go-style context)
options.detail: A cancelled wait point returns a sentinel and control goes back to the task body: recv() -> None, send() -> false, sleep() returns early. The body decides what to do. Straight-line code with no check keeps running past the cancellation, so transfer() commits after it was cancelled. A task with no wait point and no explicit check is never stopped at all. This is the model that shipped for explicit cancel today; picking A keeps it and lives with the deadline/cancel split (E3003 still unwinds).

options.name: Preemptive at the cancellation point — the task unwinds with Drop cleanup, exactly like a deadline (Trio/Kotlin-style)
options.detail: A cancelled wait point does not return to the body — it unwinds the task then and there, running every Drop-backed cleanup on the way out, and the task's result becomes Cancelled. This is byte-for-byte how E3003 deadlines already behave (deadline_context.jet). The author writes plain straight-line code; no sentinel to check. commit() past the cancelled sleep never runs, so no stray side effect, and the ledger still closes.

options.name: Preemptive by default, with an explicit shielded region for cleanup-critical sections (Trio shield / asyncio.shield / Kotlin NonCancellable)
options.detail: Default is B: cancel unwinds at the next wait point, Drop cleans up. For the rare section that must finish once started — a two-phase commit, a flush, a lock handoff — the author wraps it in a shielded region: cancellation that arrives while inside is deferred until the region exits, so the wait points INSIDE it complete normally, then the task unwinds. One mechanism (unwind at wait points) with a scoped opt-out, not a second system. Recommended: safe default, and the one expert control real cleanup code needs. Shield keyword spelling is the owner's call — candidates below.

comparisons.note: Cooperative — this is option A. ctx.Done() is a channel; a cancelled goroutine keeps running until it checks it. Forgotten checks and work-after-cancel are a well-known Go footgun and the reason context threading is boilerplate.

Preemptive — options B and C. A checkpoint (its wait points) raises Cancelled and the task unwinds through context managers (its Drop equivalent). trio.CancelScope(shield=True) is exactly option C's shielded region.
comparisons.code:
with trio.CancelScope(shield=True):
    await ledger.commit()   # runs to completion even if the outer scope is cancelled

comparisons.note: Preemptive — B/C. Suspension points throw CancellationException, finally/use blocks run cleanup, and withContext(NonCancellable) { } is the shielded region.
Preemptive — B/C. await points raise CancelledError; asyncio.shield(coro) protects a critical awaitable — option C's shield under a different name.

decisions.title: Spelling of the shielded (cancellation-deferred) region
decisions.gist: D-CANCELMODEL1 = C is ratified: cancellation unwinds a task at its next wait point, and a scoped region can defer that unwind until a critical section finishes. This ballot picks the one word a user types to open that region.
decisions.explainer: Shielded region: a block inside a task. If the task is cancelled while execution is inside the block, the cancellation is not lost — it is held until the block ends, then the task unwinds. Waits inside the block behave normally. It is the same job as Trio's CancelScope(shield=True), Kotlin's NonCancellable, and asyncio.shield. The sigil family is already established: #Unsafe("reason") { }, #Context(deadline:) { }. This name joins that family in Syntax.rs with this decision ID (I7).
decisions.story: Priya's task has won nothing: it lost the race, and cancellation is on its way. But it has already begun committing a ledger entry. She wraps the commit in the region so the commit either completes or never starts — cancellation lands the instant the block closes. The word she types should say exactly that to a reader who has never seen it: nothing stops this block early.
decisions.detail: All candidates are semantically identical; this is purely the spelling. Each shows the same commit example. Candidates avoid #Atomic (collides with the atomics/memory-ordering vocabulary) and #Critical (OS critical-section jargon, implies mutual exclusion that this block does not provide).

options.name: #Shield
options.detail: The cross-language term of art (Trio shield=True, asyncio.shield). Verb reads as an action on the block: shield it from cancellation. Short, searchable, already used in the D-CANCELMODEL1 ballot text.

options.name: #Shielded
options.detail: Adjective form: describes the state of the block rather than commanding it. Reads slightly more like prose; one character longer.

options.name: #NoCancel
options.detail: Blunt and literal: cancellation does not land here. Zero metaphor — a beginner cannot misread it. Slightly wrong to a careful reader: the cancel still happens, it is deferred, not refused.

options.name: #Uninterrupted
options.detail: Says precisely what the block guarantees: it runs start to finish. Longest candidate; reads beautifully in docs, is a lot to type at every commit site.

options.name: #Finish
options.detail: Names the promise instead of the mechanism: this block finishes. Shortest to type; pairs naturally with the sentence "cancellation lands after it finishes".

options.name: #Hold
options.detail: Aviation register: holding pattern — the cancellation circles until the block clears. Two syllables shorter than everything but #Finish; the metaphor may not be obvious without docs.

options.name: #Landing
options.detail: Aviation register: final approach — once begun, you land it; nothing aborts the sequence. Distinctively Jet; strongest metaphor, least literal.

comparisons.note: CancelScope(shield=True) — the 'shield' term of art.
withContext(NonCancellable) — the 'no cancel' phrasing.
asyncio.shield(coro) — shield again, as a function.

decisions.title: The value-tree type name a hand codec types: Data or DataTree
decisions.gist: D-SERDE2 = A gives every type a hand-writable encode(self) and decode(tree). The spec text calls the wire tree DataTree, but the only name the compiler lets a user construct and return today is Data. One of them must become the single name users type in every hand codec.
decisions.explainer: The value tree is the format-agnostic middle form: JSON/TOML/YAML/CSV all encode from and decode into it. Its variants are .Null/.Bool/.Int/.Float/.Text/.Bytes/.Array/.Object. The generated Rust type is jet_std::DataTree; the Jet-surface dynamic face is currently spelled Data (bare decode(s) yields it, Data.Text(x) constructs it). The ratified spec sentence (syntax-decisions.md, serde law) says hand-impl verbs are 'over DataTree' — code and spec disagree, and a hand codec forces the choice: the name appears in the signature `fn encode(self) -> <NAME>` of every custom codec ever written.
decisions.story: Ada writes her Email codec. The first line is the signature. Today she must write `fn encode(self) -> Data` even though the docs she read say DataTree; if she writes DataTree the compiler says nothing by that name exists. Whichever word wins is permanent taught surface.
decisions.detail: Pure naming; semantics identical. One name only either way (I8) — the loser becomes a teaching error pointing at the winner, not an alias.

options.name: Data
options.detail: Keep what the compiler already speaks. Short, matches bare decode(s) -> Data reads that already exist in examples. Spec law text is amended to say Data. Cost: 'Data' is a famously overloaded word; reads generic in signatures.

options.name: DataTree
options.detail: Rename the surface to match the ratified law text and the generated runtime type. Self-describing: it is a tree of data, distinct from any user type named Data. Cost: existing examples/goldens using Data re-bless; two more characters.

comparisons.note: serde_json::Value — the tree is named for the format; Jet's tree is format-agnostic so a format-neutral name is needed.
Codable hides the tree entirely behind Encoder/Decoder visitors; Jet exposes the tree as a value, so it needs one good name.

decisions.title: How ?-accessors compose inside a hand-written decode
decisions.gist: decode(tree) returns T ? DecodeError, but the tree accessors (.field/.at/.int/.text/…) return T ? String. Writing `tree.text()?` inside decode is today E2404: `?` cannot turn a String error into a DecodeError. The ratified surface promises ?-chaining in decode; this picks how the two error types meet.
decisions.explainer: DecodeError is the structured error { path, reason } that typed decode reports. The accessors were built for casual dynamic reads (bare decode(s) -> Data), where a plain String reason suffices. A hand codec sits between the two: it reads the tree with accessors and must return DecodeError. Something has to convert.
decisions.story: Ada's decode reads a text node and validates it: `s := tree.text()?`. Under today's types that line does not compile. She should not need a manual error-mapping incantation on every field read — the promise of the surface is that ? just works.
decisions.detail: Three distinct shapes. A changes what accessors return everywhere; B adds one blessed coercion edge; C makes the accessor error type depend on context.

options.name: Accessors return ? DecodeError everywhere
options.detail: One error type for all tree reads; the accessor fills path automatically from where it read (field name / index), which makes casual dynamic reads BETTER (structured paths for free). Cost: casual users see a struct where they saw a String; existing accessor call sites re-check.
options.code:
s := tree.text()?              // ? DecodeError, path auto-filled
age := tree.field("age")?.int()?

options.name: Blessed String -> DecodeError ? coercion
options.detail: Accessors keep ? String; the ? operator inside a fn returning ? DecodeError converts, path empty. Zero churn to existing reads. Cost: a special-case coercion edge in the ? conversion table, and hand codecs get empty paths unless they fill them manually.
options.code: s := tree.text()?              // String auto-wraps into DecodeError { path: "", reason: s }

options.name: Context-sensitive accessor error type
options.detail: Inside a Decode impl the same accessor returns ? DecodeError; elsewhere ? String. No churn, best of both surfaces. Cost: the same expression types differently by context — hardest to teach and to implement honestly (I8 tension: one spelling, two meanings).
options.code:
// inside impl T.Decode:  tree.text() : String ? DecodeError
// elsewhere:              tree.text() : String ? String

comparisons.note: All tree reads speak one error type (D::Error) — option A's shape.
errors are hand-wrapped at every read — the ceremony option A/B avoid.
comparisons.code: if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("email: %w", err) }

decisions.title: Hand-built object nodes: map literal or pair list
decisions.gist: A hand codec that encodes a record needs to build an .Object node. The compiler today takes a Map (Data.Object(map)); the D-SERDE2 ballot text showed a list of pairs. Pick the taught spelling.
decisions.explainer: This is the constructor a custom codec uses for any structured wire form. Whichever shape is taught appears in every non-trivial hand encoder. Key order matters for deterministic output (goldens, diffs, canonical forms).
decisions.story: Ada's Signup type encodes as an object with two fields. She writes the encode body once; every reader of the docs copies it.
decisions.detail: Semantics identical if the map preserves insertion order (Jet Map does). Purely which literal is taught and accepted.

options.name: Map literal
options.detail: DataTree.Object({ "name": v, … }) — matches what the compiler accepts today and how the tree prints; map literal syntax already ratified. Insertion-ordered.

options.name: Pair list
options.detail: DataTree.Object([("name", v), …]) — the ballot's illustrative shape. List-of-tuples reads slightly more wire-like; needs a new accepted constructor form and teaches a second collection spelling for the same job (I8 cost).
options.code:
DataTree.Object([
    ("name", self.name.encode()),
    ("email", self.email.encode()),
])

comparisons.note: json! macro takes map-literal shape — option A.

decisions.title: Decode an arbitrary DataTree subtree through a field type
decisions.gist: Choose the one Jet spelling that asks any Decode type to turn a DataTree subtree into that type.
decisions.story: Ada derives Decode for an Order containing an Address, a list of LineItem values, and an optional coupon. The generated Jet fragment can read each field as a DataTree, but the ratified scalar accessors cannot turn those subtrees into Address, [LineItem], or Coupon?. The derive must emit ordinary Jet that invokes the same Decode implementation Ada could write by hand, so nested validation and DecodeError paths compose without compiler-only helpers.
decisions.detail: Fixed law for every option: DataTree stays the sole tree name (D-SERDE13=B); field/element accessors return DecodeError and add their path segment (D-SERDE14=A); object construction remains the insertion-ordered map literal (D-SERDE15=A); the call dispatches the ratified Decode protocol (D-SERDE2=A), including hand codecs and primitive/List/Option/Map implementations; built-in derives emit the shown public Jet and re-enter lexer, parser, and sema (R11). No option adds a compiler-only helper, hidden alias, alternate codec, or fallback. Beginner pass: @Decode remains ceremony-free. Expert pass: generated source names the target type and ordinary protocol call, so it is inspectable and overrideable. Hybrid pass: generated and hand-written code use one dispatch mechanism.

options.name: Generic method on the DataTree subtree
options.detail: The source tree is the receiver and the requested Decode type is explicit: subtree.decode<T>(). This extends the existing field/at/scalar reader chain and mirrors the already-ratified format adapter spelling json.decode<T>(text), while dispatching the same T.Decode implementation. It works uniformly for named, primitive, List, Option, and Map targets. A missing Decode implementation is E0905 at the call, before codegen.

options.name: Static decode call on the target type
options.detail: The requested type is the receiver: T.decode(subtree). This reads like the ratified static method declaration inside impl T.Decode and makes custom named types compact. Composite type receivers remain explicit but visually heavier: [LineItem].decode(...) and Coupon?.decode(...). It is the same Decode protocol dispatch and the same E0905 failure, never a constructor or compiler intrinsic.

options.name: Generic function in core.encoding
options.detail: A public encoding.decode<T>(subtree) function performs protocol dispatch. This keeps both operands inside one call and avoids methods on DataTree or composite type expressions. It requires an import or qualified namespace in every generated fragment and places subtree decoding beside format adapters whose decode<T> consumes text or bytes, making the input medium less obvious. It still calls only T.Decode and uses E0905 for a missing implementation.

comparisons.note: Deserialize dispatch is target-directed while the deserializer supplies input. Derive-generated field code invokes the same trait a hand implementation provides; no compiler-only nested decoder exists.

A keyed container decodes a requested type from a field. The target and subtree are explicit, and nested custom Decodable implementations compose automatically. Option A keeps that source-first reading order while using Jet's existing generic-call style.
comparisons.code:
shipping = try box.decode(Address.self, forKey: .shipping)
items = try box.decode([LineItem].self, forKey: .items)

comparisons.note: decodeFromJsonElement takes an explicit serializer plus a tree element. This is closest to C, but Jet already has the type's Decode protocol and does not need a separate serializer object.

decisions.title: Complete event dispatch, failure, and hook policy surface
decisions.gist: Choose how Event and Hook expose real queued dispatch, cancellation, typed failures, and intervention outcomes.
decisions.explainer: D-EVENT1=D already fixes one compiler-known family of ordinary source-visible Event and Hook values; this ballot chooses its exact expert API, not a second event model. Every option obeys the same runtime law. An async emission moves atomically Pending -> Queued -> Running -> one terminal state. Pending means a Block producer has not been accepted. Queued means accepted and waiting for a worker. Running means one worker won ownership. Capacity counts Queued only: Running and Pending do not consume a queue slot. queued_count is exactly the number in Queued, running_count is exactly Running, and blocked_count is exactly Pending Block producers; each transition updates these facts atomically before waking observers. Terminal DispatchState is Delivered, HandlerFailed, DroppedNewest, DroppedOldest, Closed, Cancelled, or DeadlineExceeded. DispatchReport<E> contains state, accepted, delivered_handlers, failures, and trace. DropNewest completes the new attempt immediately as DroppedNewest with accepted=false. DropOldest atomically completes the oldest Queued payload's existing task as DroppedOldest with accepted=true, then accepts the new payload; it never evicts Running work. Block returns a task immediately but does not accept its payload until capacity exists; close, cancellation, or deadline wakes that producer exactly once with accepted=false. Capacity must be greater than zero or construction fails with typed EventConfigError.InvalidCapacity. AsyncEvent.close is graceful and idempotent: it rejects new and blocked producers as Closed, lets Running and Queued payloads finish, then closes workers. EventScope.cancel and owner teardown are hard, idempotent cancellation: Queued payloads become Cancelled, blocked producers become Cancelled, and Running handlers receive the same structured task cancellation at their next wait point. An inherited deadline uses DeadlineExceeded instead. The worker-versus-control race is one compare-and-set: Queued -> Running means the worker owns delivery; Queued -> Cancelled/DeadlineExceeded means no handler may observe it. A Running handler that returns before observing cancellation is Delivered or HandlerFailed; if cancellation wins at a wait point it is Cancelled/DeadlineExceeded. Thus every accepted payload reaches exactly one terminal report and is never double-delivered or double-dropped. FailurePolicy.StopFirst stops remaining handlers for that payload after the first E; the queue continues. Collect runs every handler and stores failures in stable priority/subscription order. Log runs every handler, stores no E values in the report, and emits each failure into the event trace. Ignore runs every handler and discards E values and failure trace entries. StopFirst and Collect use HandlerFailed when any E occurs; Log and Ignore use Delivered after all handlers return. A handler panic is never coerced to E: it becomes HandlerFailed with a typed DispatchFailure.Panic task-panic record and stops that payload; the queue continues. Decision hooks use DecisionHook<T,E>; each handler receives the current T and returns HookOutcome<T,E>: Continue keeps it, Transform(value) replaces it for later handlers, Cancel stops with Cancel, and Fail(error) stops with Fail(error). FirstCancelElseTransform processes stable priority/subscription order; zero handlers returns Continue(original). Worked pressure examples never depend on timing: a first handler sends on a started channel and waits on a release channel, the test receives started before enqueueing a payload that must remain Queued, then checks queued_count before the overflow or Block attempt. These laws, queue counts, reports, failures, and lifecycle transitions are debugger and Canvas facts, never reconstructed labels.
decisions.story: Maya builds a multiplayer damage pipeline. Ordinary UI clicks should stay one-line and synchronous. Network damage bursts must use a bounded queue, producers must either wait or drop by an explicit policy, cancellation and deadlines must wake blocked work, and every accepted payload must be delivered or dropped exactly once. A validation plugin must be able to transform or cancel a save, while typed handler failures remain inspectable instead of becoming background errors.
decisions.inWild:
use core.event as event

fn run() {
    owner :: event.scope()
    clicks :: event.new<Click>()
    clicks.on(owner, (click) => { ui.highlight(click.target) })
    clicks.emit(Click.{ target: "save" })

    damage :: event.async_result<Damage, DamageError>(
        event.AsyncPolicy.{ capacity: 2, overflow: event.Overflow.Block },
        event.FailurePolicy.Collect,
    )
    damage.on(owner, (hit) => apply_damage(hit))
    report :: damage.emit_async(Damage.{ amount: 12 }).join()
    print(report.state())
    print(report.failures())

    before_save :: event.decision_hook<SaveRequest, SaveError>(event.HookPolicy.FirstCancelElseTransform)
    before_save.on(owner, (request) => event.HookOutcome.Transform(normalize(request)))
    before_save.on(owner, (request) => validate(request))
    outcome :: before_save.run(SaveRequest.{ path: " notes.txt " })
    print(outcome)
}
decisions.detail: Recommendation: A. It preserves D-EVENT1's ceremony-free synchronous Event<T>/Hook<T,R> while one compiler-known companion family gives experts statically fixed return types, one queue policy per handle, and one inspectable control plane. The recommendation does not depend on implementation effort.

options.name: Typed companion handles
options.detail: Keep beginner Event<T> and Hook<T,R> unchanged and synchronous. Add AsyncEvent<T,E>, constructed by async_result, with one immutable AsyncPolicy and FailurePolicy per handle; emit_async always returns Task<DispatchReport<E>>. Add DecisionHook<T,E>, constructed by decision_hook, whose run always returns HookOutcome<T,E>. One handle therefore has one queue, one ordering domain, one lifecycle, and one statically fixed result type. This is the recommended hybrid: defaults remain tiny, while expert pressure, failure, trace, cancellation, and intervention facts are explicit without changing behavior call by call.
options.code:
drop_new_scope :: event.scope()
(start_new, started_new) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
(release_new, released_new) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
drop_new :: event.async_result<Job, JobError>(event.AsyncPolicy.{ capacity: 1, overflow: event.Overflow.DropNewest }, event.FailurePolicy.Collect)
drop_new.on(drop_new_scope, (job) => { start_new.send(job.id); released_new.receive(); handle_job(job) })
drop_new.emit_async(Job.{ id: 0 })
started_new.receive()
drop_new.emit_async(Job.{ id: 1 })
print(drop_new.queued_count())
// 1
print(drop_new.emit_async(Job.{ id: 2 }).join())
// DispatchReport(state: DroppedNewest, accepted: false, delivered_handlers: 0, failures: [])
release_new.send(0)

drop_old_scope :: event.scope()
(start_old, started_old) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
(release_old, released_old) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)

drop_old.on(drop_old_scope, (job) => { start_old.send(job.id); released_old.receive(); handle_job(job) })
drop_old.emit_async(Job.{ id: 0 })
started_old.receive()
evicted :: drop_old.emit_async(Job.{ id: 1 })
print(drop_old.queued_count())
// 1
drop_old.emit_async(Job.{ id: 2 })
print(evicted.join())
// DispatchReport(state: DroppedOldest, accepted: true, delivered_handlers: 0, failures: [])
release_old.send(0)

close_scope :: event.scope()
(start_close, started_close) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
(release_close, released_close) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
close_q :: event.async_result<Job, JobError>(event.AsyncPolicy.{ capacity: 1, overflow: event.Overflow.Block }, event.FailurePolicy.StopFirst)
close_q.on(close_scope, (job) => { start_close.send(job.id); released_close.receive(); handle_job(job) })
close_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 0 })
started_close.receive()
close_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 1 })
waiting_close :: close_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 2 })
print(close_q.blocked_count())
// 1
close_q.close()
print(waiting_close.join())
// DispatchReport(state: Closed, accepted: false, delivered_handlers: 0, failures: [])
release_close.send(0)

cancel_scope :: event.scope()
(start_cancel, started_cancel) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
(release_cancel, released_cancel) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
cancel_q :: event.async_result<Job, JobError>(event.AsyncPolicy.{ capacity: 1, overflow: event.Overflow.Block }, event.FailurePolicy.Collect)
cancel_q.on(cancel_scope, (job) => { start_cancel.send(job.id); released_cancel.receive(); handle_job(job) })
cancel_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 0 })
started_cancel.receive()
cancel_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 1 })
waiting_cancel :: cancel_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 2 })
cancel_scope.cancel()
print(waiting_cancel.join())
// DispatchReport(state: Cancelled, accepted: false, delivered_handlers: 0, failures: [])

deadline_scope :: event.scope()
(start_deadline, started_deadline) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
(release_deadline, released_deadline) :: tasks.channel<Int>(1)
deadline_q :: event.async_result<Job, JobError>(event.AsyncPolicy.{ capacity: 1, overflow: event.Overflow.Block }, event.FailurePolicy.Collect)
deadline_q.on(deadline_scope, (job) => { start_deadline.send(job.id); released_deadline.receive(); handle_job(job) })
deadline_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 0 })
started_deadline.receive()
deadline_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 1 })
#Context(deadline: time.now() + 5) {
    waiting_deadline :: deadline_q.emit_async(Job.{ id: 2 })
    print(waiting_deadline.join())
    // DispatchReport(state: DeadlineExceeded, accepted: false, delivered_handlers: 0, failures: [])
}
deadline_scope.cancel()

failure_scope :: event.scope()
failing :: event.async_result<Job, JobError>(event.AsyncPolicy.{ capacity: 2, overflow: event.Overflow.Block }, event.FailurePolicy.Collect)
failing.on(failure_scope, (job) => event.fail(JobError.Invalid(job.id)))
failing.on(failure_scope, handle_job)
print(failing.emit_async(Job.{ id: 6 }).join())
// DispatchReport(state: HandlerFailed, accepted: true, delivered_handlers: 2, failures: [Invalid(6)])

hook_scope :: event.scope()
hook :: event.decision_hook<SaveRequest, SaveError>(event.HookPolicy.FirstCancelElseTransform)
hook.on(hook_scope, (request) => event.HookOutcome.Transform(normalize(request)))
hook.on(hook_scope, (request) => event.HookOutcome.Cancel)
hook.on(hook_scope, (request) => event.HookOutcome.Fail(SaveError.Denied))

// Cancel; third handler did not run

options.detail: Use Event<T,E> and Hook<T,E> as the only nominal families; Never is implicit for beginner construction. Sync emit always returns DispatchReport<E>. Hook<T,E> uses the exact DecisionHook fold only when constructed with HookPolicy; ordinary last-result Hook<T,R> becomes the Never specialization. This resolves the return type statically with separate emit and emit_async methods, but every beginner value visibly carries the expert error parameter and reports.

options.name: Policy-specific operations
options.detail: Keep Event<T> as the only event value and create three independent scheduler lanes lazily: Block, DropNewest, and DropOldest. emit_async_block<E>, emit_async_drop_newest<E>, and emit_async_drop_oldest<E> each have their own bounded queue, FIFO order, FailurePolicy, and Task<DispatchReport<E>> result. EventScope owns all lanes and applies the shared close/cancel/deadline law to each. Cross-lane delivery order is intentionally unspecified and debugger/Canvas show the lane on every trace. Hook stays one value but run_transform<E> returns HookOutcome<T,E>; run_cancel is removed so cancellation and failure cannot become a second control plane. This makes each call explicit, but one Event can silently split related payloads into three ordering domains.
options.code:
// Every fresh Event below uses a started/release channel handler; started is received before the queued payload.
new_scope :: event.scope()
new_events :: event.new<Job>()
install_started_release_handler(new_events, new_scope, started_new, release_new)
new_events.emit_async_drop_newest<JobError>(new_scope, Job.{ id: 0 }, capacity: 1, failures: event.FailurePolicy.Collect); started_new.receive(); new_events.emit_async_drop_newest<JobError>(new_scope, Job.{ id: 1 }, capacity: 1, failures: event.FailurePolicy.Collect)
print(new_events.queued_count(event.Overflow.DropNewest))
// 1
print(new_events.emit_async_drop_newest<JobError>(new_scope, Job.{ id: 2 }, capacity: 1, failures: event.FailurePolicy.Collect).join())
// DispatchReport(state: DroppedNewest, accepted: false, lane: DropNewest, delivered_handlers: 0, failures: [])
release_new.send(0)

old_scope :: event.scope()
old_events :: event.new<Job>()

old_events.emit_async_drop_oldest<JobError>(old_scope, Job.{ id: 0 }, capacity: 1, failures: event.FailurePolicy.Collect); started_old.receive(); evicted :: old_events.emit_async_drop_oldest<JobError>(old_scope, Job.{ id: 1 }, capacity: 1, failures: event.FailurePolicy.Collect)
old_events.emit_async_drop_oldest<JobError>(old_scope, Job.{ id: 2 }, capacity: 1, failures: event.FailurePolicy.Collect)

comparisons.note: Buffer capacity and overflow are explicit, while collection runs in structured coroutine scope; Jet should retain the explicit pressure model without hiding failures in a detached collector.

Bounded mpsc send waits for capacity and wakes with an error when the receiver closes; Jet needs the same exact wake/drop law under scope cancellation and deadlines, integrated with its scheduler rather than exposed as a raw channel.
comparisons.code: tx.send(value).await?; drop(rx); // blocked sends wake with closed

comparisons.note: One owner cancellation signal removes listeners predictably; Jet's EventScope should additionally own queued payloads and blocked producers so teardown cannot leak background work.

decisions.title: Represent the shared byte-stream Reader and Writer contract
decisions.gist: Choose the real generic contract that lets one middleware implementation consume files, TCP, Unix, and TLS streams.
decisions.story: Mina writes a length-prefixed protocol reader against a file capture, then points the same code at a TCP connection and a TLS connection in production. D-NETIO1 promises that this is one generic middleware path, but Jet currently has only concrete FileReader/FileWriter methods and an unrelated binary.Reader cursor; there is no contract a generic parameter can name.
decisions.detail: D-NETIO1=D ratified generic composition while also saying to add no new trait and reuse the existing D-IO2 FileReader/FileWriter law. Repository truth has no generic Reader/Writer law to reuse: FileReader/FileWriter are concrete opaque handles, while core.binary.Reader is a consuming in-memory parser. This ballot clarifies representation without changing byte-canonical I/O, checked text projection, UDP exclusion, or socket-only inherent methods.

options.name: Public io.Reader and io.Writer traits (recommended)
options.detail: Amend the no-new-trait sentence and define two ordinary nominal core.io traits. FileReader, FileWriter, TcpStream, UnixStream, and TlsStream receive real implementations; codecs can implement or wrap them. Beginners keep calling inherent read/write methods with no ceremony. Experts can name bounds and write normal reusable middleware. The compiler uses the existing trait system, so there is no second structural dispatch mechanism.

options.name: Compiler-known structural stream contracts
options.detail: Keep the no-new-trait wording. The compiler treats any approved core handle with matching read/write signatures as Reader/Writer for generic bounds, without a user-declarable trait implementation. Beginner calls remain unchanged and built-in middleware composes, but experts cannot implement the contract for their own safe stream type; Jet gains a second, privileged conformance system beside nominal traits.

options.name: Closed core Stream sum type
options.detail: Keep concrete handles and make middleware accept a core-owned Stream value constructed from file, TCP, Unix, or TLS handles. This supplies one implementation for built-in transports but moves/boxes handles into a closed wrapper and prevents third-party stream participation. Socket-only operations require recovering the concrete handle before use.
options.code:
source :: io.Stream.from(file)
target :: io.Stream.from(tls)
io.copy(&source, &target)?

// peer_addr is unavailable until the TCP handle is recovered

comparisons.note: std::io::Read and Write are nominal traits implemented by files, TCP streams, Unix streams, and TLS wrappers; generic middleware names those bounds directly.
comparisons.code: fn copy<R: Read, W: Write>(r: &mut R, w: &mut W) -> io::Result<u64>

comparisons.note: io.Reader and io.Writer are structural interfaces; files, network connections, TLS connections, and user types compose through the same tiny contracts.
comparisons.code: func Copy(dst Writer, src Reader) (written int64, err error)

decisions.title: Exact Reader and Writer contract law
decisions.gist: Define the exact error, receiver, EOF, partial-write, close, and codec laws for the ratified core.io Reader and Writer traits.
decisions.story: Mina writes one bounded frame relay, tests it against a file capture, then runs it over TCP and TLS. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A chose public nominal traits, but did not say whether the relay preserves NetError versus IOError, whether reads and writes borrow mutably, what zero bytes mean, or whether closing belongs to generic middleware. Those details decide whether one safe implementation really works across every stream.
decisions.detail: D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A remains binding direction: public nominal traits under core.io. Clarification is required because its worked example assumed one IOError even though files, sockets, TLS, and codecs currently expose distinct typed failures. Every option below fixes exact namespace, error law, receivers, EOF/limit behavior, partial writes, write_all, close ownership, and codec conformance. All preserve D-NETIO1=D: bytes canonical, UDP excluded, socket-only facts inherent, checked text layered over bytes.

options.name: Associated Error per stream
options.detail: Exact namespace: core.io.Reader and core.io.Writer. Each has associated type Error. read(&self, limit) and write(&self, bytes) use mutable-borrow receivers because cursor/transport state advances without consuming the handle. limit must be positive; read returns at most limit bytes; empty bytes alone means clean EOF; failures retain the concrete FileError/NetError/TLSError/EncodingError. write may return any positive prefix count and zero for nonempty input is an error; write_all is one default trait method that loops until complete or returns Error. close and socket shutdown are not trait members: resource handles own inherent idempotent close, RAII remains fallback, generic middleware never steals ownership. Codecs conform only through explicit Reader/Writer adapter types whose Error is EncodingError and which delegate to one underlying stream; direct encoders/decoders do not claim byte-stream conformance.

options.name: One core.io.IOError for every stream (recommended)
options.detail: Exact namespace and receiver/EOF/limit/partial-write/write_all/close/codec laws match A, but both traits return core.io.IOError. File, TCP, Unix, TLS, and codec adapters convert their native failures into one closed IOError tree carrying operation, source category, address/path, OS code, and cause. This makes Reader-to-Writer middleware use one error type, but callers lose direct NetError/TLSError/EncodingError matching at the generic and inherent byte-operation boundary. Close remains inherent and idempotent; codecs conform only through explicit byte-stream adapters.

options.name: Universal Error at contract boundary
options.detail: Exact namespace and receiver/EOF/limit/partial-write/write_all/close/codec laws match A, but trait methods return universal Error through the ratified Fallible conversion path. Concrete inherent methods keep NetError/TLSError/etc.; only calls through a Reader/Writer bound erase to Error. write_all remains the sole default looping implementation. Close remains inherent and idempotent. Explicit codec adapters implement the traits and erase EncodingError only at the generic boundary.

comparisons.note: Read and Write use mutable receivers, empty successful read means EOF, write may be partial, write_all loops, and Close is outside both traits; Rust unifies failures as io::Error.
comparisons.code:
fn read(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize>
fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize>

comparisons.note: Protocols can preserve concrete associated types, matching Jet's existing associated-type feature and retaining transport-specific failures.

decisions.title: Attach option priority without colliding with real option keys
decisions.gist: Choose the typed source form that attaches Default, Force, or Priority(n) to one option contribution without reserving ordinary dotted keys such as filesystem.swap.fast.priority.
decisions.story: Two reusable modules choose different display managers. The baseline should be overridable, the site policy should normally win, and an emergency module may force a value. Separately, a swap device legitimately has an option named priority. Jet must distinguish precedence metadata from that real setting, show every contender in explain output, and never silently reinterpret a user's option key.

options.name: Typed contribution record
options.detail: An ordinary value remains the beginner path. An expert wraps only the contribution that needs precedence in OptionValue.{ value, priority }, where priority is .Default, .Force, or .Priority(n). The record is structurally distinct from dotted option keys, so filesystem.swap.fast.priority remains ordinary data. Explain output projects the wrapper fields but the option consumer receives only value.
options.code:
options: [
  services.displayManager: OptionValue.{ value: "sddm", priority: .Default },
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  services.audio.enable: true,
]

options.name: Priority value wrapper
options.detail: Default(value), Force(value), and Priority(n, value) wrap one contribution directly. This is compact and unambiguous, but the named tiers look like general calls and mix policy with value construction. Every supported value type must pass through the wrapper unchanged.
options.code:
options: [
  services.displayManager: Default("sddm"),
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  services.audio.enable: Force(true),
  kernel.package: Priority(2500, packages.cachyos),
]

options.name: Contribution attributes
options.detail: Attributes attach policy before one option entry. The relationship is visually clear and does not consume dotted keys, but it creates new attribute vocabulary and makes list-entry formatting carry semantic state outside the value expression.
options.code:
options: [
  #[Default] services.displayManager: "sddm",
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  #[Force] services.audio.enable: true,
  #[Priority(2500)] kernel.package: packages.cachyos,
]

comparisons.note: Nix wraps a value with mkDefault, mkForce, or mkOverride. The wrapper is unambiguous, but Jet can keep its expert form typed instead of relying on dynamically interpreted functions.
CSS attaches !important to one declaration, not to a separate property named priority. This preserves unrelated property names but provides only one override tier.

decisions.lesson:
A declarative system builds one final configuration by combining contributions from many modules. Two modules can set the same option, so the system needs a precedence rule: which contribution wins, and why? A default is a weak suggestion meant to lose to ordinary configuration. A normal value is the usual choice. A forced value is an explicit override meant to beat ordinary choices. Numeric priority adds finer ordering when three tiers are not enough.

This priority is metadata about a contribution, not part of the configured value itself. For example, the value may be the text gdm while the metadata says this is only a default. The final service receives gdm, not a wrapper or priority number. Explain output should still retain every contender and its source so a user can understand the winner.

The naming collision matters because real configuration paths may themselves end in priority, such as a swap device priority. Jet must distinguish that ordinary option key from merge metadata without guessing from its spelling. This ballot chooses the source form that makes that distinction explicit while keeping simple values simple.

decisions.title: C callback pointer and lifetime law
decisions.gist: Choose which Jet functions may become C callback pointers.
decisions.story: Mina binds an audio library whose register_processor function stores her callback and invokes it later from a real-time foreign thread, including reentrant calls while Jet is already handling an event. A captured closure could outlive its stack, race captured state, allocate on the audio thread, or unwind through C. She needs a safe callback rule without a hidden trampoline or context allocation.
decisions.detail: This ballot authorizes only C-convention callback pointers. Alternate callback conventions remain rejected even if D-CABI-PLATFORM1 permits an alternate convention on the imported function itself; imported-function ABI and callback ABI are independent. Context-pointer callbacks shaped as fn(void *ctx, ...) remain in the existing gated pointer tier plus a user/external shim. Beginner pass: a named capture-free function is enough. Expert pass: nullability, lifetime, effects, threading, reentry, panic, and storage are fixed. Hybrid pass: reuse fn(A)->R with stricter C-boundary admission. Recommendation A.

options.name: Required non-null, capture-free pure pointer
options.detail: In a C parameter, fn(A)->R is a required non-null extern-C pointer. Every parameter and return passes the same D-REPRC1/2 C-safe test. Values are monomorphic named @Pure functions or capture-free @Pure lambdas only. Callback admission adds a compiler-checked foreign-thread-safe subset without new syntax: no heap allocation, mutable/static/TLS access, scheduler/runtime handles, panic-capable operations, or calls outside the same admitted subset. Violations, bound methods, async/generators, generics deferred to C, closures, and effects are E3203. C receives one stable pointer identity, storable for the loaded program's lifetime and callable concurrently or recursively from foreign threads; this adds no Jet equality operation. Panic is forbidden statically, with abort as the boundary backstop. Capture-free lambdas receive one program-lifetime emitted symbol. No implicit context pointer, heap allocation, unregister token, null sentinel, or alternate callback ABI.

options.name: Synchronous borrowed pure callback marker
options.detail: fn(A)->R is accepted only on a parameter marked #[Callback(sync)]. The foreign contract promises same-thread calls only during the containing C call and no retention. Capture-free monomorphic @Pure functions remain required; D-EFF2 checks them normally on the same Jet thread/context. Concurrent, recursive-after-return, stored, nullable, effectful, and alternate-ABI callbacks remain E3203. Panic is forbidden statically with abort as backstop. #[Callback(sync)] is new parameter metadata and must be registered if chosen.

options.name: Keep callbacks rejected
options.detail: fn remains E3203 at every C boundary. Users bind a C-ABI shim that owns lifetime/context and exposes scalar or handle operations. This is maximally narrow but leaves direct GUI, event-loop, allocator, and native callback APIs unavailable.

comparisons.note: extern-C function pointers are capture-free; captured closures need a separately owned void* context and unsafe trampoline. Panics must not unwind.
comparisons.code:
extern "C" fn clamp(x: i32) -> i32 { x }
extern "C" { fn register(cb: extern "C" fn(i32) -> i32) -> i32; }

comparisons.note: @convention(c) closures cannot capture context; retained APIs need explicit unmanaged context ownership.
A C function pointer has no environment; user data is separate.

decisions.lesson:
A callback lets one program give another program a function to call later. In C, the basic callback value is only a machine address called a function pointer. It does not automatically carry captured variables, lifetime tracking, a garbage-collected environment, or Jet runtime state. A Jet closure that uses a local variable is therefore bigger than a bare C function pointer: it needs both code and saved context.

Lifetime asks how long that context remains valid. Threading asks which thread may call it. Reentry means C may call back while Jet is already in the middle of related work. Panic or exception unwinding through C is generally unsafe because C does not understand Jet cleanup rules. A callback stored by a library may run after the registering function returns, on another thread, or recursively.

A capture-free named function can often become one stable pointer because it needs no saved environment. Rich callbacks usually require a separate context pointer and a carefully owned trampoline. This ballot decides whether Jet admits a narrow, compiler-checkable callback subset, requires an explicit synchronous contract, or rejects direct callbacks and makes users provide a C shim.

decisions.title: Bind C status-plus-out APIs as Jet Result
decisions.gist: Decide whether Jet automatically adapts a C status return plus out pointer into Result.
decisions.story: Omar binds int store_load(uint64_t id, struct Record *out). It initializes out only for STORE_OK; every other status leaves it uninitialized. Record is a plain #Layout(c) value with no destructor. Omar wants Record ? StoreError without lying about the C call or reading uninitialized memory.
decisions.detail: Every option binds that exact header. out is last, non-null, write-only, initialized iff status==Ok; Record is fixed-size Copy/Clone #Layout(c) with no cleanup; Missing/Corrupt map one-to-one and unknown status becomes StoreError.Unknown(raw). Nullable/partial/owned outputs, cleanup functions, errno, and thread-local error text remain raw bindings. Beginner pass favors teachable conversion; expert pass requires exact initialization and ownership. Hybrid pass already exists as a raw binding plus ordinary Jet wrapper. Recommendation C.

options.name: Convention-only automatic adapter
options.detail: A C declaration returning T ? E is permitted only for fixed I32 f(args..., T *out): out is last/write-only/non-null, T is fixed-size #Layout(c) with no destructor, one configured raw integer is success and initializes out, every other listed integer maps to E, and all other integers map explicitly. Compiler uses uninitialized storage, reads only on success, never drops uninitialized storage, and emits exact store_load(id,out). Nested/growable/non-C-safe payloads are E3203. This is an adapter convention, not Result's layout.

options.name: Fully explicit adapter metadata
options.detail: Keep Result but spell exact symbol, I32 foreign return, out index/type/direction/nullability, raw statuses that initialize it, ownership/cleanup, success integers, exhaustive integer mappings, and unknown handling. Multiple outputs each define initialization and cleanup per status. Missing/overlapping facts are E3203. This creates a second FFI mini-language.

options.name: Raw header plus ordinary Jet wrapper
options.detail: Generic Result stays E3203 in C declarations. Bind I32 + *Record in the audited pointer tier.
