For this ballot's plain Record, zero initialization is valid; pass its address, ignore bytes on nonzero status, and return the value only for 0. Other headers needing true uninitialized/owned storage remain raw until their pointer contract is expressible. The wrapper owns conversion; codegen gains no adapter language.

comparisons.note: bindgen exposes status and *mut out; a safe wrapper owns MaybeUninit and assume_init.
comparisons.code:
let mut out = MaybeUninit::<Record>::uninit();
let s = unsafe { store_load(id, out.as_mut_ptr()) };

comparisons.note: Arbitrary status/out APIs remain raw and gain a handwritten throwing wrapper.
comparisons.code: var record = Record(); let status = store_load(id, &record)

comparisons.note: C import preserves pointer/status; an error union is built in Zig.
comparisons.code: var out: Record = undefined; const s = store_load(id, &out);

decisions.lesson:
Many C APIs report success in two pieces. The function returns an integer status code, while a pointer argument names memory where the successful value should be written. For example, zero may mean success and initialize Record; nonzero may mean missing or corrupt and leave that memory untouched. Jet Result expresses the same user idea more safely as either a value or an error, but C has no universal Result layout.

The hard part is initialization. Reading the output after an error can read uninitialized bytes. Destroying an uninitialized owned value can be worse. An adapter must know exactly which status initializes which output, how every status maps to a Jet error, whether the pointer may be null, and who owns or cleans up returned memory. Those facts vary by C function and cannot be inferred from pointer shape alone.

A handwritten Jet wrapper keeps the raw header visible and performs the mapping in ordinary code. An automatic adapter moves that mapping into compiler metadata. This ballot decides whether the convenience is regular and provable enough to standardize, or whether preserving the exact C declaration plus an explicit safe wrapper is the honest canonical path.

decisions.title: Alternate native calling conventions
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet marks a C function that uses a platform-specific call rule.
decisions.story: Elena connects Jet to two Windows functions. One uses the normal Windows call rule. The other uses an older 32-bit rule. Jet must call each one correctly or the program can corrupt memory.
decisions.detail: This ballot uses C-safe pointer/scalar declarations and is independent of callback ABI. #Abi changes calling convention only; = "symbol" is passed unchanged and Jet never decorates it. Vector/custom/unwind conventions are excluded. Beginner pass keeps C implicit; expert pass gets an exact matrix, inheritance, symbol, compatibility, and variadic law. Hybrid pass uses one local marker. Recommendation A.

options.name: Per-function #Abi, no inheritance
options.detail: Each function states its own call rule. Readers can see the rule beside the function, and moving the function cannot silently change it.
options.technical: Each declaration defaults independently to c. Matrix: c every target; system every target (Windows x86=>stdcall, Windows x86_64/aarch64=>native Windows, non-Windows=>c); cdecl/stdcall/fastcall Windows x86 only; win64 Windows x86_64 only; sysv64 non-Windows x86_64 only. ARM/AArch64 accept c/system only. Unknown E3212; target-invalid E3213; invalid variadic ABI E3214. Variadics only c and Windows-x86 cdecl. Symbol is exact; decoration is user/bindgen responsibility. ABI participates in direct-declaration compatibility, overlay merge, cache, and generated wrapper; conflicts E3205. Alternate-ABI functions are direct-call-only and E3203 when taken as values. Bindgen preserves declared #Abi(system) in portable source and stores resolved target ABI separately. Header types remain exact: HWND is *U8 and BOOL is I32, with a Jet wrapper converting nonzero to Bool.

options.name: Module default with local override
options.detail: A module sets one shared rule, while unusual functions override it. This removes repetition, but moving a function between modules can silently change its rule.
options.technical: #Extern(abi:X) module establishes inherited ABI; #Abi(Y) overrides one declaration. Same matrix, exact header-type fidelity, symbol, variadic, E3212-E3214, direct-call-only, E3205 compatibility, cache, and bindgen portability laws as A. Formatter prints module default/overrides; cache stores each resolved ABI. Moving declarations can change ABI.

options.name: C ABI only
options.detail: Jet supports only the standard C call rule. Users must write a C wrapper for Windows functions that use another rule.
options.technical: Every CModule function stays extern C. Any #Abi is E3215 with C-shim fix. Bindgen refuses non-C declarations. Variadic C remains only where currently supported; compatibility/cache remain C-only.

comparisons.note: Rust places the call rule on each foreign function declaration.
comparisons.code:
extern "system" { fn IsWindow(hwnd: *mut core::ffi::c_void) -> i32; }
extern "stdcall" { #[link_name = "_LegacyPing@4"] fn ping(v:i32)->i32; }

comparisons.note: Zig checks that the chosen call rule exists on the selected platform.
C and C++ headers place special call-rule words directly on each function.

decisions.lesson:
A calling convention is the low-level agreement between caller and function about how a call crosses the machine boundary. It specifies where arguments and return values go, which side cleans the stack, which registers must be preserved, and sometimes how symbols are named. ABI means application binary interface; a calling convention is one part of that interface.

C is the normal default, but platforms have historical alternatives such as stdcall on 32-bit Windows and the Win64 convention on 64-bit Windows. The word system usually means use the platform-native convention for this target. These names are target-dependent: a convention valid on one CPU and operating system may not exist on another. Variadic functions add stricter limits because caller and callee must agree on an open-ended argument list.

This is not cosmetic metadata. If Jet emits the wrong convention, the call may read the wrong registers or corrupt the stack, often before a useful diagnostic is possible. Symbol decoration is separate: Jet may call an exact exported name without inventing prefixes or suffixes. This ballot chooses where the convention is declared and whether non-C conventions are supported at all.

recommendation.why: A keeps the dangerous machine-level rule visible on the exact function it controls. It also prevents file moves from changing behavior.

whyNot.reason: B saves a little repetition but adds hidden inheritance. A harmless-looking move can then change how a function is called.
C blocks direct use of common Windows libraries even when Jet can safely support their call rules.

recommendation.tradeoff: A repeats the marker when many functions share one rule. That repetition is worth keeping this safety-critical fact local and visible.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps standard C calls marker-free, makes every unusual rule local, and lets generated bindings handle repeated expert markers.

harvest.aspect: The call rule stays beside the function it controls.
harvest.use: Keep this as the safety rule.
Use generated bindings to reduce typing without adding hidden inheritance.

harvest.aspect: Normal C calls need no extra syntax.
harvest.use: Keep C as the default when no marker appears.

decisions.title: Retire benchmark budget prototypes
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet removes the old benchmark helper without losing meaning.
decisions.story: Mina has old benchmark calls. Some only run a workload, while others use the returned true-or-false value. Jet must remove the old helper without inventing performance rules or silently changing control flow.

options.name: Narrow mechanical source migration
options.detail: Jet converts only calls whose meaning is fully clear. It preserves the workload when a matching typed budget already exists, and refuses every uncertain case.
options.technical: Before deleting the prototype, the repository migration pass may transform a call only when all of these AST conditions hold: it is a direct expression statement whose value is discarded; callee resolves exactly to core.testing.bench_budget; arguments are exactly a static string literal name, nonnegative integer literal max_ns, and a zero-parameter lambda; the lambda captures no local binding and references only package-visible functions/constants/imports; exactly one #Bench with the same name is absent; and exactly one existing BudgetSpec in the same package already has scope .Bench(name), metric .BenchTime(percentile), provider .BenchMeasurement(name), comparison .AbsoluteFrom(baseline), and limit .AtMost(max_ns ns). The pass lifts the lambda body byte-semantically into #Bench(name), deletes only the expression statement, and changes no BudgetSpec. It refuses rather than inventing a percentile, baseline, sampling policy, role, or module location. Any call used as an argument, return, condition, binding initializer, interpolation, operator operand, assertion value, or other value-producing expression is not transformed. After the repository migration, delete the Core item, sema signature, TIR/prelude helper, JET_BENCH_VERBOSE behavior, fixed 3/10 sampling, mean/stddev output, Bool result, and enforcement. All remaining calls receive the canonical unresolved Core-member diagnostic already used for absent members; no special old-syntax diagnostic remains. jet bench measures #Bench through the shared engine only.

options.name: Delete without source transformation
options.detail: Jet deletes the old helper and converts nothing automatically. Every user must rewrite the workload and performance policy by hand.
options.code:
#Bench("parse-large") { parse(large_fixture) }
Budget.{ name: "parse-large-time", scope: .Bench("parse-large"), metric: .BenchTime(.P95), comparison: .AbsoluteFrom("ci/linux-x64"), limit: .AtMost(5000000ns) }
options.technical: Keep #Bench and BudgetSpec exactly as ratified and mechanically remove every first-party prototype use during implementation. The retirement ledger maps name to Bench identity, body to #Bench body, and max_ns to the user's typed AtMost Duration intent; it records fixed warmups/trials, floating mean/stddev, stderr, environment-controlled rendering, and Bool as removed semantics with no equivalent. Delete the complete helper path. External remaining calls receive the normal unresolved-member diagnostic and require explicit user-authored percentile, baseline, and policy.

options.name: Transform workloads only, never thresholds
options.detail: Jet converts safe workloads but always drops the old time limit. Users must recreate every performance limit by hand, even when an exact typed match already exists.
options.technical: Apply A's exact discarded-result, literal, zero-capture, no-existing-#Bench AST conditions but do not require or create a matching BudgetSpec. Lift only the workload to #Bench and explicitly retire max_ns plus all old sampling/output/Bool semantics. This preserves executable benchmark coverage while forcing every performance policy choice to be authored explicitly under GRAMMAR1. Value-consuming calls are refused and later receive the canonical unresolved-member diagnostic.

comparisons.note: Mechanical migrations apply only where meaning is fixed and reject context-sensitive rewrites; A uses that same boundary without shipping a user command.
A named benchmark defines workload while the harness owns measurement; no Bool-returning threshold helper survives.

decisions.lesson:
A benchmark workload and a performance budget answer different questions. The workload says what code to measure. The budget says what metric matters, how samples are summarized, what baseline or absolute limit applies, and whether failure blocks the build. Keeping these separate lets one benchmark support different policies without hiding measurement rules inside a helper call.

The old bench_budget prototype mixed both jobs: it named and ran a lambda, chose fixed warmups and trials, computed a floating mean, printed its own report, compared nanoseconds, and returned Bool. The newer design uses #Bench as the sole workload declaration and BudgetSpec as the sole typed policy. Percentile, units, baseline, sampling, and enforcement become explicit and shared with canonical reports.

Retirement must not pretend old data means more than it did. A source migration may safely lift a clearly identified, capture-free workload, but it cannot invent a percentile or baseline the user never chose. Calls whose Bool result affects control flow also cannot be deleted mechanically. This ballot chooses the exact boundary between narrow automatic conversion and explicit removal, while ensuring no second benchmark evaluator survives.

recommendation.why: A preserves work and policy only when Jet can prove the result is the same. It removes the old evaluator without guessing about missing rules.

whyNot.reason: B is honest but discards conversions that are mechanical and fully provable.
C preserves more workloads than B, but still throws away a limit when Jet can prove an exact typed replacement.

recommendation.tradeoff: A has strict conversion rules, so many unusual calls still need manual edits. Refusing uncertain cases is safer than inventing meaning.

hybrid.synthesis: A combines strict honesty with safe workload conversion and preserves a limit only when an exact typed budget already exists.

harvest.use: Keep these narrow checks as the conversion gate.

harvest.aspect: Migration must not invent missing policy.
harvest.use: Refuse every call whose policy is not already explicit.
Lift the workload whenever the narrow checks prove it safe.

decisions.title: Retire game budget prototype
decisions.gist: Choose which old game limits become real measured performance budgets.
decisions.story: Jo wrote limits for frame time, memory, assets, and draw calls. The old object only stored those numbers. Jet must decide which limits become real measurements and which are retired.

options.name: Add exact scene asset and draw metrics
options.detail: Jet adds precise asset-size and draw-call measurements. It then converts all four old limits into budgets backed by a fixed scene test.
options.technical: Atomically amend GRAMMAR1 with SceneAssetBytes (Bytes; Scene + SceneProbe; lower better) and DrawCalls(percentile) (Count; Scene + SceneProbe; lower better). Map frame_ms to FrameTime(.P99) AtMost value*1,000,000ns; memory_mb to MemoryHighWater AtMost value*1,048,576 bytes (MiB, explicitly resolving the old ambiguous label); asset_kb to SceneAssetBytes AtMost value*1,024 bytes (KiB); draw_calls to DrawCalls(.P99) AtMost Count. Every metric uses AbsoluteFrom because backend/device/replay policy supplies statistical evidence. One SceneProbe run pins backend build, target/device, named replay/input bytes, scene-ready event, 120 warmup frames, 600 measured frames, and identical viewport/settings. FrameTime samples one integer nanosecond duration per measured frame; DrawCalls samples renderer submissions per measured frame; SceneAssetBytes samples total decoded resident bytes at the ready boundary and after each measured frame, with the run maximum as its estimator; MemoryHighWater samples process resident bytes after each measured frame, with the run maximum. REPORT1 then applies its statistical/confidence law. Old Game.Budgets construction/set/show only represented desired thresholds, never evidence; migrate the four intents and explicitly retire its stored object and GameBudgets(...) display. Delete all sema/TIR/JIT/prelude slots and paths. Remaining old calls/types receive ordinary unresolved member/type diagnostics, not performance-budget diagnostics.

options.name: Map frame and memory; retire asset and draw
options.detail: Jet converts frame time and memory because those measurements already exist. It retires asset size and draw calls, so those two limits are lost.
options.code:
migrated: frame_ms 16 -> FrameTime(.P99) AtMost(16ms)
migrated: memory_mb 128 -> MemoryHighWater AtMost(128MiB)
retired without equivalent: asset_kb, draw_calls
options.technical: Use the same pinned SceneProbe, frame samples, memory samples, old ms-to-ns and mb-to-MiB mappings as A. Explicitly retire asset_kb and draw_calls because GRAMMAR1 has no truthful metric for them. Migration refuses to claim those thresholds survived and reports both removed intents. Delete the entire Game.Budgets API and all results; no alias or second enforcement path remains.

options.name: Retire all four decorative limits
options.detail: Jet removes the old object and converts nothing. Users must write new budgets themselves, and asset size plus draw calls remain unavailable.
options.code:
$ jet migrate perf-budgets game.jet --check
Game.Budgets stored four thresholds but produced no evidence or policy result; all four require explicit typed replacement.
options.technical: Record that the old object never measured or enforced any field, delete it completely, and migrate nothing automatically. Users may author any currently ratified FrameTime or MemoryHighWater BudgetSpec explicitly. SceneAssetBytes and DrawCalls remain unavailable until separately ratified. This preserves GRAMMAR1 and removes the facade without asserting false continuity.

comparisons.note: Unity treats frame time, memory, loaded assets, and draw calls as facts from a specific test session and device.
Unreal fixes the map, replay, device, warmup, and capture window before comparing performance numbers.

decisions.lesson:
A limit written in configuration is only an intention until a real measurement proves it. The old Game.Budgets object stored numbers such as frame_ms, memory_mb, asset_kb, and draw_calls and displayed them, but did not measure a running scene or enforce those limits. Treating those numbers as historical evidence would be false.

A real scene performance budget needs a metric, unit, sampling rule, workload, and execution context. Frame time varies from frame to frame, so a percentile such as P99 asks how slow the worst one percent are. Memory high-water means the largest observed resident memory. Asset bytes need a precise boundary such as decoded resident bytes. Draw calls need a renderer-defined count. Results are only comparable when backend, device, replay input, viewport, warmup, and measured frames are pinned.

Migration can preserve threshold intent only where the new typed model can state and measure the same thing. Unit labels also matter: MB may ambiguously mean decimal megabytes or binary mebibytes. This ballot decides whether to add exact missing scene metrics, migrate only already-supported metrics, or retire every decorative field and require fresh explicit policy.

recommendation.why: A turns every old intention into a real, repeatable measurement. It keeps all four user goals while removing the decorative object.

whyNot.reason: B loses the asset and draw-call goals even though both can be defined and measured precisely.
C is truthful about the old object, but it discards all four goals and leaves two useful measurements unavailable.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds two metrics to the performance system. They belong there because they have clear units, sampling rules, and real game uses.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps only truthful old intent, uses exact existing mappings, and adds real measurements for the two useful missing metrics.

harvest.aspect: All four user goals survive as measured budgets.
harvest.use: Keep the complete measured replacement.

harvest.aspect: Frame and memory already have exact mappings.
harvest.use: Reuse those mappings unchanged.

harvest.aspect: The old object was never evidence.
harvest.use: Retire its stored display and never present old numbers as measurements.

decisions.title: Measurement provider protocol
decisions.gist: Choose how measurement code sends trusted samples to the performance budget engine.
decisions.story: Priya measures builds, benchmarks, services, and game scenes. Jet must accept complete samples, reject damaged data, and clearly distinguish a missing measurement from a broken provider.
decisions.inWild: Budget.{ name: "ready-p95", scope: .Service("api"), metric: .ServiceReadiness, provider: .ServiceProbe("api-ready"), comparison: .AbsoluteFrom("ci/linux-x64"), limit: .AtMost(2s) }

options.name: In-process typed provider registry
options.detail: Trusted Jet code gathers samples inside the main process through a typed registry. One central engine checks the data and decides every budget result.
options.code:
Error [E2906]: performance budget api-ready has no usable evidence
Why: ServiceProbe api-ready completed with insufficient-samples after 12 of 20 required trials.
Fix: restore the service probe and run `jet budget check` again.

Error [E2908]: performance budget operation failed
Why: SceneProbe level-one emitted sequence 8 after sequence 10 for request 4a….
Fix: repair the provider; no report was accepted.
options.technical: The driver owns a closed ProviderRequest and ProviderRecord API; there is no user command protocol. ProviderRequest is exactly {schema:"jet.perf-provider-request",version:1,request_id:Hex64,provider:{kind,identity},context_key:Hex64,budget_spec_hashes:[Hex64],metrics:[MetricCanonical],workload:{identity,digest},policy:MeasurementPolicy}. Arrays sort by canonical bytes; request_id hashes the remaining canonical object plus LF. Records are exactly Sample{request_id,sequence:Int,metric,budget_spec_hash,unit,value:Quantity,captured_at:RFC3339UTC}, Unavailable{request_id,reason_kind:"unsupported-host"|"missing-runtime"|"probe-not-ready"|"insufficient-samples",detail:Text}, and Complete{request_id,sample_count:Int,records_sha256:Hex64}. Sequence starts at 0 and is contiguous; Complete is last. Maximum 1,000,000 samples, 16 MiB canonical record bytes total, 4096 budget specs, and 512 UTF-8 scalars in detail; excess is E2908 before report creation. BuildArtifact resolves the one artifact target identity from the loaded package graph and reads its no-follow published file. CompilerFacts resolves the checked target and reads front-end facts. BenchMeasurement(name) resolves exactly one #Bench of that canonical package-qualified name. ServiceProbe(name) and SceneProbe(name) resolve exactly one existing named service/scene probe registered by their owning runtime subsystem; no PATH/environment command discovery. AllocationProbe(name) resolves exactly one allocation workload registered on the attached Bench/Service/Scene; absent or ambiguous identities are compile-time E2905. Runtime registries carry the pinned workload contract required by GRAMMAR1 and are hashed into workload.digest. Provider adapters may collect samples only; engine owns direction, statistics, policy, report, and baseline. A valid Unavailable or valid Complete with too few samples becomes E2906. Malformed ordering/schema/unit/context/hash, adapter panic, timeout, or registry invariant failure is E2908. Unsupported metric/provider pairs remain E2903; unresolved identity remains E2905.

options.name: Versioned subprocess protocol
options.detail: Runtime measurements run in a child process and send framed messages back. A crash is isolated, but the process protocol adds more failure cases.
options.technical: Use the same request, record variants, resolution rules, limits, ordering, hashes, E2906/E2908 boundary, and centralized evaluator as A, but registered runtime probes execute in an isolated child. stdin is one A-canonical ProviderRequest followed by LF. stdout is frames of four-byte unsigned big-endian length followed by exactly that many A-canonical JSON bytes without LF; zero length and frames over 1 MiB reject, aggregate remains 16 MiB. stderr is bounded to 1 MiB diagnostic log and never parsed. EOF before Complete, bytes after Complete, nonzero exit, timeout, or invalid UTF-8/JSON is E2908. BuildArtifact and CompilerFacts remain in-process trusted adapters. Registry entries select a compiled Jet provider target, never arbitrary PATH commands.

options.name: Signed evidence-file handoff
options.detail: Providers write signed evidence files for later reading. This supports other devices, but cross-machine trust cannot work until Jet has an attestation rule.
options.code:
.jet/perf/provider-inbox/<request_id>.json
# Canonical, create-new, local-only until attestation is ratified.
options.technical: Use the same schemas, resolution, limits, ordering, and evaluator as A. A provider writes one no-follow, create-new canonical container {request,records,complete}; the engine verifies request_id, context, record hash, ownership, mode, size, and atomic completion before reading. Missing compatible evidence is E2906; malformed, replaced, oversized, or protocol-invalid evidence is E2908. This supports remote/device capture but requires the separately gated attestation law before evidence can be trusted across machines; without attestation it is local-only.

comparisons.note: Cargo keeps machine-readable records separate from human logs.
Bazel workers use bounded request and response messages for long-running helper processes.

decisions.lesson:
A performance engine needs raw measurements before it can decide whether a budget passes. A measurement provider is the component that runs or inspects the relevant workload and emits those raw samples. The central evaluator should still own units, statistics, limits, baseline comparison, and the final report; otherwise each provider could quietly apply different rules.

The provider boundary is also a trust boundary. Every sample must belong to the requested metric, budget, workload, target, and run. Canonical encoding means the same facts always serialize to the same bytes, making hashes and replay checks reliable. Sequence numbers and a final record detect truncation or reordering. Size and sample limits prevent a faulty provider from exhausting memory. Unavailable means a valid provider cannot measure here, such as a missing runtime. Malformed means the provider violated the protocol. Those states require different diagnostics.

Provider identity must resolve deterministically; silently searching PATH could run unrelated or hostile code. In-process providers are simplest and trusted. Subprocesses add crash isolation. Evidence files help remote devices but need attestation before another machine can trust them. This ballot chooses the canonical transport while keeping one evaluator and one evidence meaning.

recommendation.why: A gives Jet one typed, deterministic path with the fewest moving parts. Providers only gather samples; the central engine keeps all policy consistent.

whyNot.reason: B adds process startup, message framing, timeouts, and crash handling before Jet needs that isolation.
C is valuable for remote devices, but Jet cannot yet prove that another machine produced trustworthy evidence.

recommendation.tradeoff: A runs trusted providers in the main process, so a provider bug can affect that process. Strict typed limits and validation reduce this risk.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps the simple typed in-process path while borrowing strict message bounds, completion records, and hashes from the transport-heavy options.

harvest.aspect: One typed registry keeps collection simple and deterministic.
harvest.use: Keep it as the primary provider boundary.

harvest.aspect: Bounded records and explicit completion expose broken output.
harvest.use: Apply those checks to in-process records without starting a child process.

harvest.aspect: Context hashes prevent evidence from being reused in the wrong run.
harvest.use: Keep the same hashes in every in-process record.

decisions.title: Performance budget integration contract
decisions.gist: Choose when commands gather performance evidence and when proof may reuse it.
decisions.story: Alex builds, runs benchmarks, starts a development service, proves a release, and opens editor views. Jet must gather measurements without surprising side effects or repeating work that is still valid.
decisions.inWild:
jet build app.jet --release
jet bench app.jet
jet dev app.jet
jet budget check
jet prove app.jet
jet inspect dossier app.jet

options.name: Intent-owned refresh with compatible slice reuse
options.detail: Each command measures the work it already owns. Proof may reuse a matching result for one exact budget, while missing results stay visibly incomplete.
options.code:
$ jet build app.jet --release
build budgets: 2 passed · report 8bdb1120b90a
$ jet prove app.jet
# Existing #240 rendering/status law applies. No budget-specific prove flag or receipt surface is added.
options.technical: jet budget check measures every applicable BudgetSpec for the current target/profile and writes the whole-policy report; update reuses that run. Every successful artifact-producing build always evaluates applicable deterministic BuildArtifact and CompilerFacts Fail budgets after atomic artifact publication and before success; failure exits 1, preserving the hard gate. jet bench measures all applicable BenchMeasurement specs whose Bench scope exists in the package, through the shared evaluator and report model. jet dev measures StartupTime on the first transition to runnable, ServiceReadiness from named service start to its declared ready event, and Scene metrics only when the existing scene/replay is explicitly started. Dev refreshes once per provider context, then only when source, BudgetSpec, workload, target, or profile digest changes; Warn never blocks, Fail blocks readiness. Dossier, Canvas, and LSP never measure and project freshness/context/report identity only. CI runs jet budget check. Prove never measures and introduces no flag, receipt type, status, field, or output. It translates each latest compatible budget result into #240's existing ProofReport Evidence representation and lets #240's existing aggregation decide pass, fail, or pass_incomplete and its existing exit behavior. A compatible passing deterministic build slice may satisfy the matching Evidence fact; statistical command slices may satisfy only the exact same BudgetSpec/context/workload fact and never imply whole-policy completion. Missing, stale, incompatible, unavailable, or unmeasured applicable evidence becomes incomplete Evidence under #240; a failed Fail budget becomes failed Evidence. Warn remains evidence detail and does not change #240 status.

options.name: Intent-owned refresh, whole-report proof reuse
options.detail: Commands still gather their own results, but proof ignores them. Only a full budget-check report can satisfy performance evidence.
options.code:
$ jet build app.jet --release
build budgets: 2 passed · slice report 8bdb1120b90a
$ jet prove app.jet
# #240 sees performance Evidence incomplete until `jet budget check` writes a compatible whole report.
options.technical: Use A's mandatory deterministic build gates, bench/dev timing, read-only projections, and prove-never-measures rule. Command slices are visible in build/dev/bench/dossier/Canvas/LSP but never satisfy ProofReport Evidence. Only a compatible whole-policy report from jet budget check contributes performance Evidence to #240; otherwise existing #240 aggregation yields pass_incomplete. Failed deterministic build budgets still prevent a successful artifact and therefore cannot be bypassed by proof.

options.name: Eager statistical refresh at owning command boundaries
options.detail: Build, development, and benchmark commands eagerly refresh every statistical measurement they can reach. This produces fresher data but makes normal commands do extra work.
options.code:
$ jet build app.jet --release
deterministic budgets: 2 passed
target statistical budgets: 1 warning
# Service, Scene, and Bench providers were not started by build.
options.technical: Keep A's hard deterministic build gates, one evaluator, read-only dossier/Canvas/LSP, and exact #240 Evidence/pass_incomplete/exit law. In addition, build refreshes applicable statistical Target scopes after deterministic gates, dev refreshes all applicable Service/Scene scopes at the same explicit start/ready boundaries, and bench refreshes all Bench scopes. Compatible slices may satisfy matching #240 Evidence exactly as A. No command runs a provider outside the target/service/scene/bench it already owns, so build does not launch services/scenes and editor views remain side-effect free.

comparisons.note: Editors show saved test state and wait for an explicit run action. All options keep editor views read-only.
Bazel reuses command facts only when their build graph and context still match.

decisions.lesson:
Performance budgets become useful only when the right commands measure them at the right time. Deterministic evidence, such as artifact size or compiler facts, should be identical for the same build inputs and can hard-gate every artifact-producing build. Statistical evidence, such as startup time or frame time, varies between runs and needs repeated samples in the runtime context that owns the workload.

Refresh means collecting new evidence. Reuse means accepting existing evidence only when its context still matches: budget definition, source, workload, target, profile, device, and provider facts. Stale or mismatched evidence must never silently pass. Read-only views such as an editor, dossier, or Canvas should display freshness and results without launching benchmarks or services as a side effect. Commands such as bench or dev already own those workloads and are natural refresh points.

Proof aggregation is separate from measurement. A proof command can reuse compatible recorded facts, mark missing required evidence incomplete, and preserve an existing failed result without becoming another hidden benchmark runner. This ballot chooses whether matching command-specific slices can satisfy proof, whether only a whole-policy check can, and how eagerly runtime-owning commands refresh statistical evidence.

recommendation.why: A measures work where users already expect it and safely reuses exact matching facts. It avoids both hidden work and needless repeated checks.

whyNot.reason: B forces a full budget check even when another command already produced the exact fact that proof needs.
C makes ordinary build and development commands run extra statistical work that users did not request.

recommendation.tradeoff: A needs strict rules for deciding when saved evidence still matches. Those checks are necessary to prevent stale results from passing.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps whole-policy checks, lets each command measure only work it owns, and reuses exact matching facts without treating a slice as full coverage.

harvest.aspect: Exact matching facts can avoid repeated work.
harvest.use: Keep fact-level reuse with strict context checks.

harvest.aspect: A full budget check remains the clearest whole-policy report.
harvest.use: Keep that command as the complete policy view.

harvest.aspect: Commands should measure only workloads they already own.
harvest.use: Keep this boundary but do not make every possible measurement eager.

decisions.title: Remove exposed Tower secrets from Git history
decisions.gist: Choose whether to rewrite the public repository's history after rotating the exposed Tower notification credentials.
decisions.lesson:
Git remembers old file contents even after a later commit deletes them. Anyone can retrieve a secret from an older public commit while that commit remains reachable.

Credential rotation makes the old private key and subscription tokens unusable. Rotation is the security fix and must happen either way. Rewriting history is a separate cleanup that removes the old bytes from ordinary clones and searches.

A history rewrite creates replacement commits without the secret. It then force-pushes the replacement history. Existing clones and open branches still contain the old commits until their owners rebase or clone again. Forks and caches may retain copies.

Because this repository is public, the exposed values must be treated as already copied. A rewrite cannot make them secret again. Its benefit is reducing future accidental discovery and preventing scanners or new clones from repeatedly surfacing revoked credentials.
decisions.story: Nate rotates Tower's notification key and resubscribes his devices. The old key can no longer send valid notifications. A new contributor then clones the public repository and searches its history. This choice decides whether that contributor still finds the revoked private key and old subscription records in normal Git history.
decisions.inWild:
$ git log -S '"d"' -- .tower/config.json
# Before cleanup: old commits contain private key material.

$ git clone https://github.com/jet-language/jet
$ git log -S '"d"' -- .tower/config.json
# After option A: ordinary reachable history contains no Tower secret material.

options.name: Rotate, then rewrite
options.detail: Rotate first, prove delivery with the new key, then remove Tower secret material from every reachable repository ref. Coordinate one force-push and require active branches to rebase or reclone. Publish the old-to-new commit mapping without publishing secret bytes.
options.technical: Scan every local and remote branch and tag, rewrite matching blobs, expire local reflogs, garbage-collect, force-push rewritten refs, and run a fresh-clone secret scan. Treat forks, caches, and old clones as permanently exposed. Never reuse the revoked values.
options.code:
$ tower notifications rotate
# owner resubscribes devices and proves one real delivery
$ git filter-repo --path .tower/config.json --replace-text /secure/tower-replacements.txt
$ git push --force --all origin
$ git push --force --tags origin
$ ./scripts/security/scan-tower-history.sh --fresh-clone
PASS: no Tower private key or subscription secret in reachable history

options.name: Rotate, keep history
options.detail: Rotate and prove the new notification path, but leave revoked values in old public commits. Record that the exposure is accepted because rotation removed their authority. New clones remain easy to search for the old bytes.
options.technical: No force-push occurs. Add the revoked key fingerprint and incident date to the private incident record, not the public repository. Secret scanners need an explicit historical finding allowance tied to the revoked fingerprint.
options.code:
$ tower notifications rotate
# owner resubscribes devices and proves one real delivery
$ ./scripts/security/scan-tower-history.sh
KNOWN REVOKED EXPOSURE: old Tower credentials remain in public commits
$ git push origin master
# no rewritten refs

comparisons.note: GitHub's model separates credential revocation from history removal. Revocation stops use; history removal reduces continued exposure but requires collaborator coordination and cannot erase forks or prior copies.
comparisons.code: revoke credential -> verify replacement -> rewrite reachable refs -> fresh-clone scan -> notify collaborators

recommendation.why: The repository is public, and the leaked values include both a private signing key and subscription secrets. Rotation removes authority; a coordinated rewrite also stops routine future disclosure.

whyNot.reason: Rotation makes the values unusable, but every new clone and secret scan still receives revoked private and subscription data from reachable public history.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rewriting changes commit IDs and requires every active branch to rebase or reclone. Accept that coordination cost once, after rotation, because public history otherwise republishes the incident indefinitely.

hybrid.synthesis: Rotate immediately, then perform one coordinated rewrite. This keeps option B's authority-first safety while gaining option A's reduced future exposure. Preserve an old-to-new commit map and migration instructions so collaborators can recover without keeping secret-bearing refs reachable.

harvest.aspect: New clones and ordinary history searches stop exposing the revoked bytes.
harvest.use: Keep the complete reachable-ref rewrite and fresh-clone scan.

harvest.aspect: Rotation removes authority without waiting for disruptive repository coordination.
harvest.use: Rotate and prove the new key before starting the rewrite.

decisions.title: `jet serve` is a literal alias of `jet dev --swap` — delete or respecialize?
decisions.gist: Two top-level verbs run the same dev loop; S14 forbids aliases.
decisions.lesson: `jet dev` is the watch loop: it re-runs your program on every save. D-DEVMODE1 guarantees its output is byte-identical to a release build. Its `--swap` flag keeps the process resident and hot-swaps type-stable edits instead of restarting (D-HOTSWAP1). D-DEV4 also ratified auto-detection: `dev` picks rerun or hot-swap by itself. `jet serve` was added as a friendlier name for the resident mode. But it ships as a one-line alias — `jet serve x.jet` literally dispatches to `jet dev x.jet --swap` (Source/main.rs:1395). S14 says no aliases, ever.
decisions.story: June is three weeks into Jet. `jet help` shows both `dev` ("watch file, re-run on save") and `serve` ("resident program, hot-swap edits"). She asks which one her web app should use and learns they are the same engine. Now she wonders what else in the manual is secretly the same thing. That doubt is exactly what the no-aliases law exists to prevent.
decisions.inWild:
# Both of these run the identical watch loop today:
jet dev app.jet --swap
jet serve app.jet

# D-DEV4 already ratified auto-detection on `dev`:
# "auto-detects rerun vs resident hot-swap; --restart/--swap/--watch=off overrides"

options.name: Delete `serve` — one dev-loop verb
options.detail: `jet dev` is the only dev loop, exactly as D-DEV4 ratified: auto-detects rerun vs resident hot-swap, with `--restart`/`--swap` as expert overrides. `jet serve` becomes a teaching error naming `jet dev`. The word `serve` stays unclaimed. A future ballot can give it real run-as-service semantics when the D-SERVICE1 story needs a CLI entry — no meaning is squatted by an alias meanwhile.
options.code:
jet dev app.jet            # magic: picks rerun or hot-swap for you
jet dev app.jet --swap     # expert: force resident hot-swap
$ jet serve app.jet
error[E2101]: `serve` is not a jet command
  the dev loop is `jet dev app.jet` (hot-swap: `--swap`)

options.name: Respecialize `serve` — it runs a service, not a dev loop
options.detail: `jet serve` stops being a dev verb. It builds and runs the project's server target the way production would: no watcher, no interpreter, release profile by default. So `dev` means iterate and `serve` means run-as-service — a memorable beginner story. It costs a real design now: a program with no server target gets an error naming `jet run`. And it mints service semantics before the D-SERVICE1 runtime work has proven what `serve` should do.
options.code:
jet dev api.jet            # iterating: watch + hot-swap
jet serve api.jet          # running: release build, resident, no watcher
$ jet serve script.jet
error[E2XXX]: `script.jet` defines no server target
  `jet serve` runs long-lived services; for a one-shot program use `jet run script.jet`

comparisons.note: The JS ecosystem's split is option B's shape: `vite dev` iterates, `vite preview` serves the built artifact.
comparisons.code:
vite dev
vite preview   # serve the production build locally

comparisons.note: Cargo has one verb per job and no aliases; `cargo watch` is a separate tool, not a second spelling of the same one.

recommendation.why: D-DEV4 already ratified auto-detection, so the alias adds no capability — only a second spelling for the same loop. S14 is absolute. Deleting now also keeps `serve` free for a real future job.

whyNot.reason: It invents run-as-service semantics ahead of the D-SERVICE1 runtime that would define them; a verb ratified before its behavior exists invites a second reconciliation later.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users who learned `serve` retype `dev` once, guided by the teaching error.

hybrid.synthesis: A and B are compatible over time: delete the alias now, and re-mint `serve` later as B's run-as-service verb once the service runtime ships and proves the need. A is the hybrid's first step.

harvest.use: adopted now

harvest.aspect: serve as a genuine run-as-service verb
harvest.use: deferred to a future ballot gated on D-SERVICE1 shipping

decisions.title: `#Wasm` / `#Js` duplicate `#Target(Wasm)` / `#Target(Js)` — merge into one marker family?
decisions.gist: Two marker spellings pick an item's web compilation target; one family should own it.
decisions.lesson: A hybrid web build (D-WEBKIND1) splits one program across two emitted artifacts: WASM for compute-heavy functions, JS for DOM glue. Item-level markers say which side an item lands on. D-OSTARGET1 ratified `#Target(…)` accepting `Web`, `Browser`, `Wasm`, `Js`, and `Os.Linux/Macos/Windows`. Syntax.rs additionally ships bare `#Wasm` and `#Js` markers from the earlier D-WASM1 work — same job, second spelling. `#WasmExport` names an exported symbol surface; that is a different job and not part of this question.
decisions.story: Marcus builds a hybrid web app: image filtering should compile to WASM, DOM glue to JS. One doc example shows `#Wasm fn blur(...)`; another shows `#Target(Wasm) fn blur(...)`. He asks his teammate which one is right. The answer is "both" — so now every codebase picks a house style, which is the guess I8 exists to eliminate.

options.name: `#Target(…)` owns the axis; `#Wasm`/`#Js` die
options.detail: One marker family for all target partitioning, exactly as D-OSTARGET1 ratified: `#Target(Wasm)`, `#Target(Js)`, `#Target(Web)`, `#Target(Os.Linux)`. `#Wasm` and `#Js` become ordinary unknown-marker errors — greenfield, no teaching residue. `#WasmExport` is untouched. The OS axis and web axis read identically, so a reader learns one shape that also fits every future axis (plugin, embedded profiles).
options.code:
#Target(Wasm)
fn blur(pixels: [U8], radius: Int) -> [U8] { ... }

#Target(Js)
fn wire_ui() { web.on("#go", "click", (e) => render()) }

$ jet check app.jet   # after the break
error[E0061]: unknown marker `#Wasm`
  target partitioning is `#Target(Wasm)`

options.name: Short markers own the web axis; `#Target` narrows to OS only
options.detail: `#Wasm`/`#Js` stay as the web-partition spellings — shortest for the most-typed case in hybrid apps. `#Target(…)` narrows to the OS axis (`#Target(Os.Linux)`), and `#Target(Wasm/Js/Web/Browser)` becomes an error. This saves five characters per marker. The cost: two families for one concept, and a reader must learn that the web and OS axes use different mechanisms for no semantic reason.
options.code:
#Wasm
fn blur(pixels: [U8], radius: Int) -> [U8] { ... }

#Target(Os.Linux)
impl LinuxBackend { ... }

$ jet check app.jet
error[E0061]: `#Target(Wasm)` is not a target axis
  web partitioning uses `#Wasm` / `#Js`

comparisons.note: Rust spells every target condition through one attribute family, cfg. Nobody writes `#[wasm]`; the axis is an argument, not a marker name.
Swift likewise: one `#if os(...)` / `#if arch(...)` conditional family for all axes.

recommendation.why: Axis-as-argument already won for OS targeting and generalizes to every future target. A deletes a whole marker pair from the surface and makes the two axes read identically.

whyNot.reason: It preserves five characters at the cost of a second mechanism — a trade the ranked priorities never make.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hybrid-heavy files type `#Target(...)` more verbosely on every partitioned item.

hybrid.synthesis: If hybrid-app practice ever proves the verbosity painful, a future ballot could bless a shorthand inside an already-`#Target(Web)` file. Nothing today needs it, so A ships alone.

harvest.aspect: one marker family, axis as argument
harvest.use: adopted now

harvest.aspect: brevity for the hot hybrid case
harvest.use: deferred; revisit only with real-use evidence of pain

decisions.title: One noun for the package store: hangar, store, or both?
decisions.gist: Two ratified decisions gave the package store two different CLI nouns; one must win.
decisions.lesson:
The hangar is Jet's shared content-addressed package store at /etc/jet/hangar/ — the same job as Nix's /nix/store. Store commands verify objects, copy them between machines, list generations, and reclaim disk.

Two decisions ratified on 2026-07-10 collided. D-CLI-SURFACE1=B created a `jet store` command group and put `gc` inside it. D-JPK-STORECLI1=D put the physical verbs under `jet hangar` instead. It also re-affirmed your 2026-07-03 amendment that `jet clean` is the only GC intent. The shipped CLI has all three spellings plus a bare `jet gc` alias. S14 says one canonical spelling per construct, no aliases ever.
decisions.story: Ray's CI disk fills up. He wants to check the shared package store for corruption, clean unused entries, and copy a verified object to an air-gapped builder. The manual shows him `jet store verify`, `jet hangar verify`, and `jet clean`. He runs `jet store gc` — a command one ratified decision created and another says must not exist. He cannot tell whether the other spellings do something different or the same thing.
decisions.inWild:
# CI maintenance script — which of these is real?
jet store verify          # D-CLI-SURFACE1=B says this group exists
jet hangar verify         # D-JPK-STORECLI1=D says hangar owns physical verbs
jet store gc              # D-CLI-SURFACE1=B lists gc under store
jet clean                 # owner amendment 2026-07-03: the ONLY gc+optimize intent
jet gc                    # shipped silent alias — S14 says no aliases, ever

options.name: Hangar wins — `jet store` group dissolves
options.detail: `jet hangar` owns every physical store verb: verify, repair, copy, import, export, dump/restore, sign, rollback, generations, du. `jet clean` stays the sole GC+optimize intent. Project-side verbs leave the group: `jet fetch` stays flat, and script locking folds into `jet fetch --lock <script.jet>`. `jet store …` and bare `jet gc` become teaching errors naming the real spelling. One noun survives, and it is the product's own name.
options.code:
jet hangar verify
jet hangar copy --to ssh://builder /etc/jet/hangar/abc123
jet hangar generations
jet clean                       # gc + optimize, unchanged
jet fetch --lock tool.jet       # was: jet store lock
$ jet store verify
error[E2101]: `jet store` is not a jet command group
  the store lives under `jet hangar` — try `jet hangar verify`

options.name: Store wins — hangar stays a product name, not a CLI noun
options.detail: `jet store` absorbs D-JPK-STORECLI1's verb list: verify, repair, copy, import, export, dump/restore, sign, rollback, generations. `store gc` dies per your amendment; `jet clean` stays the GC intent. "Hangar" remains the store's name in prose and paths (/etc/jet/hangar/) but is never typed as a command. `jet hangar du` respells as `jet store du`. The generic word is easier to guess, but Jet then types a different word than it says.
options.code:
jet store verify
jet store copy --to ssh://builder /etc/jet/hangar/abc123
jet store generations
jet clean
$ jet hangar verify
error[E2101]: `jet hangar` is not a jet command group
  physical store verbs live under `jet store` — try `jet store verify`

options.name: Split by audience — `jet store` project-facing, `jet hangar` physical
options.detail: `jet store` keeps the verbs a developer runs against their project's resolved view: fetch, lock, verify, rollback, generations. `jet hangar` keeps the administrator verbs against the shared physical store: repair, copy, import, export, dump/restore, sign, du. `jet clean` stays the GC intent. Two nouns survive with distinct jobs. But the verify/rollback boundary between them is genuinely fuzzy, and users must memorize which side a verb lives on.
options.code:
jet store verify            # my project's resolved store view
jet hangar repair           # the shared physical store
jet hangar copy --to ssh://builder abc123
jet clean

comparisons.note: Nix splits `nix store` from `nix profile`/`nix flake` and users routinely cannot guess which noun owns a verb. Its third gc spelling is the exact confusion Jet should not replicate.
comparisons.code:
nix store verify --all
nix store optimise
nix-collect-garbage   # third spelling for gc

comparisons.note: Cargo has no store noun at all — one `cargo clean` intent; everything else is invisible. Jet already matches that beginner ceiling with `jet clean`.

recommendation.why: D-JPK-STORECLI1 is the more specific, verb-by-verb law and already chose hangar. Hangar is the product's own aviation name, the word users already see in every store path. A store/hangar synonym pair is exactly the two-names-one-thing confusion I8 exists to kill.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the generic word but breaks the product's own vocabulary: paths, docs, and errors all say hangar while the CLI refuses the word.
Two nouns for one store makes every verb placement a memorization test; the project/physical boundary is too fuzzy to teach.

recommendation.tradeoff: `hangar` is a Jet-ism newcomers must learn once; the teaching error on `jet store` teaches it at first contact.

hybrid.synthesis: A already absorbs B's single-noun virtue and C's clean physical/project split: physical verbs live under one noun, project verbs stay flat daily verbs. No compatible idea remains outside A.

harvest.aspect: hangar as the one physical-store noun
harvest.use: adopted wholesale
A keeps one noun too — it just picks the product's own name

harvest.aspect: project verbs separate from physical verbs
harvest.use: A keeps fetch/lock flat on the daily ring instead of minting a second noun

decisions.title: Complete the CLI verb map: 18 verbs still outside the ratified ring and groups
decisions.gist: Every jet verb needs a ratified home; 18 have none and 4 are silent aliases the law forbids.
decisions.lesson:
D-CLI-SURFACE1=B (2026-07-10) fixed a two-ring CLI. About 20 daily verbs stay flat (run, build, test, dev, repl, fmt, ...). The long tail lives under four groups: `jet registry`, `jet inspect`, `jet store`, `jet self`. A moved verb's bare spelling must be a teaching error, never a silent alias.

Separately, D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1=C ratified product ownership: jet owns the language and dev loop, jetpack owns packages/env/build substrate, jetos owns OS workflows. Eighteen shipped verbs were in neither decision's table. Four of them (doctor, devtools, gc, toolchain) are silent duplicates of grouped verbs — the exact thing SURFACE1 banned.
decisions.story: Priya prints `jet help` to learn the tool. She expects the promised small daily ring plus four groups. The real listing also shows env, fetch, search, info, logs, outdated, clean, push, trust, bridge, services, image, os, config, toolchain, doctor, devtools, and gc floating outside both. She types `jet doctor` and it silently works, even though the law says that spelling moved to `jet self doctor`.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet doctor          # works — but law says `jet self doctor`
$ jet devtools bless  # works — but law says `jet self devtools bless`
$ jet gc              # works — but `jet clean` is the sole GC intent
$ jet toolchain       # works — but law says `jet self toolchain`
# and 14 more verbs with no ratified ring/group row:
# env fetch search info logs outdated clean push trust bridge services image os config

options.name: Product-split placement — jet keeps the dev loop, engine verbs go to their owners
options.detail: Daily developer verbs join the flat ring: env, fetch, search, info, outdated, clean. Already-ratified product verbs stay put: `jet trust` (D-JPK-GRANTCMD1) and `jet os` (D-JPK-OSVERB1). Engine and ops verbs move to the owning binary: `jetpack push/bridge/services/image/config/logs`, each with a jet-side teaching shim. The four silent aliases die as teaching errors naming `jet self doctor`, `jet self devtools`, `jet clean`, and `jet self toolchain`.
options.code:
# flat ring gains (daily-loop):
jet env    jet fetch    jet search    jet info    jet outdated    jet clean
# stays (already ratified):
jet trust grant ...     jet os switch ...
# moves to the engine binary:
jetpack push prod-fleet
jetpack services up
$ jet doctor
error[E2101]: `doctor` moved — try `jet self doctor`

options.name: Everything stays on jet; unplaced verbs get grouped
options.detail: No verb leaves the jet binary. The four aliases die. Ops verbs group under existing nouns: `push`, `bridge`, `services`, `image`, `config` under `jet os`; `search`, `info`, `logs`, `outdated` under `jet inspect`. `env`, `fetch`, and `clean` join the flat ring. One binary to learn. But `jet inspect search` is heavier than daily discovery deserves, and `jet os services` stretches the os noun past its ratified meaning.
options.code:
jet env    jet fetch    jet clean
jet inspect search http
jet inspect info core.http
jet os push prod-fleet
$ jet gc
error[E2101]: `gc` moved — try `jet clean`

options.name: Freeze the status quo minus aliases
options.detail: All 14 real verbs stay flat top-level on jet; only the four silent aliases become teaching errors. Smallest motion. But the flat surface stays at roughly 35 verbs. That is the crowding D-CLI-SURFACE1 was ratified to end — the ring stops meaning anything.
options.code:
jet push prod-fleet     # stays flat
jet bridge flake        # stays flat
$ jet devtools
error[E2101]: `devtools` moved — try `jet self devtools`

comparisons.note: git's porcelain/plumbing split is the survivable big CLI: ~20 daily verbs in `git help`, the long tail behind `git help -a`. SURFACE1 chose this shape; this ballot finishes it.
comparisons.code:
git help        # 21 common verbs
git help -a     # everything else, grouped

comparisons.note: nix-env/nix-store/nix-collect-garbage grew ungoverned top-level spellings for years. The 2.x `nix <noun> <verb>` redesign is the cleanup Jet can do before 1.0 instead of after.
comparisons.code:
nix-env -e pkg           # legacy flat sprawl
nix profile remove pkg   # governed redesign

recommendation.why: A is the only option consistent with both prior ratifications at once: SURFACE1's small ring and PRODUCT-SPLIT1's ownership. Daily verbs stay one keystroke; fleet/ops verbs sit with the binary that owns their behavior.

whyNot.reason: It bloats `jet inspect` and `jet os` with verbs those nouns don't own, trading noun coherence for single-binary purity nobody asked for.
A 35-verb flat surface abandons the ratified ring; the help screen stops teaching what matters daily.

recommendation.tradeoff: Fleet and service users retype `jetpack push` etc. once, guided by teaching shims. Store-group rows here stay agnostic: D-CLI-STORE2 on the same card picks the store noun independently.

hybrid.synthesis: A is already the hybrid: it takes B's group discipline for jet-owned verbs, C's zero-motion for the daily six, and PRODUCT-SPLIT1's ownership for engine verbs. No stronger compatible combination remains.

harvest.use: adopted wholesale

harvest.aspect: grouping discipline on the jet binary
harvest.use: A applies it to jet-owned verbs (self/inspect groups) only
A promotes the daily six into the ring untouched

decisions.title: C++ binder depth: `cpp.*` — opaque classes, laundered exceptions, on-demand templates
decisions.gist: Decide how deep the C++ binder goes: classes, exceptions, and templates across the boundary.
decisions.lesson:
The C binder (S59) is shipped law, but the world's performance libraries are C++: OpenCV, LLVM, TensorRT, Qt, game physics. C++ has no stable ABI, so every language binds it by generating a C shim layer underneath.

D-FFI-UNIFY1 already fixes the user surface: `cpp.<lib>` with script/project/overlay tiers and a `jet inspect bind cpp` binder. This ballot picks the binder's depth: what happens to classes, exceptions, and templates — the three things C++ has that C doesn't. The swift binder (D-FFI-SWIFT1) set the precedent shape: opaque ref-counted handles, throws mapped to Result.
decisions.story: Grace needs OpenCV's image pipeline. Python users type two lines. Today she would hand-write a C wrapper around every C++ method she touches, recreating the shim layer pybind11 generates automatically for Python.
decisions.inWild:
use cpp.opencv as cv               // project tier: opencv: cpp@"4.10" in pkg.jet

img :: cv.imread("scan.png")?      // cv::Exception -> `? CppError`
blur :: img.gaussian_blur(kernel: 5)?
files.write_bytes("out.png", blur.encode(".png")?)?

options.name: Full depth — opaque classes, `? CppError`, on-demand template instantiation
options.detail:
The binder (clang-based) emits a generated C shim crate per library, cached content-addressed like every bridge. Classes become opaque owned handles with RAII mapped to Jet scope cleanup (S63); methods become ordinary Jet methods on the handle type. Exceptions are caught at the shim and surface as `T ? CppError` — fallibility is visible at every call site.

Templates instantiate on demand: `cpp.vector<Int>` asks the binder to instantiate `std::vector<int64_t>` in the shim on cache miss. Overloads collapse to argument labels (S61); operator overloads become named methods. The overlay tier corrects any wrong guess.
options.code:
use cpp.opencv as cv

img :: cv.imread("scan.png")?        // handle; frees at scope end (S63)
out :: img.gaussian_blur(kernel: 5)?

$ jet check vision.jet   # exception type not convertible
error[E32xx]: `cv.imread` can throw `cv::Exception`
  the call is fallible — write `cv.imread("scan.png")?` and handle `CppError`

options.name: C-surface only — bind `extern "C"` symbols, classes stay out
options.detail:
The cpp binder binds only what the C binder already understands: free functions with C linkage. Libraries exposing C APIs (many do) work day one; anything class-shaped needs a hand-written C wrapper, exactly like today.

Honest and small, but it concedes the actual C++ ecosystem: OpenCV, Qt, and LLVM are class-first. The gap between Jet and Python/Swift interop stays visible in every migration conversation.
options.code:
use cpp.sqlite3 as sq       // works: C API
use cpp.opencv as cv        // fails:
$ jet check vision.jet
error[E32xx]: `opencv` exposes no C-linkage surface
  the cpp binder binds extern "C" symbols only; write a C wrapper for classes

options.name: Full depth minus templates — classes and exceptions, no generic instantiation
options.detail: Everything in A except template instantiation: template types appear only where a library already instantiates them in its own headers. Cuts the binder's hardest surface. Users hit the wall exactly at `std::vector<T>` returns and Eigen-style math libraries — common in the target workloads — and fall back to overlay-tier hand shims.
options.code:
use cpp.opencv as cv
img :: cv.imread("x.png")?          // fine: concrete class
hist :: img.histogram()?             // fails if return is std::vector<float>
error[E32xx]: `histogram` returns `std::vector<float>` — no instantiation support
  add an overlay shim, or vote template support

comparisons.note: pybind11 proved the full-depth model: opaque class handles, exceptions translated, templates instantiated at binding time. It is why C++ libraries feel native from Python.
Swift's C++ interop (5.9+) also chose classes-as-values/handles with throws mapping — the same shape D-FFI-SWIFT1 already ratified for Swift itself.
comparisons.code:
import CxxOpenCV
let img = try cv.imread("scan.png")

recommendation.why: The C++ ecosystem is the single biggest performance-library pool Jet can absorb, and it is class-first. Full depth is what makes `use cpp.opencv` two lines instead of a wrapper project; pybind11 proved the model at scale.

whyNot.reason: It binds the part of C++ that is already C and concedes the actual target — every class-first library stays a manual wrapper project.
Template returns pervade the exact math/vision libraries this binder exists for; stopping there moves the wall two steps back instead of removing it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The binder owns a clang toolchain dependency (jetpack-provisioned, never in Source/ — I6) and template instantiation lengthens first-compile cache misses.

hybrid.synthesis: A ships staged along B→C→A internally — C-linkage binding lands first, classes/exceptions next, templates last — but the ratified surface is A so no intermediate stage becomes accidental law.

harvest.use: ratified as the contract
first internal stage; already proven by the shipped C binder
second internal stage; overlay tier covers gaps until templates land

decisions.title: Bare project verbs: run/dev/debug/bench/check/build with no file argument
decisions.gist: Whether the six build verbs work with no file argument inside a package, resolving the entry the way run and test already do.
decisions.lesson:
Terms first. A single .jet file is a whole program; you run it with `jet file.jet` and it never needs a manifest. A package is a directory with a pkg.jet manifest that declares one or more targets (buildable entry points). Inside a package the entry is already known: pkg.jet lists targets, and an omitted target is inferred from a top-level `fn run()` (decision D-ILE1). A workspace holds several packages; you pick one member with `-p <member>`.

Today two verbs already run bare inside a package. `jet test` collects the package's #Test blocks with no argument. `jet fmt` discovers workspace, package, or current-directory scope on its own. But `jet run`, `jet dev`, `jet debug`, `jet bench`, `jet check`, and `jet build` still demand a file argument even when the package entry is unambiguous. So a beginner who scaffolds a project and types `jet run` gets a usage error instead of their program.

This choice is whether those six verbs learn the same entry-resolution rule the rest of the tool already uses.
decisions.story: Marcus Bell finishes the Jet tutorial and scaffolds his first real project. He runs `jet new weather-cli`, cd's in, opens the generated main file, and types the command every other language taught him: `jet run`. Instead of his program, he gets a usage error telling him to name a file. He knows the file is right there. He knows the project knows. He types the path by hand, and again the next twenty times.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet new weather-cli
  created weather-cli/ (pkg.jet, Source/Main.jet)
$ cd weather-cli
$ jet run
error: no input file
  usage: jet run <file.jet>

# pkg.jet already names the entry:
package: weather-cli
targets:
  main: { entry: Source/Main.jet }

options.name: One shared entry-resolution rule for all six verbs
options.detail: run, dev, debug, bench, check, and build all become bare-capable inside a package. With no file, each resolves the entry the same way: the package's declared targets, falling back to an inferred `fn run()` (D-ILE1). One declared target runs directly. Several targets with no default is an error that lists them and shows how to pick. An explicit file or `-p <member>` always wins. Outside a package, bare use stays today's usage error. One rule, learned once, applied everywhere.
options.code:
$ cd weather-cli
$ jet run
  weather-cli 22C, clear

# two targets, none default:
$ jet build
error: package has 2 targets; name one
  targets: main, bench-tool
  pick with:  jet build -p main
  or a file:  jet build Source/Main.jet

$ jet build -p main
  built target 'main'

options.name: Only run and dev go bare
options.detail: The two most-typed verbs, run and dev, become bare-capable inside a package. debug, bench, check, and build keep requiring an explicit file. The everyday loop gets shorter, but the tool now has two classes of verb. Some read the manifest for you; some make you name the file even though the manifest is right there. A beginner learns `jet run` works bare, assumes `jet check` does too, and hits the wall.
options.code:
$ cd weather-cli
$ jet run
  weather-cli 22C, clear
$ jet check
error: no input file
  usage: jet check <file.jet>
$ jet check Source/Main.jet
  no errors

options.name: Status quo: file always required
options.detail: All six verbs keep demanding an explicit file, even inside a package whose entry is declared. Nothing new to learn about resolution, but every beginner keeps typing the path the manifest already knows, and the tool stays inconsistent with test and fmt, which resolve scope on their own.
options.code:
$ cd weather-cli
$ jet run
error: no input file
  usage: jet run <file.jet>
$ jet run Source/Main.jet
  weather-cli 22C, clear

comparisons.note: `cargo run` and `cargo build` read Cargo.toml and need no path; `--bin <name>` disambiguates. Jet already has the manifest and the `-p` selector; option A finishes the same convenience for its build verbs.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo run
   Running `target/debug/app`
$ cargo run --bin other

comparisons.note: `go run .` and `go build` operate on the current package by directory, no file named. The bare-verb ergonomics beginners expect are the norm, not a special case.

recommendation.why: One entry-resolution rule across every verb is the ceremony-free default a beginner expects: cd into a project and `jet run` just works, same as test and fmt already do. It stays honest about ambiguity by listing targets, and it never removes expert control because an explicit file or `-p` always wins.
recommendation.tradeoff: A package with several targets and no default gets an error on bare use instead of guessing. That is the safe direction: it names the real targets and shows the exact pick, so the one-time friction lands on the ambiguous case, not the common one.

whyNot.reason: Splitting verbs into bare-capable and not creates two classes the beginner cannot predict. Learning `jet run` works bare teaches the wrong lesson about `jet check`. Inconsistent surface, against one-path.
Keeps every beginner typing a path the manifest already holds, and leaves the tool inconsistent with test and fmt. It fixes nothing the card exists to fix.

hybrid.synthesis: Adopt one shared entry-resolution rule for all six verbs (A). It already contains B's win, since run and dev are simply two of the six, and it answers C's only virtue, predictability, with a single rule instead of a per-verb table.

harvest.aspect: One rule for all six verbs, explicit file or -p always wins
harvest.use: The core mechanism: bare resolves via targets then inferred fn run(); ambiguity errors with the target list.

harvest.aspect: run and dev are the highest-value verbs to shorten
harvest.use: They are included first-class in A; the everyday loop gets the shortest path without inventing a special case.

harvest.aspect: Predictability and no new resolution surprises
harvest.use: A delivers this through a single rule shared with test and fmt, so there is nothing per-verb to memorize.

decisions.title: One spelling for discarding a fallible or must-use result: .drop(reason) vs #Suppress region
decisions.gist: Whether discarding an ignored result stays the per-value `.drop("reason")` only, or also keeps the block-wide `#Suppress(MustUse) { ... }` region that ships alongside it.
decisions.lesson:
Terms first. Some Jet calls return a result you are not allowed to silently throw away. These are fallible results (they might carry an error) and @MustUse values (the caller must look at them). Discarding one requires visible intent, so the reader sees you meant to (decisions D-IGNORERET1 and D-IGNORERET2). Ignore one by accident and you get error E0402 or E0419.

Right now the code ships two ways to say the same thing. The recorded spelling is `.drop("reason")`, written on the value: `cleanup_temp().drop("best-effort")`. But the parser and sema also ship a region form, `#Suppress(MustUse) { ... }`, which suppresses those same errors for every statement in the block. That is two spellings for one semantic job, which invariant I8 forbids: one canonical mechanism per job.

This choice picks which one is canonical, or ratifies them as genuinely distinct jobs.
decisions.story: Priscilla Hoffman writes a test-helper file full of teardown calls whose results nobody checks. She wraps the whole file's noisy section in `#Suppress(MustUse) { ... }` and moves on. Months later a teammate adds a real fallible call inside that same block, `db.commit()`, and forgets the return matters. The commit fails in CI, returns an error, and the region silently swallows it. No E0419, no diagnostic, a green test over a broken write.

options.name: Per-value .drop("reason") only; #Suppress region is removed
options.detail: `.drop("reason")` on the value is the one canonical discard. Each site names why it is safe to ignore, so intent is auditable per result and grep-able. The `#Suppress(MustUse)` region leaves the language; writing it becomes an ordinary unknown-marker error with no special teaching residue. A fallible call added later without its own `.drop` still triggers E0419, so nothing gets silently swallowed by proximity.

options.name: Keep both, ratified as distinct jobs
options.detail: Declare the two forms serve different jobs and keep both. `.drop("reason")` discards one value with a reason; `#Suppress(MustUse) { ... }` marks a scaffolding or test block where many known-noisy results are discarded together. Convenient for teardown-heavy files, but it means one semantic intent, 'I mean to discard this result', has two spellings, and the region keeps swallowing any new fallible call dropped into the block.

options.name: Region only; .drop is removed
options.detail: `#Suppress(MustUse) { ... }` becomes the one discard mechanism; `.drop` leaves the language. Discarding a single value then means wrapping one statement in a region, which is noisy for the common case and still hides any later fallible call inside the block. The per-site reason string is lost, so audits cannot see why each result was ignored.

comparisons.note: Rust's must-use discard is per-value (`let _ = x;`) with no block-wide suppression; #[allow(unused_must_use)] on an item is the escape hatch and is known to hide later real cases. Jet's `.drop("reason")` improves on `let _ =` by requiring a stated reason.
comparisons.code: let _ = cleanup_temp();  // per value, no reason recorded

comparisons.note: Go discards per-value with `_ =`, never a region. The blank identifier is deliberately one assignment at a time, so a newly added error return is a fresh, visible discard, not something a wrapper already covers.

recommendation.why: The per-value reason string keeps intent auditable at the exact discard site and reads clearly for the common case of ignoring one result. It satisfies I8 with a single canonical mechanism and keeps the greenfield break clean: the retired region becomes an ordinary error with no teaching residue.
recommendation.tradeoff: Teardown-heavy files repeat `.drop("reason")` per line instead of wrapping once. That repetition is the point: each ignored result carries its own visible reason, and a later fallible call cannot hide behind a block that already suppresses the check.

whyNot.reason: Two spellings for one intent violates I8, and the region's real danger stays: a fallible call added inside the block later is silently swallowed with no E0419. The convenience buys a safety hole.
Loses the per-site reason string, makes single-value discard noisy, and keeps the same swallow-later-calls hazard as B. It removes the safer, clearer form and keeps the risky one.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep the per-value `.drop("reason")` as the sole discard (A). B and C both trade less typing against a checked boundary. The repetition A costs is a feature: every discard states its own reason, and no future call hides inside a suppression.

harvest.aspect: Per-value discard with a mandatory reason string
harvest.use: The canonical mechanism; auditable at each site and safe against later-added fallible calls.
Answered without a region: `.drop("reason")` per line stays terse and keeps each discard's intent visible.
A also gives exactly one mechanism, but keeps the reason string and avoids wrapping single statements in a block.

decisions.title: Debug derivation: auto-derive like Printable/Equatable, or opt-in @Debug marker
decisions.gist: Whether the Debug view of a value is derived automatically when every field qualifies, or requires a hand-written @Debug marker on the type.
decisions.lesson:
Terms first. Printable is the pretty, user-facing rendering of a value; Debug is the developer-facing dump you use while diagnosing, selected in interpolation with `{value@Debug}`. Equatable means the type supports `==`. A derive is the compiler writing one of these for you when every field already supports it, so you write no boilerplate. A field marked `#[Redact]` renders as "[redacted]" in Debug so secrets never leak into logs (D-DEBUG-REDACT).

Two ratified rules disagree. S55, the built-in derive policy, says Printable and Equatable auto-derive silently when every field qualifies, and lists other derives, including `@Debug`, as explicit opt-in markers. D-DISPLAYDBG1 says the opposite for Debug: 'Debug is dev-facing and auto-derived; `{value@Debug}` selects it.' One says add a marker to get Debug; the other says it is already there.

This choice settles which rule is law.
decisions.story: Deborah Nguyen is chasing a bad total on an order. She drops a print into her handler, `print("order: {order@Debug}")`, exactly as the tutorial showed. One doc page told her Debug is auto-derived and just works; another told her she must first add an `@Debug` marker to the Order type. Depending on which rule is real, she either sees her struct dumped or gets a compile error mid-debug, pointing at a marker she did not know she needed.

options.name: Debug auto-derives like Printable and Equatable
options.detail: Debug derives automatically whenever every field qualifies, matching Printable and Equatable under S55. `{value@Debug}` always works in development with no marker. A hand-written Debug impl still overrides the derived one, and `#[Redact]` still renders sensitive fields as "[redacted]". The standalone opt-in `@Debug` marker leaves the derive list, since it now selects nothing you did not already have. Inspecting your own struct needs no ceremony.

options.name: Opt-in @Debug marker stays required
options.detail: Debug stays explicit opt-in per S55's list. Using `{value@Debug}` on a type without an `@Debug` marker is a compile error carrying a fix-it that adds the marker. The surface is explicit: you can point at exactly which types are debuggable. The cost is ceremony on every struct you inspect, paid during debugging when friction hurts most.

comparisons.note: Rust makes Debug opt-in with `#[derive(Debug)]` and errors if you `{:?}` a type without it. It is a frequent beginner speed bump; you interrupt debugging to annotate the type. Jet's redaction removes the usual reason to keep Debug off by default.

Python gives every object a default repr with zero ceremony; you can always print something while debugging. Auto-derive brings that friction-free inspection while `#[Redact]` keeps secrets out of the dump.

recommendation.why: Debug is a dev-facing tool. Requiring a marker before you can inspect your own struct fights priority two, the beginner experience, at the exact moment friction hurts, mid-debug. Auto-derive matches how Printable and Equatable already behave, so the model stays consistent, and #[Redact] carries the secrets-in-logs safety story.
recommendation.tradeoff: Auto-derive means every qualifying type carries a Debug view whether or not it is ever printed.
