That view exists only for developer inspection, redaction protects sensitive fields, and a hand-written impl overrides it, so the cost is a capability you never see until you ask for it.

whyNot.reason: Puts ceremony on the debugging path itself: you hit a compile error mid-diagnosis and must annotate the type before you can look at it. The usual reason for opt-in, secret leakage, is already handled by #[Redact], so the friction buys little.

hybrid.synthesis: Auto-derive Debug (A) and keep the two controls B's explicitness relied on: a hand-written impl still overrides, and #[Redact] still hides sensitive fields. That preserves expert control over the exact dump without making every beginner annotate a type just to print it.

harvest.aspect: Ceremony-free Debug that matches Printable and Equatable
harvest.use: The default: `{value@Debug}` works everywhere in dev, consistent with the other auto-derives.

harvest.aspect: Explicit control over what the Debug dump shows
harvest.use: Kept via hand-written impl override and #[Redact], so experts still shape or hide fields without a mandatory opt-in marker.

decisions.title: core.archive vs core.compress: split stream codecs from container formats, or merge
decisions.gist: Whether gzip's two current homes resolve by splitting stream codecs from container formats, or by merging everything compression-ish into one module.
decisions.lesson:
Terms first. A byte-stream codec transforms one stream of bytes into a smaller stream and back: gzip and zstd are codecs. A container format holds many named entries in one file: zip and tar are containers. They are different jobs; a codec never names an entry, a container never has to compress.

Right now two registered core modules overlap on gzip. `core.archive` (D-DEP-ARCHIVE1) offers gzip, zip, and tar over a flate2-family FFI bridge. `core.compress.gzip` and `core.compress.zstd` (D-CODECS1) register the same codecs standalone. So gzip lives in two places and a reader cannot tell which import is canonical.

This choice picks the shape that removes the overlap.
decisions.story: Frank Castellano ships a service that compresses a rolling log stream with zstd, then, in the same afternoon, unpacks a vendor release tarball to read its manifest. He reaches for compression and finds gzip exported from both `core.archive` and `core.compress`. He cannot tell which is the real one, imports both to be safe, and ends up with two spellings of the same call in one file.

options.name: Split by job: compress owns codecs, archive owns containers
options.detail: `core.compress` owns stream codecs (gzip, zstd, and future additions). `core.archive` owns container formats (zip, tar). A compressed tarball composes the two: archive builds the tar, compress gzips the stream. archive's standalone gzip helpers move to core.compress as a clean break, so gzip has exactly one home. Each name states its real job, and a reader always knows which import to reach for.

options.name: Merge: archive absorbs the codecs, compress dies
options.detail: `core.archive` absorbs gzip and zstd; `core.compress` leaves the language. Everything compression-related lives behind one import. The cost is a lie in the name: `core.archive.zstd` labels a codec that never archives anything. The module name stops describing its members, and the codec-vs-container distinction disappears from the API.

comparisons.note: Python keeps them separate for exactly this reason: `gzip`/`zlib`/`lzma` are stream codecs, `zipfile`/`tarfile` are containers. The split maps to how the two jobs actually differ, and tar.gz composes tarfile with a gzip stream.
comparisons.code:
import gzip, tarfile
data = gzip.compress(log_bytes)
tf = tarfile.open('release.tar')

comparisons.note: Rust's ecosystem splits the same way: `flate2`/`zstd` are stream codecs, `tar`/`zip` are container crates, and a tar.gz is a tar writer wrapped in a gzip encoder. Option A mirrors this composition.

recommendation.why: Splitting by job mirrors the ratified one-adapter-identity shape (D-ENCSTREAM1) and keeps every name truthful: codecs live where the name says codec, containers where it says archive. A reader always knows which module is canonical, and tar.gz composes cleanly instead of one module owning two unrelated jobs.
recommendation.tradeoff: A compressed tarball now touches two modules, archive to pack and compress to gzip. That composition is the accurate model: it names each step for what it is, so nothing hides a codec under an archive label or an archive under a codec one.

whyNot.reason: Puts a codec under a name that lies about it: `core.archive.zstd` never archives anything. It erases the codec-vs-container distinction from the surface and keeps one module owning two different jobs, against the truthful-naming and one-job goals.

hybrid.synthesis: Split by job (A), keeping B's one virtue, discoverability, through clean composition rather than a merged module. tar.gz is written as compress-over-archive, so both jobs stay reachable and each name still tells the truth about its members.

harvest.aspect: Truthful split: codecs in compress, containers in archive
harvest.use: The canonical shape; gzip gets one home and each module name matches its members.

harvest.aspect: One obvious place to find compression
harvest.use: Answered by composition: core.compress is the single home for codecs, and tar.gz is compress applied over an archive, so nothing is scattered.

decisions.title: Inline foreign code: a fourth FFI tier with the Jet signature as the checked contract
decisions.gist: Let a Jet file carry a small foreign function body inline, type-checked against a Jet signature.
decisions.lesson:
D-FFI-UNIFY1 gives every foreign language three tiers. Script tier binds a foreign file (`use "raylib.h" as rl`). Project tier pins a dependency (`use py.h5 as h5`). Overlay tier corrects generated bindings. All three bind code that lives in another file.

Nothing covers ten lines of foreign code that belong inside one Jet file — a checksum kernel, one intrinsic, one tricky syscall wrapper. Today you create a separate header or dependency for it. Other languages solve this with inline blocks: Rust has `asm!`, C++ has `asm`, Zig has inline assembly and C import. None type-check the boundary as a real signature.
decisions.story: Walter ports a hash function whose reference implementation is 12 lines of C. The algorithm is stable; wrapping it as a whole vendored library is absurd. He wants those 12 lines next to the Jet code that calls them, with the call boundary checked like any Jet function.

options.name: `#Foreign(<lang>)` fn — one directive shape for every language
options.detail:
A fourth D-FFI-UNIFY1 tier. The declaration is an ordinary Jet `fn` signature; the body is one multi-line string of foreign source. Sema checks every call site against the Jet signature. The language's existing binder compiles the body on cache miss and generates the same safe marshaling as the script tier.

A body/signature mismatch is a Jet diagnostic naming both sides — no foreign compiler error reaches the user unlaundered (I2). Effects declare like any extern; unsafe-language bodies (c, cpp, asm) additionally require the enclosing `#Unsafe("reason")` gate (S58). One shape, reused by every current and future language.

options.name: No inline tier — script tier is enough
options.detail:
Keep the ratified three tiers. Small foreign snippets live in a sibling file bound by the script tier (`use "./crc32.h" as c`). The surface stays smaller and every foreign line stays in a file its own toolchain can open directly.

The cost: the ten-line case keeps real friction — a second file, a header/source split for C, and pkg wiring for anything the script tier can't bind. The friction pushes people toward vendoring or toward not using the best tool.

options.name: Typed-text values — foreign code as a checked string type
options.detail: Reuse D-TYPEDTEXT1: a string literal in a `C`/`Py` typed position becomes a checked foreign-code value, compiled and invoked through a Core call. Symmetry with `Sql`/`Html` is elegant. But code-as-value blurs the boundary: the signature lives in a turbofish, call sites read like dynamic strings, and the `#Unsafe` audit gate has no natural declaration to attach to.
options.code:
kernel: C<fn([U8], U32) -> U32> :: """
  uint32_t crc32(const uint8_t* d, size_t n, uint32_t s) { … }
"""
sum :: kernel.call(bytes, 0)?

comparisons.note: Zig's `@cImport` binds headers (Jet's script tier already matches it). Zig still has no inline foreign bodies except asm.
Rust inline is asm-only and the operand contract is spelled in strings, not a function signature. cc/cxx crates need build scripts for anything more.
comparisons.code: unsafe { asm!("rdtsc", out("rax") lo, out("rdx") hi); }

recommendation.why: The signature-as-contract shape is what makes Jet's FFI safer than every host language: sema owns the boundary, binders own the body, and the same spelling scales from asm to Python. It completes D-FFI-UNIFY1 with one rule instead of per-language hacks.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the highest-frequency FFI case (a few lines) with the highest ceremony, which is backwards for a language selling ergonomic interop.
Code-as-value hides the declaration: no natural home for the #Unsafe gate, effects, or docs, and call sites stop looking like ordinary Jet calls.

recommendation.tradeoff: Foreign bodies inside .jet files get editor support only through injected-language regions; the binder cache must rebuild the snippet when the body string changes.

hybrid.synthesis: A absorbs B's discipline: bodies compile through the same binder and cache as script-tier files. It also keeps C's checked boundary — the check just lives on a real fn declaration.

harvest.aspect: one directive shape, signature as contract
harvest.use: adopted

harvest.aspect: binder + cache reuse, no second compilation path
harvest.use: A compiles inline bodies through the exact script-tier binder machinery
A keeps the check, attached to the fn signature where audit gates and effects already live

decisions.title: Inline assembly: the `asm` instance of the inline tier, gated by #Unsafe
decisions.gist: Give experts real inline assembly with typed operands, behind the existing #Unsafe gate.
decisions.lesson:
Master-of-ALL bottoms out in assembly: cycle counters, cache-line tricks, crypto with constant-time guarantees, kernel entry stubs, intrinsics the SIMD lane types (D-SIMD1) don't cover. Jet has no asm story today — the expert hits a wall and reaches for C or Rust.

The low-level tier already has the right gates: `use core.mem` for discovery, `#Unsafe("reason")` for audit (S58). Rust lowers inline asm through `asm!`, which rustc verifies per target — Jet's generated-Rust backend can reuse that verification while keeping the user-facing surface and diagnostics Jet-owned (I2).
decisions.story: Dale profiles a hot loop and needs the CPU's cycle counter, not wall-clock time. `core.time` has no such call. In Rust he would write three lines of `asm!`. In Jet today his only path is an FFI round-trip through a C file for one instruction.
decisions.inWild:
use core.mem

#Unsafe("cycle counter — no Core surface exists")
#Foreign(asm) fn rdtsc() -> U64 {
    """
    rdtsc
    shl rdx, 32
    or  rax, rdx        ; -> return
    """
}

start :: rdtsc()
hot_loop()
print("cycles: {rdtsc() - start}")

options.name: `#Foreign(asm)` — asm is a language in the inline tier
options.detail:
Assembly reuses D-FFI-INLINE1's shape exactly: a Jet `fn` signature is the operand contract — parameters map to input registers, the return value to outputs, per a small documented convention with named `; -> return` anchors. Requires `use core.mem` plus an enclosing `#Unsafe("reason")`. Bodies are per-target; the existing `comptime if build.os ==` and `#Target` machinery select variants.

Lowering emits Rust `asm!`, so rustc verifies register/clobber facts per target while every user-facing error stays a Jet diagnostic naming the Jet span (I2). No new sigil, no new block form — the inline tier absorbs asm as just another language.

options.name: Intrinsics library only — no user-visible asm
options.detail:
Instead of asm syntax, `core.mem.intrinsics` grows curated functions (cycle counters, prefetch, CAS variants, crc32 hardware ops), each internally implemented with vetted asm. Beginners never see assembly; every operation is named, documented, and effect-tagged.

The ceiling is real: an expert who needs an instruction Core hasn't wrapped is stuck writing C again. The library also chases every new ISA extension forever, always behind.
options.code:
use core.mem

start :: mem.intrinsics.cycle_count()
hot_loop()
print("cycles: {mem.intrinsics.cycle_count() - start}")

// need CLDEMOTE? not wrapped yet — back to C FFI

comparisons.note: `asm!` is string templates with operand constraints spelled inline; powerful, but the contract is not a function signature and beginners meet it in library code.
Zig treats asm as an expression with typed outputs — closest to option A's spirit; Jet goes further by making the whole fn signature the contract.

recommendation.why: A removes the last wall between an expert and the machine while staying inside gates that already exist. The signature-as-contract convention makes Jet asm more checkable than C's or Rust's, and rustc's verifier rides underneath for free.

whyNot.reason: A curated library is a ceiling, not a floor — the expert one instruction past the catalog falls back to C, which is the outcome this ballot exists to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: Per-target bodies are the user's responsibility; a program using #Foreign(asm) gives up target portability for those functions and must gate variants explicitly.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A as the floor and let B grow on top. `core.mem.intrinsics` wraps popular cases as ordinary functions implemented with the same #Foreign(asm) mechanism. Beginners meet named functions; the expert path never hits a ceiling.

harvest.use: adopted as the mechanism

harvest.aspect: curated named intrinsics for the common cases
harvest.use: grows in Core on top of A; beginners meet only the named functions

decisions.title: Go host model — `go.*` binder
decisions.gist: How Go libraries run when you call `go.*` from Jet — Go's runtime in-process, or in a separate worker.
decisions.lesson:
Jargon. A binder is the tool that turns a foreign library into typed Jet functions. cgo is Go's official bridge for calling Go from C. c-archive is a Go build mode that produces a static library with C entry points.

A goroutine is Go's lightweight thread. Go has a garbage collector (GC) that frees memory automatically; Jet uses ownership instead. A sidecar is a separate helper process. Handle pinning tells Go's GC not to move or free an object Jet still holds.

An effect like `#(Go)` is a tag on a function's type recording that it can block on Go's runtime; the compiler tracks it up the call chain.
decisions.story: Walter Briggs runs a backup service. He needs MinIO's Go client for S3-compatible object storage — the mature, battle-tested one. He types `use go.minio as s3` and expects typed upload calls, not a rewrite of a cloud SDK in Jet.
decisions.inWild:
use go.minio as s3

client :: s3.new("play.min.io", key, secret)?
client.put_object(bucket: "backups", name: "2026-07.tar", data: bytes)?  #(Go, IO)

options.name: c-archive static shims (in-process)
options.detail: The binder runs `go build -buildmode=c-archive` and links the archive into your program. Go's runtime rides in-process. Blocking Go calls carry a `#(Go)` effect so the compiler tracks them. Handle pinning lets Go's GC and Jet ownership coexist; goroutines are bounded by call-scoped contexts.

options.name: Sidecar worker process
options.detail: Go runs in a separate worker; Jet talks to it over a typed message boundary. A Go panic crashes only the worker, not your program. But every call and every array copies across the process boundary, and Go's real draw is its library estate, not runtime isolation.

comparisons.note: cgo's `-buildmode=c-archive` is Go's own supported way to expose Go to a C ABI. It emits a static library with C entry points and is proven at scale.
comparisons.code:
$ go build -buildmode=c-archive -o libminio.a ./minio
# emits libminio.a + libminio.h with C entry points

comparisons.note: Go's `gomobile bind` wraps a package as an Android AAR or iOS framework using the same c-archive machinery. Millions of shipped apps embed Go's runtime in-process this way.
comparisons.code: $ gomobile bind -target=ios ./mypkg   # Go runtime rides in-process, in production apps

recommendation.why: Go's value to a Jet user is its libraries — MinIO, Kubernetes clients, cloud SDKs — not runtime isolation. c-archive links that estate in-process with the least overhead and no per-call copy.
recommendation.tradeoff: In-process means a Go runtime bug shares your address space. Handle pinning and call-scoped goroutine contexts contain that coexistence. A panic is still laundered to a typed Jet error.

whyNot.reason: Sidecar buys crash isolation Go rarely needs and taxes every call and array with a process-boundary copy — the opposite of why anyone reaches for Go's fast libraries.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship c-archive in-process as the one host model. Keep the sidecar as a future opt-in switch, exactly like `py@embed` inverts Python's default — same call sites, one flag, no new surface.

harvest.use: The default host: links Go's library estate with no per-call copy, effects tracking blocking calls.
Reserved as an opt-in `go@worker` tier for the rare case that wants a crashy Go library fenced off.

decisions.title: JVM host model — `java.*` binder (Kotlin, Scala ride along)
decisions.gist: How the JVM runs when you call `java.*` from Jet — embedded in-process, or in a separate worker.
decisions.lesson:
Jargon. The JVM is the Java Virtual Machine — the runtime that executes Java, Kotlin, and Scala, which all compile to the same bytecode. So one `java.*` binder reaches all three.

JNI is Java's Native Interface, the official bridge between the JVM and native code. Its invocation API lets native code create and drive a JVM in the same process. An opaque handle is a Jet reference to a Java object whose fields Jet never touches directly.

A checked exception is a Java error the compiler forces you to handle. Zero-copy means passing an array without duplicating its bytes. jetpack is Jet's package manager; it provisions the JVM so it never enters the compiler's own sources (I6).
decisions.story: Priscilla Hoffman maintains an invoicing tool. She needs Apache PDFBox — the reference Java library for reading PDF forms — and there is no equal elsewhere. She types `use java.pdfbox as pdf` and wants `doc.text()` to just work.
decisions.inWild:
use java.pdfbox as pdf

doc :: pdf.load(files.read_bytes("form.pdf")?)?  #(Jvm)
print(doc.text())

options.name: Embedded JVM in-process (JNI invocation API)
options.detail: The JVM starts in-process on the first `java.*` call, created lazily by the JNI invocation API. Java classes become opaque handles; checked exceptions become `T ? JavaError` at the call site. jetpack provisions the JVM — it never enters the compiler's sources (I6).

options.name: Sidecar JVM worker
options.detail: The JVM runs in a separate worker over a typed message boundary, like Python's default. A JVM crash or memory blowup stays fenced off. But each call pays a message round-trip, and arrays copy across the boundary — no zero-copy for the data workloads that justify the JVM.

comparisons.note: Py4J connects Python to a JVM over a socket — the sidecar model. It is why calling heavy JVM libraries from Python is slow: every object and array crosses a socket.
comparisons.code:
# Py4J: JVM in a separate process, socket boundary
gateway = JavaGateway()                     # socket to a running JVM
arr = gateway.jvm.java.util.ArrayList()     # each op = a socket round-trip

comparisons.note: GraalVM runs multiple languages in one process with shared memory, proving in-process polyglot embedding is mature and fast. Jet's JNI-embed host targets the same in-process, zero-copy goal.

recommendation.why: Embedding a JVM in-process is mature and standard, and zero-copy array passing is exactly what the numeric and data libraries — the reason to reach for the JVM — depend on.
recommendation.tradeoff: An embedded JVM shares your address space and its GC pauses affect the whole program. The sidecar stays available as a future opt-in when a project wants that library fenced off.

whyNot.reason: Sidecar copies every array across a process boundary. That kills the zero-copy path the JVM's data libraries exist to provide, and isolation is the rarer need.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the embedded JVM as the one host model. Keep the sidecar as an opt-in `java@worker` tier, mirroring Python's `py@embed` inversion — one surface, one flag, call sites unchanged.

harvest.use: Default: in-process JVM, zero-copy arrays, checked exceptions mapped to `T ? JavaError`.
Opt-in `java@worker` tier for fencing off a memory-hungry or crash-prone JVM library.

decisions.title: .NET host model — `cs.*` binder (C#, F# ride along)
decisions.gist: How the .NET runtime runs when you call `cs.*` from Jet — embedded in-process, or in a separate worker.
decisions.lesson:
Jargon. .NET is Microsoft's runtime; C# and F# both compile to it, so one `cs.*` binder reaches both. An assembly is a compiled .NET library file (a `.dll`).

hostfxr and hostpolicy are .NET's official hosting APIs — the supported way for a native program to load and run the .NET runtime in-process. A Task is .NET's unit of async work, like a future.

NuGet is .NET's package registry. jetpack resolves NuGet packages as a provider, fetches them into the hangar, and hash-pins them — the runtime never enters the compiler's sources (I6).
decisions.story: Raymond Callahan automates finance reports. He needs ClosedXML — the go-to .NET library for writing real Excel spreadsheets with formulas and styles — and wants `sheet.cell(...)` calls, not an Excel-format rewrite. He types `use cs.closedxml as xl`.
decisions.inWild:
use cs.closedxml as xl

book :: xl.workbook()
sheet :: book.add_sheet("Q3")
sheet.cell("A1").value = "Revenue"
book.save("q3.xlsx")?  #(Dotnet)

options.name: hostfxr/hostpolicy embed (in-process)
options.detail: The .NET runtime loads in-process through hostfxr — Microsoft's first-party hosting API. .NET classes become opaque handles; a .NET async `Task` bridges to a Jet task at the boundary. jetpack's NuGet provider resolves and hash-pins assemblies.

options.name: Sidecar dotnet worker
options.detail: The runtime runs in a separate worker over a typed message boundary. A .NET crash stays contained. But every call round-trips through the boundary and spreadsheet data copies across it, and .NET async loses its natural in-process bridge to Jet tasks.

comparisons.note: hostfxr is the API Microsoft's own tools use to launch .NET — the documented, supported path to embed the runtime in a native process. Building on it means no unofficial hosting hacks.
Python.NET embeds the CLR inside the Python process so `import clr` calls run in-process with no worker. It proves in-process .NET embedding is stable, and it is why those calls are fast.
comparisons.code:
import clr                       # CLR loaded in-process
clr.AddReference("ClosedXML")    # direct in-process calls, no subprocess
from ClosedXML.Excel import XLWorkbook

recommendation.why: hostfxr is Microsoft's supported in-process hosting API, and the in-process bridge lets .NET's `Task` async map cleanly onto Jet tasks — the same reasoning as the JVM binder.
recommendation.tradeoff: The in-process runtime shares your address space and adds .NET's GC to the picture. A sidecar stays available as a future opt-in for fencing off a suspect assembly.

whyNot.reason: A worker copies spreadsheet data across a process boundary every call and severs the clean async bridge between .NET Tasks and Jet tasks. Isolation is the rarer need.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship hostfxr embed as the one host model. Keep the sidecar as an opt-in `cs@worker` tier, matching the JVM and Python pattern — one surface, one flag, call sites unchanged.

harvest.use: Default: in-process CLR, .NET Tasks bridged to Jet tasks, NuGet assemblies via jetpack.
Opt-in `cs@worker` tier to fence off a crash-prone or untrusted .NET assembly.

decisions.title: Fortran binder — dedicated `fortran.*` root or C-wrap
decisions.gist: Whether Fortran gets its own `fortran.*` binder root, or users hand-wrap it through the existing C binder.
decisions.lesson:
Jargon. Fortran is the classic scientific-computing language; BLAS and LAPACK — the linear-algebra libraries under nearly all numerical software — are written in it.

ISO_C_BINDING is Fortran's standard feature for exposing routines to C. `BIND(C)` marks a routine as callable across that C interface. gfortran is the GNU Fortran compiler.

Column-major and row-major describe array memory order: Fortran stores columns first, most other languages store rows first. Getting the order wrong silently transposes a matrix. A `Tensor<T>` is Jet's typed multi-dimensional array.
decisions.story: Marjorie Vance writes climate models. She needs LAPACK to solve linear systems — the fifty-year-old reference implementation everything else wraps — and does not want to hand-write C glue for every routine. She types `use fortran.lapack as la`.

options.name: ISO_C_BINDING bridge (dedicated `fortran.*` root)
options.detail: The binder drives gfortran to emit `BIND(C)` interfaces, then generates typed Jet wrappers over them. Arrays cross as `[T]` or `Tensor<T>`. The binding records each routine's column-major order as a checked fact — a mismatched order is a diagnostic, never a silent transpose.

options.name: No dedicated root — hand-wrap through the C binder
options.detail: No `fortran.*` root. Users write a Fortran routine with `BIND(C)` by hand, then bind the resulting C header through the shipped `c.*` binder. It works, but every routine needs hand-written glue and the column-major order is on the user to get right.

comparisons.note: f2py is how SciPy wraps Fortran BLAS/LAPACK into Python. It auto-generates the C bridge and handles array order — proving a dedicated Fortran binder is the standard, not hand-glue.
comparisons.code:
$ f2py -c dgesv.f -m lapack   # auto-generates the C bridge + array marshaling
>>> import lapack; lapack.dgesv(a, b)   # order handled by the wrapper

comparisons.note: NumPy carries an explicit `order='F'` flag because Fortran-order bugs are a known, costly trap. Recording layout as a checked fact turns that runtime footgun into a compile error.
comparisons.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1,2],[3,4]], order='F')   # 'F' = Fortran/column-major, opt-in
# forget order='F' before a LAPACK call and results are silently wrong

recommendation.why: A first-class Fortran root unlocks BLAS, LAPACK, and decades of scientific code with typed calls and a checked layout fact — the replacement story the north star needs.
recommendation.tradeoff: A `fortran.*` root is one more binder to carry. It earns its place: it turns the column-major transpose footgun — silent in every hand-wrapped path — into a compile error.

whyNot.reason: Hand-wrapping forces the exact per-routine C glue and manual column-major bookkeeping that D-FFI-UNIFY1 exists to abolish, and leaves transpose bugs silent at runtime.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the `fortran.*` root with layout facts as law. The C-wrap path still exists for any exotic routine the binder cannot yet project — but it is the fallback, not the expected workflow.

harvest.use: The default: typed Fortran calls, arrays as `[T]`/`Tensor<T>`, column-major mismatch caught at compile.
Remains available via the shipped `c.*` binder for a one-off routine outside the Fortran binder's projection.

decisions.title: Lua host model — in-process VM vs sidecar worker
decisions.gist: Decide how Lua runs when a Jet program calls `lua.*`. Option A runs Lua inside the Jet binary. Option B runs it as a separate supervised process, matching the Python precedent.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. A **VM** (virtual machine) is the small engine that executes Lua code. **In-process** means that engine lives inside your Jet binary and shares its memory. A **sidecar worker** means Lua runs as a separate operating-system process, and Jet talks to it over a typed channel.

An **effect root** is a tag like `#(Lua)` the compiler stamps on any function that touches Lua, so a caller sees the dependency in the type. A **table** is Lua's one data structure, a key/value map; `[K: V]` is Jet's map type.

Lua was built to be embedded. Its whole reason to exist is being a tiny engine you drop inside a host program.
decisions.story: Marcus Bell ships a tower-defense game written in Jet. The engine core is Jet, but he wants designers to tune enemy waves without a full rebuild, so wave logic lives in small Lua scripts beside `core.game`. On a busy wave the loop spawns hundreds of enemies per frame, and every spawn reads a value the Lua script produced.

options.name: In-process VM — Lua lives inside the Jet binary
options.detail: The Lua VM is embedded in your program. Lua tables become zero-copy `[K: V]` views, so reading `e["pos"]` hundreds of times a frame costs no serialization. Every Lua call carries the `#(Lua)` effect. No extra process, no channel, no copy on the hot path.
options.code:
use lua.waves as w

spawns :: w.tick(0.016)     // [Str: Dyn] view straight over the Lua table
core.game.spawn(spawns[0]["kind"], at: spawns[0]["pos"])
// reads hit the Lua table in place — no copy, no IPC

options.name: Sidecar worker — Lua runs as a separate process
options.detail: Lua runs in its own process behind a typed message boundary, exactly like Python (D-FFI-PY1). Uniform with `py.*`, crash-isolated. But every table crossing the boundary is serialized and copied, and the per-frame call now blocks on IPC. That forfeits the one property Lua was designed for.

comparisons.note: Redis embeds a Lua VM directly in the server so `EVAL` scripts run atomically next to the data, with no cross-process hop. That in-process choice is why Lua scripting in Redis is fast enough to run on the request path.
comparisons.code:
> EVAL "return redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])" 1 counter
// Lua runs inside the redis-server process, no IPC

comparisons.note: OpenResty embeds LuaJIT inside each Nginx worker so request handlers run in-process. Every high-throughput Lua host embeds the VM; none of them shell out to a Lua daemon per call.
comparisons.code:
location /hi { content_by_lua_block { ngx.say("hi") } }
// Lua handler runs inside the nginx worker

recommendation.why: Lua exists to be embedded. In-process is what makes zero-copy table views and per-frame calls viable, which is the reason a beginner reaches for Lua scripting in the first place. The `#(Lua)` effect keeps the dependency honest without a process boundary.
recommendation.tradeoff: You give up crash isolation: a bug in a Lua script can fault the host process. Lua's tiny, well-contained VM makes that risk small, and the expert `@embed`-style escape stays available for the rare script that needs a wall.

whyNot.reason: A sidecar copies and serializes every table across a process wall, so the per-frame call that motivates Lua scripting becomes an IPC round-trip. Uniformity with `py.*` is not worth forfeiting the embedding property Lua is chosen for.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship in-process as the default so the beginner gets fast zero-copy tables with no ceremony. Keep a supervised out-of-process mode as an explicit opt-in for scripts a team wants walled off, reusing the same `lua.*` surface so call sites never move.

harvest.use: The default host: embedded VM, `[K: V]` table views, `#(Lua)` effect on every call.
Offered as an opt-in tier (same `use lua.X` surface) for untrusted or crash-prone scripts that need a wall.

decisions.title: Ruby host model — sidecar worker vs in-process embed
decisions.gist: Decide how Ruby runs when a Jet program calls `ruby.*`. Option A runs Ruby as a separate supervised process, matching the Python precedent. Option B embeds libruby inside the Jet binary.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. **In-process embed** means the Ruby interpreter (libruby) runs inside your Jet binary and shares its memory. A **sidecar worker** means Ruby runs as a separate operating-system process that Jet talks to over a typed channel.

The **GVL** (Global VM Lock) is a lock inside Ruby that lets only one thread run Ruby code at a time. Ruby also keeps large **global interpreter state**, so two Rubies in one process fight over it. A **gem** is a Ruby library; **RubyGems** is its registry.

A **provider** is a jetpack backend that resolves and fetches packages from a foreign registry (D-JPK-EXTPROV1).
decisions.story: Dana Whitfield runs a Jet web service that renders user-authored email templates. A mature Ruby gem, Liquid, already does safe templating well, and rewriting it is not on the roadmap. She wants to call Liquid from a request handler and get a rendered string back, without a Ruby bug taking down the service.
decisions.inWild:
Reusing the Liquid gem from a Jet request handler:

```jet
use ruby.liquid as liquid       // pinned in pkg.jet: liquid: ruby@"5.5"

render :: fn(tpl: Str, ctx: [Str: Str]) -> Str ? RubyError #(Ruby) {
    liquid.Template.parse(tpl)?.render(ctx)?
}
```

options.name: Sidecar worker — Ruby runs as a separate process
options.detail: Ruby runs in its own supervised process behind a typed message boundary, exactly like Python (D-FFI-PY1). A Ruby crash or segfault cannot take the Jet service down; it restarts the worker. The `#(Ruby)` effect marks every call. RubyGems becomes a jetpack provider for `liquid: ruby@"5.5"`.

options.name: In-process embed — libruby inside the Jet binary
options.detail: Embed libruby directly. Avoids the per-call process hop, but Ruby's GVL serializes all Ruby work onto one thread, and its large global interpreter state makes multiple isolated Rubies in one process hostile. A gem crash faults the whole host.

comparisons.note: Teams that need one gem from another language shell out to a `ruby -e` subprocess and parse stdout. That is an untyped, unsupervised sidecar. The `ruby.*` worker is the same isolation with a typed boundary and laundered errors.
comparisons.code:
$ ruby -e 'require "liquid"; print Liquid::Template.parse($stdin.read).render'
// ad-hoc process + stdout parsing — what the worker replaces

recommendation.why: Ruby's GVL and heavy global state make a clean in-process embed hostile, and the sidecar matches the ratified Python host model (D-FFI-PY1) for a uniform mental model. Crash isolation protects the Jet service from a gem fault.
recommendation.tradeoff: Each call crosses a process boundary, so a value returned from a gem is serialized and copied. For template rendering and typical gem reuse that cost is negligible next to the work done inside Ruby.

whyNot.reason: Embedding libruby inherits the GVL bottleneck and shared global state, so it cannot run isolated Rubies well, and a gem segfault faults the whole host. The saved process hop does not justify losing crash isolation and the py-uniform model.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the supervised sidecar as the sole default, identical in shape to the Python host, so a beginner reuses a gem safely with no ceremony. RubyGems rides in as a jetpack provider. No embed tier until a real project proves it needs one.

harvest.use: The default host: typed message boundary, `#(Ruby)` effect, crash isolation, `liquid: ruby@"…"` resolution.
Deferred; revisit only if a project needs shared-memory zero-copy and can tolerate the GVL, offered later on the same `use ruby.X` surface.

decisions.title: Perl host model — sidecar worker vs in-process embed
decisions.gist: Decide how Perl runs when a Jet program calls `perl.*`. Option A runs Perl as a separate supervised process, matching the Python precedent. Option B embeds libperl inside the Jet binary.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. **In-process embed** means the Perl interpreter (libperl) runs inside your Jet binary and shares its memory. A **sidecar worker** means Perl runs as a separate operating-system process Jet talks to over a typed channel.

A Perl interpreter keeps large **global state**; running several isolated interpreters in one process (its multiplicity model) is fragile and rarely used. **CPAN** is Perl's package registry, decades deep in sysadmin and bioinformatics modules.

A **provider** is a jetpack backend that resolves and fetches packages from a foreign registry (D-JPK-EXTPROV1). A **module** here is a Perl library.
decisions.story: Ray Holloway maintains a genomics pipeline. A trusted CPAN module, Bio::SeqIO, already parses the sequence formats his lab uses, and it has been correct for fifteen years. He wants to call it from a new Jet pipeline stage and get typed records back, without porting the parser or wrapping it in a brittle shell script.
decisions.inWild:
Calling a CPAN bioinformatics module from a Jet pipeline stage:

```jet
use perl."Bio::SeqIO" as seqio     // pinned in pkg.jet: "Bio::SeqIO": perl@"1.7"

records :: fn(path: Str) -> [SeqRecord] ? PerlError #(Perl) {
    seqio.read_fasta(path)?           // returns typed records across the boundary
}
```

options.name: Sidecar worker — Perl runs as a separate process
options.detail: Perl runs in its own supervised process behind a typed message boundary, like Python (D-FFI-PY1). A decades-old CPAN module runs unmodified; a crash in it restarts the worker, not the pipeline. The `#(Perl)` effect marks every call. CPAN becomes a jetpack provider for `"Bio::SeqIO": perl@"1.7"`.

options.name: In-process embed — libperl inside the Jet binary
options.detail: Embed libperl directly. Avoids the per-call hop, but a Perl interpreter's global state makes multiple isolated interpreters in one process fragile, and a module crash faults the whole host. The estate this targets is legacy scripts, which value isolation over shared memory.

comparisons.note: Sysadmin and bioinformatics shops hold enormous, correct Perl estates they cannot afford to rewrite. Today they invoke those scripts through `system()` or a bare subprocess. The `perl.*` worker keeps them callable as-is, with a typed boundary and laundered errors.
comparisons.code:
$ perl -MBio::SeqIO -e '...' < reads.fa   // today: ad-hoc subprocess
// worker: use perl."Bio::SeqIO"; typed records, supervised

recommendation.why: The value here is a huge legacy CPAN estate callable without a rewrite, and the sidecar keeps those scripts running as-is with crash isolation. It matches the ratified Python host (D-FFI-PY1) for one uniform model across scripting languages.
recommendation.tradeoff: Each call crosses a process boundary and copies its result. For pipeline stages that call a module once per file, or per batch, that overhead disappears against the work Perl does inside.

whyNot.reason: Embedding libperl inherits fragile interpreter multiplicity and shared global state, and a legacy module fault would take the host down. Legacy estates value isolation, so the saved hop does not justify losing it or the py-uniform model.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the supervised sidecar as the sole default, shaped like the Python host, so a legacy CPAN module is callable with no rewrite and no ceremony. CPAN rides in as a jetpack provider. No embed tier until a concrete project proves the need.

harvest.use: The default host: typed boundary, `#(Perl)` effect, crash isolation, `"Bio::SeqIO": perl@"…"` resolution.
Deferred; revisit only if a project needs shared-memory Perl and can accept the multiplicity risk, later on the same `use perl.X` surface.

decisions.title: PHP host model — sidecar worker pool vs embed SAPI
decisions.gist: Decide how PHP runs when a Jet program calls `php.*`. Option A runs a supervised pool of PHP worker processes, in the spirit of PHP-FPM. Option B embeds PHP in-process via its embed SAPI.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. **In-process embed** means the PHP engine runs inside your Jet binary through the **embed SAPI** (Server API — PHP's pluggable host interface). A **sidecar worker** means PHP runs as a separate operating-system process Jet talks to over a typed channel.

**PHP-FPM** (FastCGI Process Manager) is PHP's standard production host: a supervised pool of worker processes, one request per worker at a time, recycled after use. A **pool** lets many requests run concurrently across workers.

**Packagist** is PHP's package registry (used via Composer). A **provider** is a jetpack backend that resolves and fetches from a foreign registry (D-JPK-EXTPROV1).
decisions.story: Priya Nair is porting a PHP monolith to a new Jet server one endpoint at a time. The order-pricing logic is thousands of lines of battle-tested PHP she will migrate last. Until then, the new Jet endpoints must call the existing PHP pricing code and get typed results, while serving many requests at once.
decisions.inWild:
New Jet server calling existing PHP domain logic during a piecewise migration:

```jet
use php."app/Pricing" as pricing    // pinned in pkg.jet: "app/Pricing": php@"local"

quote :: fn(cart: Cart) -> Money ? PhpError #(Php) {
    pricing.price_cart(cart)?          // runs in a pooled PHP worker
}
```

options.name: Sidecar worker pool — PHP-FPM-style process pool
options.detail: PHP runs in a supervised pool of worker processes, the model every PHP shop already runs in production. Many Jet requests price carts concurrently across workers; a fatal PHP error recycles one worker, not the server. The `#(Php)` effect marks every call. Packagist becomes a jetpack provider.

options.name: In-process embed — PHP embed SAPI in the Jet binary
options.detail: Embed PHP through its embed SAPI. Avoids the process hop, but PHP's request-scoped global lifecycle assumes one request per interpreter, so concurrency inside one process is awkward, and a fatal PHP error faults the whole server. It fights the FPM model PHP shops already trust.

comparisons.note: Essentially every production PHP deployment uses FPM: a supervised worker pool, one request per worker, recycled on fault. Matching that model makes the `php.*` host behave the way PHP operators already expect and tune.
comparisons.code:
; php-fpm.conf
pm = dynamic
pm.max_children = 32   // the pooled-worker model the sidecar mirrors

recommendation.why: A worker pool is how PHP already runs in production, so concurrency and fault recovery match operator expectations, and a fatal PHP error recycles one worker instead of the Jet server. It fits the ratified sidecar model from Python (D-FFI-PY1).
recommendation.tradeoff: Calls cross a process boundary and results are copied. For request-scoped domain logic during a migration, that cost is trivial next to the pricing work, and the pool absorbs concurrency the way FPM does.

whyNot.reason: PHP's request-scoped global lifecycle assumes one request per interpreter, so an embedded engine handles concurrency poorly and a fatal error faults the whole server. The saved hop is not worth fighting the FPM model PHP shops rely on.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the supervised FPM-style worker pool as the sole default so migrations call existing PHP concurrently with familiar fault behavior. Packagist rides in as a jetpack provider. No embed tier until a concrete project proves it is needed.

harvest.use: The default host: pooled workers, `#(Php)` effect, per-worker fault recovery, `"app/Pricing": php@"…"` resolution.
Deferred; revisit only for a single-threaded embed use case, later on the same `use php.X` surface.

decisions.title: R binder host model — sidecar R worker vs in-process embed
decisions.gist: The `r.*` root is already reserved (D-DATA-BRIDGE1). This ballot decides only how R runs behind it. Option A runs R as a separate supervised process. Option B embeds libR in-process.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. The `r.*` namespace is already reserved by D-DATA-BRIDGE1; this ballot picks its host, not the name. **In-process embed** means the R engine (libR) runs inside your Jet binary. A **sidecar worker** means R runs as a separate process Jet talks to over a typed channel; **Rserve** is R's established protocol for exactly that.

A **data.frame** is R's table type; **`core.data.Table`** is Jet's, so a round-trip maps columns both ways. **CRAN** is R's package registry. A **glm** is a generalized linear model, a common R fitting routine.

R runs as a single global interpreter with heavy shared state (D-DATA-PLOT1 defines Jet's SVG plot values, which R plots can return into).
decisions.story: Ellen Park, a data scientist, keeps her feature engineering in Jet `core.data` but trusts R's `glm` for the actual model fit. She has a Jet `Table` of loan records and wants to fit a logistic regression in R, then read the coefficients back as typed Jet values, plus the diagnostic plot.
decisions.inWild:
Fitting an R glm on a Jet Table and reading typed coefficients back:

```jet
use r.stats as stats            // CRAN-provided, pinned in pkg.jet
use core.data

fit :: fn(t: core.data.Table) -> [Str: Float] ? RError #(R) {
    model :: stats.glm(t, formula: "default ~ income + age", family: "binomial")?
    model.coefficients()          // typed [Str: Float] back across the boundary
}
```

options.name: Sidecar R worker — Rserve-style separate process
options.detail: R runs in its own supervised process behind a typed message boundary, in the spirit of Rserve. A Jet `core.data.Table` round-trips to an R data.frame and back column-typed. A plot returns as an SVG value compatible with D-DATA-PLOT1. CRAN becomes a jetpack provider. The `#(R)` effect marks every call.
options.code:
use r.stats as stats

m :: stats.glm(table, formula: "y ~ x", family: "binomial")?
coefs :: m.coefficients()   // [Str: Float] — typed round-trip from the data.frame
plot :: m.residual_plot()   // returns an SVG value (D-DATA-PLOT1)

options.name: In-process embed — libR inside the Jet binary
options.detail: Embed libR directly. It avoids the process hop for large frames, but R is a single global interpreter with heavy shared state and is not built for concurrent embedding. A fault in R code takes the host down, so it is fragile next to the isolated worker.

comparisons.note: rpy2 embeds R in-process for Python. It is powerful but famously fragile: R's single global interpreter and shared state cause hard-to-debug crashes and threading limits. The sidecar trades that fragility for isolation.
comparisons.code:
import rpy2.robjects as ro
ro.r('glm(y ~ x, family=binomial)')   // in-process embed — fragile under load

comparisons.note: Rserve runs R as a supervised server other languages connect to over a typed protocol, giving isolation and clean marshaling of frames and results. The `r.*` worker follows this proven shape.
comparisons.code:
// client connects to a supervised R server, ships a data.frame, gets typed results
Rconnection c; c.eval("glm(y ~ x, family=binomial)");

recommendation.why: R is a single global interpreter with heavy shared state, so isolating it in a supervised worker gives clean data.frame round-trips, SVG plots into D-DATA-PLOT1, and crash safety. It matches the ratified Python host model (D-FFI-PY1).
recommendation.tradeoff: A large Table is serialized crossing the boundary. For a model fit, the copy is small next to the fit itself, and the isolation prevents an R fault from crashing a data pipeline mid-run.

whyNot.reason: Embedding libR inherits R's single-global-interpreter fragility and no real concurrent embedding, and an R fault crashes the host — exactly rpy2's well-known pain. The saved copy on large frames does not justify losing isolation.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the Rserve-style supervised worker as the sole default so a data scientist fits an R model on a Jet Table with typed round-trips and safe crashes. CRAN rides in as a jetpack provider, plots return as D-DATA-PLOT1 SVG. No embed tier until proven.

harvest.use: The default host: supervised R, `data.frame ↔ core.data.Table`, SVG plots, `#(R)` effect, CRAN resolution.
Deferred; revisit only for a single-threaded huge-frame case that can accept R's global-state fragility, on the same `use r.X` surface.

decisions.title: Shell as typed text (`Sh`) vs explicit argv-list API
decisions.gist: Decide how a Jet program builds a command line. Option A adds `Sh` as a third typed-text instance beside `Sql` and `Html`, so holes become safe argv items. Option B offers only an explicit argv-list API.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. **Typed text** (D-TYPEDTEXT1) is the ratified mechanism where a string literal in a position expecting `Sql` or `Html` becomes a checked value. Each `{hole}` is a bound parameter (Sql) or an escaped insertion (Html), never raw text. A runtime `String` reaching such a position is error **E0149**.

**argv** is the list of arguments a program receives; a shell splits a command string into argv by whitespace and expands globs like `*`. **Injection** is when attacker data in a string is reparsed as extra commands or arguments.

**Word-splitting** breaks a value on spaces; **glob expansion** turns `*` into filenames. This proposal adds `Sh` as a third typed-text instance: a hole is exactly one argv item, never split or globbed. `Sh.raw` is the sole audited escape; `sh"…"` is the prefix form (D-TYPEDTEXT2).
decisions.story: Tom Ferraro writes a Jet backup tool. It runs `rsync` with a source and destination the user supplies on the command line. A directory called `my backups` or a crafted value like `; rm -rf ~` must never break the command apart or run anything extra. Tom wants to write what looks like a shell line and stay safe.
decisions.inWild:
A user-supplied path with a space, plus the error when a plain `String` reaches the position:

```jet
use core.process

cmd: Sh :: "rsync -a {src} {dest}"   // src = "my backups"; becomes ONE argv item
core.process.run(cmd)?               // exec's rsync directly — no shell parses src
```

```
error[E0149]: a runtime String cannot be used where `Sh` is expected
  |
5 |     core.process.run(user_input)
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^^ this String was never checked as a command
  = help: write it as a typed literal `sh"rsync -a {src} {dest}"`,
          or wrap an audited raw fragment with `Sh.raw(...)`
```

options.name: `Sh` typed text — third D-TYPEDTEXT1 instance
options.detail: A literal in a `Sh` position becomes a checked command; each `{hole}` is exactly one argv item, never word-split or glob-expanded. `core.process.run` exec's the program directly, so no shell ever parses user data — injection is impossible by construction. Same engine as `Sql`/`Html` (I8). `Sh.raw` is the audited escape.

options.name: Explicit argv-list API only — no typed text
options.detail: No `Sh` type. The only safe call passes a program and an argument list: `process.run("rsync", args: ["-a", src, dest])`. Safe, but verbose, and it reads nothing like a shell line. Beginners paste real shell lines into one string, which then needs a shell to run — reopening the injection path this was meant to close.

comparisons.note: `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True)` with an f-string is the classic injection footgun; the safe form is a list, `run(["rsync", "-a", src])`. Python makes the safe path the ugly one and the footgun the easy one. `Sh` makes the shell-looking path the safe one.
comparisons.code:
subprocess.run(f"rsync -a {src}", shell=True)   # injection if src is hostile
subprocess.run(["rsync", "-a", src])            # safe list form

comparisons.note: `Sh` is the same ratified typed-text engine as `Sql` and `Html` (D-TYPEDTEXT1), just a third instance. Sql holes become bound parameters, Html holes become escaped insertions, Sh holes become single argv items — one mechanism, three safe surfaces (I8).
comparisons.code:
q: Sql :: "select * from t where id = {id}"   // id -> bound parameter
c: Sh  :: "rsync -a {src} {dest}"             // src -> one argv item

recommendation.why: `Sh` makes the shell-looking line the safe line: holes are single argv items, no shell parses user data, so injection is impossible by construction. It reuses the ratified `Sql`/`Html` engine, so it is one mechanism, not a new one (I8).
recommendation.tradeoff: `Sh` only builds an argv vector, so genuine shell features (pipes, glob, redirection) need explicit APIs or an audited `Sh.raw`. That is the point: the easy path stays safe, and reaching for shell semantics is a visible, audited choice.

whyNot.reason: An argv-list-only API is safe but reads nothing like a command. Beginners fall back to pasting shell lines into a string that needs a shell to run, reopening the exact injection path. It leaves the footgun as the natural default.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship `Sh` typed text as the default safe surface for building commands, and keep the explicit argv-list form as the lower-level primitive `Sh` elaborates into. Beginners write the shell-looking literal; experts can drop to the list or `Sh.raw` when they truly need shell semantics.

harvest.use: The default: `Sh` literal, holes as argv items, E0149 on unchecked String, `Sh.raw` audited escape, `sh"…"` prefix.
Kept as the primitive `Sh` lowers to and the expert entrypoint for programmatic argument building, not the beginner-facing default.

decisions.title: Live queries: effect-tracked server functions with automatic subscription invalidation
decisions.gist: A pure Db.Read server function becomes a live query: clients subscribe, and committed transactions that touch its data push fresh results automatically.
decisions.lesson:
Convex made backends feel magic with one loop. Server queries are deterministic and their database reads are tracked. So the platform knows exactly which client results a write changed, and pushes updates. Nobody writes cache invalidation or websocket plumbing, and no UI goes stale.

Jet already owns every ingredient as ratified law. Effect rows prove a function only reads the database (D-EFF1, D-EFFTREE1). `@Pure` proves determinism (S60). `#Transact` is the write boundary (D-TXN1-4). `core.reactive` gives Signals (D-REACT1). The app graph is sema-known (D-WEBAPP1) and `core.ws` is the push channel (D-WS1=B). This ballot decides whether Jet wires them into a language-level live-query loop.
decisions.story: Frank builds a support dashboard. Ticket lists must update the moment a teammate closes one. Today he writes websocket handlers, invalidation keys, and refetch logic — and still ships a stale-list bug. In Convex this whole layer does not exist. Frank wants that in Jet, self-hosted, without a platform.

options.name: Compiler-integrated live queries
options.detail:
`app.live(query, args)` accepts only a function whose effect row is inside `Db.Read` and whose body is `@Pure` modulo those reads. Sema records the query's read footprint; the runtime binds it to the argument values. A committed `#Transact` whose write set intersects a live footprint invalidates exactly those subscriptions, re-runs them, and pushes results over `core.ws` into a client `Signal<T>`.

Passing an unqualified function is a compile error naming the offending effect. No invalidation keys exist anywhere. This runs in `jet dev` and any self-hosted server — no platform dependency.
options.code:
tickets :: app.live(open_tickets, team)

$ jet check app.jet   # query does I/O beyond Db.Read
error[E07xx]: `open_tickets` cannot be a live query
  its effect row includes `Net` (http fetch at line 14)
  a live query may only read the database — move the fetch to an action

options.name: Library subscriptions with manual invalidation keys
options.detail:
Core ships `app.subscribe(key, fetch)` and `app.invalidate(key)`. The developer names a key per query and calls invalidate in every mutation that affects it. No compiler involvement.

This is the Redis/Firebase pattern every stack already has. The failure mode is the famous one: a new mutation forgets an invalidate call and some client goes stale. The compiler knows the read and write sets and would just not be telling anyone.

options.name: Polling reactivity
options.detail: `app.live` re-runs the query on an interval and pushes when the result differs. No tracking, no invalidation, works with any function. Latency is the poll period, load grows with subscriber count times poll rate, and a write is visible only on the next tick. It is the shape teams settle for, not the one they want.
options.code:
tickets :: app.live(open_tickets, team, every: 2000ms)
// close() commits… clients see it up to 2s later

comparisons.note: Convex tracks read sets in deterministic V8 isolates and retries mutations on conflict. It proved the model but requires their cloud; Jet can prove the same facts in sema and stay self-hosted.
comparisons.code:
export const openTickets = query(async ({ db }, { team }) =>
  db.query("tickets").withIndex("team", q => q.eq("team", team)).collect());

comparisons.note: LiveView pushes server-rendered updates but invalidation is hand-wired PubSub topics — option B's failure mode with nicer plumbing.

recommendation.why: Jet already paid for the proofs — effect rows, purity, transaction boundaries, the sema-known app graph. A is the first feature that spends them on something no mainstream language has: stale-free realtime by construction, self-hosted. It is the strongest possible answer to what a language-level effect system is for.

whyNot.reason: Manual keys reintroduce the exact bug class the ingredients exist to kill, while the compiler silently holds the answer.
Polling trades correctness timing for simplicity Jet does not need, and collapses under subscriber count.

recommendation.tradeoff: The runtime carries a footprint index and re-run scheduler; queries that want liveness must actually be @Pure + Db.Read, which constrains how people write them (the constraint is the feature).

hybrid.synthesis: A can expose B's primitives underneath as the expert floor. `app.subscribe`/`app.invalidate` stay public for exotic sources the tracker cannot see. C's `every:` becomes an expert option for non-tracked queries. Beginner magic on top, manual valves below.

harvest.use: the default loop
public expert floor for sources outside the tracker
expert `every:` option for queries that opt out of tracking

decisions.title: Schedule-as-code: a declarative #Every marker on #Task functions
decisions.gist: Let code declare its own schedule next to the function, consumed by dev, services, and jetos from one declaration.
decisions.lesson:
Recurring work — prune sessions nightly, refresh a cache every five minutes — needs a schedule. Jet has runtime timers (`tasks.interval`, D-TASKRUNTIME1) and jetos has service timers, but no way for an application to declare a schedule as source.

Today the schedule lives wherever the deployment lives: a jetos timer, a cron entry, or a hand-rolled loop. The function and its cadence drift apart. Convex put the schedule next to the function and it reads like the requirement. Jet already ratified the task surface this could ride: a task is an ordinary `#Task fn` (D-JPK-TASKRUN1).
decisions.story: Susan ships a session store. The requirement says expired rows vanish nightly at 3am. She writes the delete in Jet, then leaves the repo to write a systemd timer that shells back into her own binary. Six months later someone renames the task and the timer silently runs nothing.

options.name: `#Every(…)` marker on `#Task fn`
options.detail:
One directive marker on the already-ratified task surface. `#Every(5min)` takes a duration literal (D-UNITLIT1); `#Every("03:00")` takes a daily wall-clock time; both are checked at compile time (unknown shape is an error, not a runtime surprise). Every consumer reads the same declaration. `jet dev` runs due tasks in the dev loop, the service runtime (D-SERVICE1) schedules them in production. A jetos generation projects them as real timer units.

The schedule lives in source, versioned and reviewed with the function it drives. Renaming the fn cannot orphan the schedule.
options.code:
#Task #Every("03:00")
fn prune_sessions() { db.exec("DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expired")? }

$ jet check jobs.jet
error[E13xx]: `#Every("3am")` is not a schedule
  write a daily time as "HH:MM" (e.g. "03:00") or a duration literal (5min)

options.name: Manifest field — schedules in pkg.jet
options.detail: Schedules live in the manifest: `tasks: { prune_sessions: { every: "03:00" } }`. Deployment data stays out of code, and an operator can change cadence without touching source. The cost is the drift Susan hit: the schedule names a function from far away, the rename hazard survives, and a reader of the function cannot see it runs nightly.

options.name: Runtime API only — status quo
options.detail: No declarative surface. A long-lived service loops on `tasks.interval` and calls the work itself. This already works and stays fully general. But every consumer difference is hand-built: `jet dev` cannot list or run due jobs, jetos cannot project a timer unit, and one-shot deploys need a resident process just to own a loop.

comparisons.note: Convex crons are code beside the functions they schedule — the readability this ballot transplants.
Timer units are powerful but live in a different language and directory from the code they invoke — the drift-by-distance option B inherits.

recommendation.why: The schedule is a fact about the function, so it belongs on the function — same reasoning that put effects and contracts on signatures. One declaration feeding dev, services, and jetos is exactly the one-mechanism law (I8) applied to time.

whyNot.reason: Manifest schedules keep the rename hazard and hide cadence from the function's reader; operators can still override at the jetos layer, which is where operational overrides already live.
A resident loop per app re-implements a scheduler everywhere and gives tooling nothing to read, list, or project.

recommendation.tradeoff: Complex calendars (cron expressions, timezones, jitter) are deliberately out of the v1 marker; those cases keep the runtime API or a jetos timer.

hybrid.synthesis: A is the declaration. C's runtime API stays as the expert floor for dynamic schedules. B's operational override survives where it already lives — jetos/service deployment can re-time a declared task with provenance.

harvest.aspect: schedule as a checked source fact on the task
harvest.use: the default surface
stays at the jetos/service layer with explain provenance, not in pkg.jet
tasks.interval remains for schedules computed at runtime

decisions.title: The override law: warnings never block by default; every bypass is spelled and recorded; teams add walls via policy
decisions.gist: One law for every expert escape hatch: the tool advises, the human decides, the record remembers, and only team policy builds walls.
decisions.lesson:
Jet already has expert escape hatches, each minted separately: `#Unsafe("reason")` (S58), `--try-anyway` (D-DEV1), `--allow-impure` (D-CTEFFECT1), `--allow-<root>` effect flags, `assume_deterministic { }` (D-DET1), `#[allow(lint)]` (D-DECIMAL1). They behave similarly by accident, not by law.

Your stated principle: we are not their parents. An expert may ignore warnings, effects, or determinism without being babied. Enterprises still need enforcement and audit. Memory and type safety are never in this conversation — I1 has no override and this ballot does not touch it.

The missing piece is the law that keeps the next ten gates consistent, the way D-MARKER-FAMILY1 made every sigil predictable.
decisions.story: Carl prototypes a scraper on a Saturday. The build nags about an unused fallible result and a float in a money-named field. He does not care yet; he wants to see data flow. At work on Monday, his team's CI must hard-fail those exact lints. Today the first experience depends on each lint's ad-hoc mood, and the second needs tribal knowledge.

options.name: Codify the three-point override law
options.detail:
One law, binding on every current and future gate. First: warnings and lints never fail a build by default — errors are reserved for programs Jet cannot compile safely or unambiguously. Second: every bypass is spelled at the site or on the command line, never in hidden config, and lands in the audit record (`jet inspect dossier`, effect-budget provenance, build facts). Third: walls are team policy only — the ratified `policy:` namespace (D-JPK-POLICYSURFACE1) gains `lints: { deny: [...] }`, joining effect budgets and trust; host/org policy narrows, never widens (already law).

Existing gates keep their spellings; the law standardizes their behavior and every future gate's design.
options.code:
$ jet build --allow-impure          # solo expert: builds, bypass recorded
$ jet inspect dossier build | grep bypass
  bypass: comptime impure (flag --allow-impure, 2026-07-11T14:02)

$ jet build                          # same code under team policy:
error[E13xx]: lint `float_money` is denied by policy (pkg.jet:12)
  price: Float in struct Invoice — use Decimal (core.numeric)
  policy owner: pkg.jet `policy.lints`

options.name: Deny-by-default lints, per-site suppression
options.detail: Default-on lints fail the build; the expert writes `#[allow(...)]` at every site. Codebases stay loud-clean and nothing ships un-acknowledged. It is also the babying your principle rejects: the Saturday prototype fights its tools, and beginners meet walls before they meet the language. Rust's clippy-in-CI culture shows the result — suppression attributes everywhere, signal lost.
options.code:
$ jet run scraper.jet
error[L0504]: float in money-named field
  #[allow(float_money)] to proceed
// …repeat per site, per lint, before anything runs

options.name: Status quo — each gate decides alone
options.detail: No law. Every future gate re-litigates blocking behavior, spelling, and audit. The surface stays inconsistent exactly where consistency teaches trust: some bypasses are flags, some markers, some silent; some are recorded, some vanish. Carl's Saturday and Monday stay unpredictable.
options.code:
// today: six gates, six shapes
#Unsafe("reason") { … }      // marker + reason, audited
--try-anyway                  // flag, unrecorded
#[allow(float_money)]         // attribute, silent

comparisons.note: Permission flags proved explicit-bypass ergonomics, but Deno records nothing — the audit half is missing. Jet already has the audit rails.
gofmt/vet advise and never block a local build; teams enforce in CI. Twelve years of evidence that advise-by-default plus team walls keeps both audiences happy.
comparisons.code: go vet ./...   # exit code matters only where the team says so

recommendation.why: It turns your principle into enforceable law: freedom by default, walls by team choice, memory on everything. Every existing rail is already ratified — this ballot only forbids future gates from drifting.

whyNot.reason: Deny-by-default is parenting: it taxes the solo expert and the beginner to serve the enterprise, which policy already serves better.
No law means the next ten gates each invent their own bypass shape, and the audit story stays accidental.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some real bugs ship in solo projects that a blocking lint would have caught. The bet: respect plus a recorded advisory beats a wall. Teams that disagree get their wall in one line of policy.

hybrid.synthesis: A already contains B for those who want it — `policy.lints.deny` IS deny-by-default, scoped to the people who chose it. C's per-gate freedom survives as spelling variety only; behavior and audit become uniform.

harvest.use: the law
available verbatim through policy.lints.deny for teams and CI
kept — the law fixes behavior and audit, not the sigil

decisions.title: cobol.* binder — call the COBOL estate in place
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a cobol.* binder so Jet code can call existing COBOL programs directly.
decisions.lesson:
COBOL is a business programming language from 1959. It still runs core batch jobs at banks, insurers, and government agencies, and almost nobody writes new COBOL. A copybook is a COBOL include file that describes a record layout: fixed-width fields at fixed byte offsets, with money often stored as a packed decimal (called COMP-3), not a floating-point number.

GnuCOBOL is an open-source COBOL compiler that translates COBOL into C and exposes each program through the C calling convention (the C ABI).

D-FFI-UNIFY1 is Jet's ratified rule that every foreign language mounts as `<lang>.<lib>`, generates safe wrappers, and turns foreign toolchain errors into normal Jet diagnostics. @Codable is Jet's ratified struct marker for types that map to an external wire format. Decimal is Jet's exact base-10 number type from core.numeric; Float is binary and rounds, so it is wrong for money.
decisions.story: Marcus Bell maintains payroll for a county government. The gross-to-net calculation lives in a 1980s COBOL program, PR-CALC, that nobody dares rewrite: it encodes decades of tax and pension rules, and it is correct. Marcus wants a new Jet web portal to show each employee their net pay, computed by the exact same code the nightly batch uses. Today he would shell out to the batch job or reimplement the rules and risk a mismatch.
decisions.inWild:
A Jet payroll service calls the county's COBOL net-pay program with a typed copybook struct and gets an exact Decimal back, no reimplementation.

```jet
use cobol.payroll as pay

// copybook PR-EMP-REC imported as a struct; money is Decimal, not Float
rec :: pay.PrEmpRec.{
    emp_id: "004821",
    gross:  Decimal("5320.00"),
    filing: .married,
}
net :: pay.pr_calc(rec)?          // calls the real COBOL PR-CALC
print("net pay: {net.take_home}") // net pay: 4187.63
```

options.name: GnuCOBOL C-ABI binder
options.detail: `use cobol.<lib>` compiles the COBOL source with GnuCOBOL on a cache miss and calls each program through the generated C ABI, exactly like the ratified C binder (S59). Copybooks import as @Codable structs: each field carries fixed-width offset and length facts, and COMP-3 money fields become Decimal from core.numeric, never Float. Wrappers are safe by construction (I1); a GnuCOBOL compile error becomes a Jet diagnostic (I2), never raw compiler output.
options.code:
$ jet inspect bind cobol ./payroll
cobol.payroll → .jet/bindings/cobol/payroll.jet
  PR-CALC        program → fn pay.pr_calc(rec: PrEmpRec) -> PrResult
  PR-EMP-REC     copybook → struct PrEmpRec  (@Codable, #[Layout(cobol)])
    EMP-ID   PIC X(6)          → emp_id: String   @ off 0  len 6
    GROSS    PIC S9(7)V99 COMP-3 → gross: Decimal @ off 6  len 5 (packed)

// A bad field type is a Jet diagnostic, not a GnuCOBOL error:
$ jet build
error[JT0412]: money field bound to Float loses cents
  --> portal/pay.jet:9
   |
 9 |     gross: Float,
   |            ^^^^^ COMP-3 field GROSS is exact base-10
   = fix: use Decimal; COMP-3 stores packed decimal, Float rounds

options.name: No binder — hand-wrap or rewrite
options.detail: Jet ships no COBOL support. Teams keep doing what they do today: call the batch job over a file or queue, hand-write a C shim, or rewrite the program in another language. The estate stays a black box behind a batch boundary, and any migration is big-bang because there is no way to call one program at a time from Jet.

comparisons.lang: IBM watsonx Code Assistant for Z
comparisons.note: IBM's flagship COBOL story is AI-assisted rewrite to Java — a translation project that leaves two codebases to reconcile. The binder path instead calls the proven COBOL in place, so the running logic never forks.
comparisons.code:
// watsonx: COBOL --(AI translate)--> Java, then reconcile behavior.
// Jet binder: Jet --(C ABI)--> the same COBOL, no second codebase.

comparisons.note: The standard safe-migration pattern wraps a legacy system, then replaces it piece by piece behind a stable interface. The cobol.* binder is the wrapping step; D-FFI-UNIFY1 in-situ replacement is the piece-by-piece step.

recommendation.why: The binder turns an untouchable estate into a set of callable, typed programs. Marcus calls the real PR-CALC from Jet with a typed copybook struct, gets exact Decimal money, and never reimplements a tax rule. It reuses the ratified C-ABI binder wholesale, so COBOL is just another D-FFI-UNIFY1 language.
recommendation.tradeoff: GnuCOBOL becomes a provisioned runtime dependency, acquired only when a project uses cobol.*, hash-pinned and jetpack-managed like CPython for py.*. That cost buys safe, gradual, call-site-stable access to code that otherwise stays behind a batch wall.

whyNot.reason: Leaves every team hand-writing C shims and packing copybook bytes by hand under #Unsafe, where one wrong offset or a Float cent is a silently wrong paycheck. It forces big-bang rewrites because no single program can be called in isolation.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the GnuCOBOL C-ABI binder as the one COBOL surface. Option B is not a second mechanism to keep; it is the status quo the binder replaces. The binder subsumes B's only real use — reaching the estate — while removing its footguns.

harvest.aspect: Typed copybooks + Decimal money over the C ABI
harvest.use: The shipped mechanism: programs become functions, copybooks become @Codable structs with layout facts, COMP-3 money is Decimal, errors are Jet diagnostics.

harvest.aspect: The estate must stay callable in its current form
harvest.use: Kept as the binder's guarantee: call in place with no rewrite, so migration is gradual and the running COBOL logic is never forked.

decisions.title: octave.* sidecar — call MATLAB-compatible .m code from Jet
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships an octave.* root that runs existing .m scripts in a sidecar and marshals matrices to typed Jet values.
decisions.lesson:
MATLAB is a commercial numerical computing environment used heavily in engineering and academia; its programs are `.m` script files built around matrix math. GNU Octave is an open-source language that runs most MATLAB `.m` code unchanged and needs no MATLAB license.

A sidecar is a separate helper process Jet talks to over a typed message boundary, so a crash or bug in it cannot corrupt Jet's own memory. Jet already uses this model for Python (D-FFI-PY1) and R.

`Matrix<M,N>` is Jet's fixed-size numeric matrix type and `Tensor<T>` its N-dimensional array. An effect root is Jet's way of marking that calling into a subsystem carries a tracked effect, like `#(Py)` for Python. jetpack is Jet's package manager; it provisions foreign toolchains so the user never installs them by hand.
decisions.story: Diane Fletcher is a controls engineer. Her team's flight-surface filter was designed years ago in MATLAB as `designNotchFilter.m`, validated against flight data, and treated as ground truth. She is writing the new control loop in Jet. She wants to call that exact filter-design function during startup, get its coefficient matrix, and run the loop natively. Buying MATLAB seats for the whole team, or porting math she does not want to re-validate, are both off the table.

options.name: Sidecar Octave worker
options.detail: `use octave.<lib>` runs a supervised Octave worker in a sidecar, exactly like the ratified py and R roots. Matrices round-trip as typed values: an Octave matrix becomes `Matrix<M,N>` when the shape is known, or `Tensor<T>` otherwise, and Jet matrices marshal back the same way. Any `.m` script is callable. Calls carry an `#(Octave)` effect. Octave is provisioned by jetpack, acquired only when a project uses octave.*. Octave errors are laundered into Jet diagnostics (I2).
options.code:
$ jet inspect bind octave ./filters
octave.filters → .jet/bindings/octave/filters.jet
  designNotchFilter.m → fn flt.design_notch_filter(freq: F64, q: F64)
                        -> Matrix<2, 3>  #(Octave)

// A shape mismatch is a Jet diagnostic, not an Octave stack trace:
$ jet build
error[JT0431]: matrix shape mismatch at boundary
  --> loop/ctl.jet:5
   |
 5 |     coeffs: Matrix<3, 3> :: flt.design_notch_filter(freq: 60.0, q: 30.0)?
   |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ script returns 2x3, binding declares 3x3
   = fix: annotate Matrix<2, 3>, or Tensor<F64> for a dynamic shape

options.name: No octave root — export to C or rewrite
options.detail: Jet ships no Octave support. To reach MATLAB logic, Diane either runs it through MATLAB Coder (a proprietary tool that generates C from a licensed MATLAB install) and binds the C, or rewrites the algorithm in Jet. The open path is a full manual port; the automated path requires paid MATLAB seats, the exact cost the team is trying to avoid.

comparisons.note: rpy2 proved the sidecar bridge model: run the foreign numeric runtime in a companion process and marshal arrays across a typed boundary. Jet's octave root is the same shape as its already-shipped py and R roots, so it is a fourth instance of one mechanism, not a new one.
comparisons.code:
# rpy2: robjects.r['designNotchFilter'](60, 30) -> R matrix -> numpy
// Jet:  flt.design_notch_filter(freq: 60.0, q: 30.0) -> Matrix<2,3>

comparisons.note: MathWorks' own bridge requires a licensed MATLAB runtime on every machine that calls it. The Octave sidecar gives the same MATLAB-compatible call surface with an open runtime jetpack provisions, so there is no per-seat license gate.
comparisons.code:
// Engine API: needs MATLAB installed + licensed to run at all.
// octave.*: jetpack fetches Octave; no license, same .m surface.

recommendation.why: The sidecar lets Diane call her validated `.m` filter design straight from Jet, get a typed Matrix, and run the loop natively — no rewrite, no MATLAB seats. It slots into the existing py/R sidecar precedent, so octave.* is just another D-FFI-UNIFY1 language with crash isolation for free.
recommendation.tradeoff: Octave becomes a jetpack-provisioned runtime dependency, acquired only when a project uses octave.*. Sidecar calls cross a process boundary, so hot inner loops should marshal once and compute in Jet. That is how the worked example uses it: fetch coefficients once, run the loop natively.

whyNot.reason: Both of its paths are dead ends for this team. MATLAB Coder demands the paid seats they are avoiding. A hand rewrite means re-deriving and re-validating flight-critical math where a single sign error is a safety hazard.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the sidecar Octave worker as the one octave surface. Option B is not a second mechanism; it is the status quo the root replaces. The sidecar delivers B's goal — reaching MATLAB logic — without the license gate or the re-validation risk.

harvest.aspect: Typed matrix round-trip over a crash-isolated sidecar
harvest.use: The shipped mechanism: .m scripts become effect-carrying functions, matrices map to Matrix<M,N>/Tensor<T>, Octave provisioned by jetpack, errors laundered.

harvest.aspect: MATLAB-compatible surface without a MATLAB license
harvest.use: Kept as a design requirement the sidecar satisfies: the open Octave runtime runs the same .m code, so no seat cost and no forced rewrite.

decisions.title: Source-level importer framework — jet import <lang> <dir>
decisions.gist: The law every per-language source importer must obey when it translates foreign source code into editable Jet.
decisions.lesson:
Jet already imports foreign metadata: `jet import <ecosystem> <path>` (D-JPK-IMPORTCMD1) reads a manifest — an npm package.json, a PyPI project, a Cargo.toml — and writes canonical, editable Jet describing the project. Nothing imports the actual source code.

This ballot fixes the framework law for source importers, not any one language; each per-language importer (cobol2jet, py2jet, c2jet, and so on) ships later under this law.
