hybrid.synthesis: A absorbs B's concern inside the plane: `#Live` needs no reason argument, so the beginner-adjacent case stays ceremony-free while joining the family.

harvest.use: adopted

harvest.aspect: live is lighter than the expert escapes
harvest.use: #Live takes no reason argument; #Nondeterministic does
rejected — the churn is three spellings, paid once, greenfield

decisions.title: One meaning for `policy`: respell the in-source module floor as #Policy(…)
decisions.gist: The word policy names two unrelated surfaces — a module allocation floor in source and the manifest governance namespace; give it one meaning.
decisions.lesson:
`policy no_alloc` is a bare item inside a module file (D-NOALLOC-SEM1). It floors that one module: four allocation-shaped expressions become error E0921 inside it. Nothing else reads it.

`policy:` in the manifest is the governance namespace (D-JPK-POLICYSURFACE1): trust, providers, licenses, replacements — and D-LINTPOLICY1 just added `lints:` to it. It governs the whole workspace and feeds prompts, locks, and audit.

Same word, two homes, two scopes, two jobs. A directive that changes what compiles inside a scope is the `#` plane's exact definition (D-MARKER-FAMILY1).
decisions.story: Owen reads a teammate's PR: `policy no_alloc` at the top of a module. He has just configured `policy: { lints: … }` in pkg.jet, so he assumes this is the same system reaching into source, and looks for the module's entry in the manifest. There isn't one. Two features are sharing one name and he learned the wrong lesson first.

options.name: Respell the module floor as `#Policy(no_alloc)`
options.detail:
The in-source item becomes a module-level directive: `#Policy(no_alloc)`. Future floors ratified for modules (D-MEM1 names `no_alloc` as the first) arrive as arguments, not new keywords. The bare `policy` keyword leaves the grammar; the word means the manifest namespace, alone.

The directive plane is the honest home: it changes what compiles in a scope, exactly like `#Unsafe` changes legality in a block.
options.code:
#Policy(no_alloc)

fn mix(a: F32x4, b: F32x4) -> F32x4 { … }

$ jet check hot_path.jet   # after the break
error[E0003]: unknown statement `policy`
  module floors are `#Policy(no_alloc)`; manifest governance is pkg.jet `policy:`

options.name: Keep both spellings, document the difference
options.detail: Zero churn; the reference docs explain that source `policy` and manifest `policy:` are different systems. The collision stays: every new reader resolves it the hard way, and future module floors keep the keyword growing in parallel with the namespace.

comparisons.note: Go compiler directives are comments-with-shape (`//go:noinline`), never keywords — scope-local build behavior stays off the keyword list.

recommendation.why: One word, one meaning is the cheapest kind of simplicity, and the directive plane is this feature's definitionally correct home. The floor mechanism also gains a growth path (new floors are arguments) instead of new keywords.

whyNot.reason: Documentation cannot un-collide a word; the confusion re-occurs per reader, forever, and the keyword still grows in parallel with the namespace.

recommendation.tradeoff: One retired spelling; the D-NOALLOC-SEM1 checker is untouched, only its trigger respells.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps B's zero-semantic-change property — the local-only walk, E0921, and the ratified scope cut all survive verbatim; only the spelling moves plane.

harvest.use: adopted
preserved — checker and diagnostics unchanged

decisions.title: One meaning for `drop`: rename the linear consume to `consume(x)`
decisions.gist: Two unrelated features share the word drop — discarding a result and consuming a linear value; rename the rarer one.
decisions.lesson:
`.drop("reason")` discards a fallible or `@MustUse` result with visible intent (D-IGNORERET, just re-ratified as the sole discard spelling). It is everyday surface.

`drop(x)` is something else entirely. A `#SingleUse` value (D-LIN1) must be consumed exactly once on every path — passed by `^`, returned, or explicitly finished with `drop(x)` inside an `#Unsafe("reason")` block. That is the expert linear-types tier, and its `drop` does not discard an unwanted result; it satisfies a consumption obligation.

One word, two semantics. Every language that overloaded a common word this way (Rust's `drop` function versus Drop trait versus drop glue) pays in forum confusion forever.
decisions.story: Hank learns `.drop("best-effort")` in week one — the discard verb. In month three he handles a `#SingleUse` session token and reads `drop(token)` in the expert docs. He assumes it discards the token's result and wonders what error he is suppressing. It suppresses nothing; it fulfills a linearity proof. The word taught him wrong.

options.name: Rename the linear consume to `consume(x)`
options.detail:
The linear finisher becomes `consume(x)` — the law it satisfies already says "must be consumed exactly once", so the word teaches itself. `.drop("reason")` keeps sole ownership of the discard meaning. The retired `drop(x)` spelling becomes an ordinary unknown-identifier error inside the gate.

Blast radius is tiny: `consume` only exists inside `#Unsafe` blocks on `#SingleUse` values — the narrowest expert surface in the language.
options.code:
#Unsafe("token retired before handoff")
{ consume(token) }

cleanup_temp().drop("best-effort")   // unchanged, sole meaning

$ jet check session.jet   # after the break
error[E0104]: unknown function `drop`
  a #SingleUse value is finished with `consume(x)`;
  discarding a result is `.drop("reason")`

options.name: Status quo — context disambiguates
options.detail: Keep both. The call shapes differ (method with a string versus free function in a gate), so the compiler is never confused — only people are. The Rust precedent says the confusion is permanent and generates the same explanation in every teaching thread.

comparisons.note: Rust's `drop` names a free function, a trait, and compiler glue; "what does drop actually do here" is a perennial forum thread. The overload never stopped costing.
comparisons.code:
drop(x);            // the function
impl Drop for X {}  // the trait — related but not the same thing

recommendation.why: One word, one meaning — bought at the smallest possible price, since the linear tier is the least-typed surface in the language and `consume` states the obligation it fulfills.

whyNot.reason: The compiler never needed the fix; readers do, and they pay per reader forever while the fix costs one tiny expert spelling once.

recommendation.tradeoff: One expert spelling retires; D-LIN1 diagnostics re-bless with the new word.

hybrid.synthesis: Nothing to combine — B is the absence of A. The teaching text in A's error message carries B's only asset: the reminder that the two features exist.

harvest.use: adopted
true under A as well — only the word changes

decisions.title: One spelling for the generated Rust: the emit verb; the --emit-rust flag dies
decisions.gist: A verb and a global flag both print the generated Rust; keep the verb.
decisions.lesson:
Jet compiles to Rust internally (I2 hides it; experts sometimes want to see it). Two surfaces expose it today. `jet emit --rust <file>` is a verb whose whole job is emitting generated output. The global flag `--emit-rust` additionally prints the generated Rust during another command, like `jet check`.

S14 says one canonical spelling per construct. D-CLI-SURFACE1 put `emit` in the ratified daily ring. The flag predates the ring and now duplicates it.
decisions.story: Peggy suspects a codegen bug. One teammate tells her `jet emit --rust tool.jet`; another says `jet check tool.jet --emit-rust`. She runs both, gets the same Rust twice, and files the mental note every duplicate spelling costs: which one is the real one, and is the other subtly different?
decisions.inWild:
$ jet emit --rust tool.jet          # the verb (ratified ring member)
$ jet check tool.jet --emit-rust    # the flag — same bytes, second spelling

options.name: Verb only — `--emit-rust` becomes a teaching error
options.detail: `jet emit --rust <file>` is the one spelling. The global flag leaves the table; using it names the verb. Scripts pipe the verb's stdout, which is already its contract. One place to document, one behavior to pin in CLI transcripts.
options.code:
$ jet emit --rust tool.jet > tool.rs

$ jet check tool.jet --emit-rust
error[E2102]: unknown flag `--emit-rust`
  the generated Rust comes from `jet emit --rust tool.jet`

options.name: Flag only — fold the verb's job into every command
options.detail: Kill the `emit` verb instead; any command accepts `--emit-rust`. This inverts the ratified ring (D-CLI-SURFACE1 lists `emit` as a daily verb) and couples an output mode into every command's contract — each verb's transcript now has a with-flag variant to pin.
options.code:
$ jet check tool.jet --emit-rust
$ jet build tool.jet --emit-rust   # every verb grows the mode

comparisons.note: Go exposes compiler internals through dedicated tool verbs, not flags scattered across commands — one place to look.
comparisons.code: go tool compile -S main.go   # the one spelling for assembly output

recommendation.why: The verb is already ratified ring surface with the right contract (emit to stdout); the flag is the stray duplicate. Removing it costs nothing but the S14 violation.

whyNot.reason: It deletes a ratified ring verb to keep the stray, and multiplies every command's transcript surface by the output mode.

recommendation.tradeoff: Anyone using the flag in a script retypes it once as the verb, guided by the teaching error.

hybrid.synthesis: B's convenience — seeing the Rust for exactly what you just checked — survives under A as two commands in a row, or a shell pipeline; no flag needed.

harvest.use: adopted
run `jet emit --rust` beside `jet check`; same bytes, one spelling

decisions.title: One math home: fold core.numeric (BigInt, Decimal) into core.math
decisions.gist: Numbers live in two modules — functions in core.math, arbitrary-precision types in core.numeric; fold them into one home.
decisions.lesson:
`core.math` is the canonical callable math surface (D-MATHLIB2): libm functions plus the checked/saturating/wrapping integer families, already width-generic (D-FLOATW1).

`core.numeric` holds exactly two types: `BigInt`, the arbitrary-precision integer (D-BIGINT1), and `Decimal`, the exact base-10 number for money (D-DECIMAL1). Nothing else lives there and nothing else is planned there.

A user who needs big or exact numbers is doing math; the split makes them learn a second module name for two types. Go put arbitrary precision inside math (`math/big`) and the placement never confused anyone.
decisions.story: Cora computes compound interest. She imports `core.math` for `pow`, then discovers `Decimal` lives somewhere else and goes hunting. Completion offers `core.numeric` — a name she has to guess means "the other half of math". Two imports, one domain.
decisions.inWild:
use core.math
use core.numeric          // the other half of math

principal: Decimal :: Decimal("10000.00")
rate :: math.pow(1.05, years.to_float())

options.name: Fold — `BigInt` and `Decimal` move into core.math
options.detail: `core.math` becomes the one numbers home: functions and the two arbitrary-precision types together. `core.numeric` leaves the registry (ordinary unknown-module error, clean break). Construction spellings are untouched — `BigInt(…)`, `Decimal("…")`, the no-auto-promotion law (E0130–E0133), and the L0504 money lint all survive verbatim.
options.code:
use core.math

principal :: Decimal("10000.00")
big :: BigInt("9999999999999999999999")
rate :: math.pow(1.05, years.to_float())

$ jet check ledger.jet   # after the break
error[E0606]: unknown core module `core.numeric`
  BigInt and Decimal live in `core.math`

options.name: Keep the split — functions versus types
options.detail: The boundary is at least statable: math holds functions, numeric holds types. But it is not a boundary users need — nobody benefits from filing `Decimal` away from `pow` — and it costs a guessed module name plus a second import in every financial file.

comparisons.note: Go nests arbitrary precision inside math as math/big; fifteen years, zero placement confusion.
Python splits decimal, fractions, and math as flat top-level modules — the sprawl users memorize rather than derive.
comparisons.code:
import math
import decimal   # a placement you just have to know

recommendation.why: One domain, one home, and the freed top-level slot serves the D-CORENS2 admission law. The types keep every ratified behavior; only their address changes, while the language is still greenfield.

whyNot.reason: The functions-versus-types boundary is real but useless — it optimizes the registry's tidiness over the user's import list.

recommendation.tradeoff: One clean import break for files using core.numeric today.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps B's only virtue — a statable rule — by upgrading it: the rule becomes "numbers live in math", which is both statable and useful.

harvest.use: adopted
survives as the simpler rule: numbers live in math

decisions.title: One membership word: contains for elements, contains_key for keys; Bag's has dies
decisions.gist: Membership is asked three ways — contains, contains_key, and has; unify on the contains pair.
decisions.lesson:
Asking "is this in the collection?" is spelled three ways. `Set`, `SortedSet`, and `BitSet` use `contains(value)`. Maps and `Lru` use `contains_key(key)` — precise, because a map could plausibly be asked about keys or values. `Bag` uses `has(item)`, and Bag's method list (`add`, `remove`, `has`, `count`) sits in ratified law (D-TAG1).

The element/key pair (`contains`/`contains_key`) is one family with a stated reason. `has` is a third word for the element case that already has a word.
decisions.story: Ray writes `if tags.contains("urgent")` for a Set, then swaps in a Bag to count duplicates. The compile error tells him Bag spells the same question `has`. Nothing about counted membership changes the question; the word changed anyway.
decisions.inWild:
tags.contains("urgent")        // Set / SortedSet / BitSet
scores.contains_key(name)       // map / Lru — key membership, precise
inventory.has("arrow")          // Bag — third word, same question

options.name: Contains pair only — Bag.has renames to contains
options.detail: `contains(value)` is the element-membership word everywhere; `contains_key(key)` stays the keyed question on maps and caches. `Bag.has` renames to `contains` — one clean break on one type. The pair enters stdlib-api-laws.md Law 1 as the membership rule, so future collections cannot mint a fourth word.
options.code:
inventory.contains("arrow")     // Bag joins the element rule
scores.contains_key(name)        // unchanged

$ jet check quiver.jet   # after the break
error[E0104]: no method `has` on `Bag<String>`
  membership is `contains(value)`

options.name: Has everywhere — the shorter word wins
options.detail: Rename the whole family: `set.has(v)`, `map.has_key(k)`, `bag.has(v)`. Shorter and JavaScript-familiar, but it respells the larger shipped surface (every set-like plus every map) to spare one Bag method, and `has_key` reads worse than `contains_key`.
options.code:
tags.has("urgent")
scores.has_key(name)
inventory.has("arrow")

options.name: Status quo — three words
options.detail: Keep all three. The Bag outlier stays as precedent, and Law 1's guessability promise keeps one standing exception the docs must explain.
options.code:
tags.contains("urgent")
scores.contains_key(name)
inventory.has("arrow")

comparisons.note: Rust ships exactly the contains/contains_key pair across every collection; the consistency is why nobody looks it up twice.
JS ships has on Map and Set but includes on Array — the living example of what a third word costs.
comparisons.code:
set.has(v);
arr.includes(v);   // same question, different word

recommendation.why: The contains pair is the majority shipped surface and carries its own reason (element vs key). One rename on one type buys a zero-exception membership rule.

whyNot.reason: It respells the majority to match the outlier — maximum churn for a two-letter saving.
The exception survives as precedent, and the next counted collection will cite it.

recommendation.tradeoff: One clean break on `Bag.has`, amending the D-TAG1 method list.

hybrid.synthesis: Nothing of B survives contact with the churn math; C's no-churn instinct is honored everywhere except the single outlier the rule exists to fix.

harvest.aspect: contains/contains_key as the closed membership pair
harvest.use: adopted into Law 1
rejected; two letters do not buy a respell of the majority surface
kept — exactly one method moves

decisions.title: Law 1 says `length`, the shipped surface says `len()` — reconcile the naming law with ratified law
decisions.gist: The Core API rubric bans abbreviations and names len as its example, but len() is the ratified, shipped spelling everywhere; one text must bend.
decisions.lesson:
Two ratified texts disagree. The Core API rubric (D-STDRUBRIC1=A, Law 1) says names are plain English words, not abbreviations — its own example is "`length`, not `len`".

The shipped, ratified surface says otherwise: S41 ratifies `s.len()` for string length; S76 ratifies `.len` as the compile-time constant on fixed lists; every collection ships `xs.len()`. The rubric and the surface cannot both be law.

This matters beyond one method: the rubric is the review gate for every future Core API, so its examples teach reviewers what to reject.
decisions.story: Ted reviews a new Core API against the rubric checklist. Law 1's example tells him to reject `len`-style names. The very first file he opens uses `xs.len()` — ratified, golden-tested, everywhere. He now has to guess whether the rubric or the surface is the real law, which is the guess a review gate exists to remove.

options.name: Amend Law 1 — `len` joins the blessed vocabulary
options.detail: Law 1 keeps its plain-English rule but swaps its example. It gains a short blessed-abbreviation list: programmer vocabulary shared across every mainstream language (`len`, plus the module names `fmt`, `args`, `env`). The shipped surface is untouched. The rubric stops contradicting the code it reviews, and the blessed list is closed — additions need a ballot.

options.name: Rename the surface — `.length()` everywhere
options.detail: The rubric wins: `len()` becomes `length()` across strings, collections, and the fixed-list constant. Plain-English purity, at the cost of respelling the single most-typed method in the language and re-blessing every example, snapshot, and golden. Go, Rust, and Python all chose the short word; no mainstream precedent supports the long one.
options.code:
count :: names.length()
size  :: buffer.length

$ jet check app.jet   # after the break
error[E0104]: no method `len` on `[String]`
  the length method is `length()`

comparisons.note: Go's builtin is len() — the abbreviation IS the plain word for programmers; Go's own style guide bans other abbreviations while keeping it.
Rust ships .len(); Python ships len(x). Three ecosystems agree the short form is the universal spelling.

recommendation.why: `len` is not an abbreviation to its audience — it is the cross-language word for length, which serves Law 1's actual goal (guessable names) better than `length` would. A closed blessed list keeps the rubric's teeth for real abbreviations like `rm`.

whyNot.reason: It respells the most-typed method in the language against every mainstream precedent, to satisfy a rubric example rather than a user need.

recommendation.tradeoff: Law 1 gains a small exception list reviewers must know; the list is closed and ballot-gated.

hybrid.synthesis: A absorbs B's discipline by making the exception list closed and ballot-gated — plain English stays the default, and the next `rm`-style name still gets rejected.

harvest.use: adopted
kept as the default rule; the blessed list is the only carve-out and it is closed

decisions.title: One storage verb: add — upsert by default, add_new for no-overwrite; insert and put die
decisions.gist: One verb stores into every collection: add upserts and reports what it displaced, add_new refuses collisions; insert and put both die.
decisions.lesson:
Storing into a Core collection is spelled three ways today. Maps use `insert(key, value)`. `Set`, `SortedSet`, and `Bag` use `add(value)`. The `Lru` cache uses `put(key, value)`.

Your direction: the verb is `add`, and experts need both collision behaviors — overwrite-by-default and only-if-new. The two behaviors are real semantics: an upsert replaces silently; a unique-add must leave the existing value untouched and say so.
decisions.story: Ellen caches sessions. Most writes should just land — latest wins. But when two workers race to claim a job id, the second must NOT overwrite the first; it must learn it lost. Today she gets `put` with one behavior and hand-rolls the other with a get-then-put race.
decisions.inWild:
scores[name] = 10               // map index-write (S39) — stays the literal upsert
scores.add(name, 10)             // method form, same upsert
tags.add("urgent")               // element containers, same verb
claims.add_new(job_id, worker)   // only-if-absent — the race-safe claim

options.name: add upserts and returns the displaced value; add_new refuses collisions
options.detail:
One verb family on every collection; `insert` and `put` both die. Keyed containers: `add(key, value) -> T?` upserts and returns the displaced old value (`None` means the key was fresh) — the expert reads the collision from the return, free. `add_new(key, value) -> Bool` stores only if the key is absent; `false` means it existed and was left untouched.

Element containers: `add(value) -> Bool` (`Set`/`SortedSet`: `true` if newly added; `Bag`: always `true`). `S39` index-writes stay the literal upsert. The rule enters Law 1.

options.name: Two verbs by container kind — insert for keyed, add for elements
options.detail: The earlier shape: keyed containers spell storage `insert(key, value)`, element containers spell it `add(value)`; `Lru.put` renames to `insert`. The keyed/element split is teachable, but it keeps two verbs where one now suffices, and it leaves the only-if-new behavior unspecified — the gap your question names.
options.code:
scores.insert(name, 10)
tags.add("urgent")
recent.insert(user_id, page)   // and no race-safe claim exists

options.name: Status quo — insert, add, and put coexist
options.detail: Keep all three per-type verbs. Zero churn; the memorization tax stays, the collision behavior stays implicit per type, and the next cache-like type mints a fourth verb.
options.code:
scores.insert(name, 10)
tags.add("urgent")
recent.put(user_id, page)

comparisons.note: Rust's insert returns Option<old> — the displaced-value trick A adopts; the only-if-new case needs the separate entry API most users never find.
comparisons.code:
let old = map.insert(k, v);          // Some(prev) on collision
map.entry(k).or_insert(v);            // the hidden only-if-new path

comparisons.note: .NET ships exactly A's pair: the indexer upserts, TryAdd refuses collisions and returns bool — race-safe claims are one call.
comparisons.code:
dict[k] = v;            // upsert
dict.TryAdd(k, v);      // false if present, untouched

recommendation.why: It answers the requirement exactly: one guessable verb, magic upsert default, and both collision behaviors first-class — the return value gives experts collision visibility on the default path, and add_new makes the race-safe claim a single call.

whyNot.reason: Two verbs where one now suffices, and it never answers the only-if-new requirement.
Three verbs, implicit collision behavior, and the gap stays open per type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two clean breaks (map.insert and Lru.put respell to add); Set.add gains a Bool return.

hybrid.synthesis: A absorbs B's keyed/element distinction inside one verb — the signature (key + value vs value) carries it — and adds the collision pair B lacked.

harvest.use: adopted; enters Law 1
carried by the signature, not the verb
two renames total; index-write upsert untouched

decisions.title: Constructor-idiom law: codify when bare Type(…), .new, .over, and .from_* each apply
decisions.gist: Four construction idioms ship across Core with an implicit pattern; write the pattern down so it binds reviews.
decisions.lesson:
Core constructs values four ways today. Bare type-name calls build a value from its components: `Vec3(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)`, `F32x4(…)`, `BigInt("…")`, `Severity(raw)?`. `.new()` makes a fresh, usually empty, stateful container: `Set.new()`, `Pool<T>.new()`, `Shared.new(x)`, `Scene.new()`. `.over()` wraps a view around existing data without owning it: `Reader.over(bytes)`, `Cursor.over(s)`. `.from_*()` converts from another representation: `F32x4.from_array(…)`.

Each idiom is individually ratified, and the pattern is real — but it is nowhere written down. The API rubric (D-STDRUBRIC1) only says literals use `Type.{ }` and factories use `Type.from_*`, which under-describes the shipped surface. Unwritten patterns drift: the next contributor picks by taste.
decisions.story: Gene adds a `RingLog` type to Core. Should construction be `RingLog(capacity)`, `RingLog.new(capacity)`, or `RingLog.over(buf)`? He greps Core, finds all three idioms, and picks by coin flip. Review argues about it for a day because the rubric has no line to point at.
decisions.inWild:
v :: Vec3(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)          // bare call: value from components
ids :: Pool<Marker>.new()          // .new: fresh stateful container
r :: Reader.over(bytes)            // .over: view over existing data
lanes :: F32x4.from_array(vals)    // .from_*: conversion
// four idioms, zero written law

options.name: Codify the four-idiom law as shipped
options.detail: One rubric rule, matching every ratified constructor. Bare `Type(…)` applies when the arguments ARE the value (components; fallible where narrowing, like `Severity(raw)?`). `.new(…)` makes fresh stateful containers. `.over(…)` wraps non-owning views of existing data. `.from_*(…)` converts between representations. `Type.{ }` stays the literal for plain data records (D-DOTCTOR1). Nothing shipped changes; the law enters stdlib-api-laws.md and the review checklist.

options.name: Collapse toward one idiom — .new everywhere
options.detail: Every non-literal construction becomes `.new(…)`: `Vec3.new(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)`, `Reader.new(bytes)`, `BigInt.new("…")`. One idiom to learn, but it erases distinctions the current surface communicates. A Reader borrowing bytes reads identically to a Pool owning slots. It also respells the ratified math/SIMD/numeric constructors beginners type most.
options.code:
v :: Vec3.new(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)
r :: Reader.new(bytes)      // owning? borrowing? the name stopped saying

options.name: No law — reviews keep arguing
options.detail: Status quo. The pattern stays folklore; each new type re-litigates construction in review, and drift accumulates exactly where beginners form first impressions.
options.code:
// next quarter, plausibly:
buf :: RingLog.create(512)   // a fifth idiom arrives unballoted

comparisons.note: Rust's new/from/with conventions are API-guideline law, not folklore — the written rule is why the ecosystem converged.

recommendation.why: The surface already agrees with itself; the cheapest possible act — writing the pattern down — locks the consistency in and ends the per-review argument. Zero churn, one rubric rule.

whyNot.reason: It buys uniformity by deleting information the idioms carry (owning vs viewing vs converting) and respells the constructors beginners meet first.
Folklore drifts; the fifth idiom arrives with the next contributor.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more rule in the review checklist; genuinely new construction shapes need a ballot to extend the list.

hybrid.synthesis: A gives B's one-rule learnability at the meta level — one LAW covering four idioms — while keeping the information each idiom encodes.

harvest.use: adopted into stdlib-api-laws.md + review template
achieved as a single derivation rule instead of a single spelling
survives as the ballot path for genuinely new construction shapes

decisions.title: Ambient-surface admission law: one closed registry for every no-prefix name
decisions.gist: The names usable without any import are scattered across three decisions; write the closed list once and gate additions with ballots.
decisions.lesson:
The ambient surface is what a Jet file can call with no `use` line — the very first thing a beginner meets. Today it is defined in pieces. D-PRELUDE1=B makes `print` and `input` ambient. S36 adds `panic` and `require` as prelude builtins. The comptime tier adds `embed_file`, `embed_bytes`, `find`, and `fetch` under their effect gates (D-CTIO1, D-CTEFFECT1). Keywords like `copy` are separate grammar.

Each piece is ratified; no single text says "this is the whole list." D-PRELUDEX1 already guards one direction — libraries can never inject ambient names — but nothing guards growth from inside Core. The registry pattern is proven: namespaces (D-CORENS2), metadata (D-MARK-META1), constructors (D-API-CTOR1) all just gained closed admission laws.
decisions.story: Ann audits what her students can type on day one. She finds `print` and `input` in one decision, `panic` and `require` in another, and the comptime quartet in a third. When a teammate proposes an ambient `dbg()` helper, there is no single law to point at — just an archaeology exercise across three documents.

options.name: One registry, ballot-gated admission
options.detail: A single normative list enters the spec: ambient always — `print`, `input`, `panic`, `require`; ambient under comptime gates — `embed_file`, `embed_bytes`, `find`, `fetch`. The existing shadowing law (user definitions win) and D-PRELUDEX1 (libraries never inject) are restated beside it. Any addition or removal is a ballot. Nothing shipped changes; the scattered law gains one home and one growth gate.

options.name: Status quo — the pieces stay where ratified
options.detail: Each decision keeps its own fragment; readers assemble the list themselves. The library-injection guard still holds, but Core-side growth has no gate, and the day-one surface — the one list that most deserves a single source of truth — remains an archaeology exercise.
options.code:
// the answer to "what can I call with no import?" spans
// D-PRELUDE1, S36, D-CTIO1/D-CTEFFECT1 — and whatever ships next

comparisons.note: Go's predeclared identifiers are one spec section, famously short; everyone can recite it, and additions (min/max, clear) each took a proposal.
comparisons.code: // Go spec, one list: len cap new make append copy delete panic recover print println …

recommendation.why: The ambient list is the beginner's whole world on day one and the tightest surface in the language — it deserves the same closed-registry law every other growth axis just received. The cost is one spec table.

whyNot.reason: An unlisted surface grows by accretion; the next convenient helper lands ambient because no law says it cannot.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more registry for reviewers to know — the same shape as the namespace, metadata, and constructor laws, so it amortizes.

hybrid.synthesis: A is B plus one table and one gate; every ratified fragment keeps its authority and gains a shared index.

harvest.use: adopted
kept — the registry indexes the decisions, it does not replace them

decisions.title: One artifact-extension law — and .jreplay is two different formats today
decisions.gist: Jet's tool artifacts use two extension families, and one extension names two unrelated formats; fix the law and the collision.
decisions.lesson:
Jet tools write typed artifact files. Ratified today: `.jetmap` (the Jet-to-Rust line table, D-OBS2), `.jetnb` (notebooks, D-NOTEBOOK-DOC1), `.jproof` (proof evidence, D-JPROOF1), `.jtrace` (profiler sessions, D-PERFSESSION1), and `.jreplay`.

Two problems. First, two naming families coexist: `jet`-prefixed (`.jetmap`, `.jetnb`) and `j`-prefixed (`.jproof`, `.jtrace`, `.jreplay`). Second, `.jreplay` is ratified twice for different formats: `game.Replay.record(".jreplay")` writes a game input replay (D-GAME-REPLAY1), while `jet prove --replay` consumes a capability-bound proof replay (D-JREPLAY1). A file picker, an OS association, or a user cannot tell which kind a `.jreplay` is.
decisions.story: June profiles a game. Her folder holds `session.jtrace`, `run.jreplay` from the replay recorder, and `traces/panic.jreplay` from `jet prove`. She passes the game replay to `jet prove --replay` — the wrong kind — and gets a parse error instead of the type-level distinction the extensions were supposed to carry.
decisions.inWild:
$ ls artifacts/
app.jetmap        # jet-prefixed family
notes.jetnb       # jet-prefixed family
run.jproof        # j-prefixed family
session.jtrace    # j-prefixed family
run.jreplay       # game input replay (D-GAME-REPLAY1)
panic.jreplay     # proof replay (D-JREPLAY1) — same extension, different format

options.name: `.jet*` family everywhere; the proof replay renames
options.detail:
One law: every Jet tool artifact is `.jet<kind>` — `.jetmap`, `.jetnb`, `.jetproof`, `.jettrace`. The collision fix rides along: game replays take `.jetreplay` and proof replays take `.jetproof-replay`. Distinct, self-describing, greppable as one family. New artifact kinds need a ballot (closed family, like every other growth law).

The `jet`-prefix wins because it is the product name users already know; three characters of clarity over the `j`-prefix.
options.code:
app.jetmap
notes.jetnb
run.jetproof
session.jettrace
replay.jetreplay          # game input replay
panic.jetproof-replay     # proof replay — collision gone

$ jet prove app.jet --replay replay.jetreplay
error: `replay.jetreplay` is a game replay, not a proof replay
  proof replays are `.jetproof-replay` files written by `jet prove`

options.name: `.j*` family everywhere; the game replay renames
options.detail: The short family wins: `.jmap`, `.jnb`, `.jproof`, `.jtrace`, `.jreplay` stays the proof replay, and game replays become `.jgame` or `.jinput`. Shorter names, but `.j*` collides more easily with other ecosystems' extensions, and the two most user-visible artifacts (`.jetmap`, `.jetnb`) respell away from the product name.
options.code:
app.jmap
notes.jnb
run.jproof
session.jtrace
panic.jreplay          # proof replay keeps the name
replay.jinput          # game replay renames

options.name: Fix only the collision; families stay mixed
options.detail: Rename one of the two `.jreplay` kinds and stop. The dangerous ambiguity dies; the cosmetic split (`jet` vs `j` prefixes) survives, and the next artifact ballot picks a family by taste.
options.code:
run.jreplay            # game replay (unchanged)
panic.jproof-replay    # proof replay renames
app.jetmap             # families still mixed

comparisons.note: Cargo artifacts converged on one recognizable family (Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, .crate); the consistency is why tooling and humans identify them at a glance.

recommendation.why: The collision is a real footgun with two ratified owners, and the family split will only widen as prove/perf/notebook artifacts multiply. One product-named family plus a closed admission rule ends both permanently.

whyNot.reason: It optimizes for brevity over recognizability and respells the two artifacts users see most, away from the product name.
It fixes the sharp edge but ratifies the cosmetic fork, so every future artifact re-argues the family.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three ratified extensions respell once (.jproof, .jtrace, plus one .jreplay kind); artifacts are machine-written, so the break is one re-record away.

hybrid.synthesis: A contains C (the collision fix is its first clause) and takes B's one-family principle — just anchored on the product name instead of the shortest string.

harvest.use: adopted
adopted with the jet prefix
A's first clause; the family law rides the same break

decisions.title: WASI entropy retry allocation identity
decisions.gist: Resolve a contradiction in D-CRYPTO-RNG1: a general allocator may reuse an address after a zeroized buffer is dropped, so Jet cannot guarantee both one live attempt buffer and a never-reused pointer.
decisions.lesson:
An allocation has two identities. Its logical identity is the ownership lifetime: a new Vec is a new allocation request even when the allocator later returns the same numeric address. Its physical identity is that address. Once an old buffer is zeroized and freed, a normal allocator may legally reuse its address.

Preventing address reuse requires retaining old storage, padding buffers, or owning a custom arena. Those choices contradict D-CRYPTO-RNG1's other requirements that each WASI attempt use exactly one full-size buffer and that at most one attempt buffer exist at a time. Address reuse after complete volatile zeroization does not reuse entropy state; it only reuses memory.
decisions.explainer: D-CRYPTO-RNG1 requires each WASI EINTR retry to allocate a distinct fresh full-size buffer, forbids allocation or pointer reuse, and also permits at most one attempt buffer at a time. Those statements cannot all hold under Rust's allocator: after zeroization and drop, the next exact-size Vec may receive the same address. The current attempted workaround allocates count plus padding and passes a shifted slice, which makes pointer values differ but violates the exact full-size allocation rule and proves no security property. Every option preserves the security law: exactly count zero-initialized bytes reach random_get; any non-success volatile-zeroizes the whole attempt; only success returns bytes; at most seventeen calls; no fallback.
decisions.story: A WASI host interrupts random_get twice before succeeding. Jet must throw away every tainted attempt and begin again without exposing partial bytes. The implementation must also be mechanically testable without pretending that a shifted slice pointer is a fresh allocation.
decisions.detail: This decision amends only WASI allocation identity language in D-CRYPTO-RNG1. It does not change providers, retry count, error type, cap, cancellation, supported targets, or zeroization. Tests use an injected provider and allocation-generation counters owned by the test seam; they never treat numeric address inequality as evidence of fresh entropy.

options.name: Fresh lifetime, address reuse allowed
options.detail: Recommended. Each retry constructs a new exact-count zeroed Vec after the prior Vec has been fully volatile-zeroized and dropped. Numeric address reuse is allowed because allocators own addresses; no bytes, capacity object, provider state, or reference crosses lifetimes. Tests prove generation count, one live attempt, exact length, full taint zeroization, seventeen-call cap, and no output on failure.

options.name: Reserve old allocations
options.detail: Keep each zeroized failed Vec allocated until the request ends, forcing the allocator to choose a different live address for the next Vec. This preserves physical pointer inequality but amends the one-live-buffer rule and can retain up to seventeen MiB for a maximum-size request.

options.name: One monotonic retry arena
options.detail: Allocate one bounded arena and give each retry a distinct exact-count slice. This preserves distinct provider pointers and one provider-visible attempt at a time, but amends the rule that every retry owns a separate allocation and reserves up to seventeen times the requested memory.

comparisons.note: Dropping a Vec ends its ownership lifetime but does not reserve its address. A later Vec may legally reuse that address, so address inequality cannot define freshness.
comparisons.code: drop(old); let next = vec![0u8; count]; // next.as_ptr() may equal old_ptr

comparisons.note: The host fills the caller's slice or returns an errno. Security comes from discarding and zeroizing failed attempts, not from comparing allocator addresses.

recommendation.why: A preserves every security property with exact-size bounded memory and states the allocator contract honestly. Freshness means a new cleared ownership lifetime and a new provider call, not a numeric address promise the allocator cannot make.
recommendation.tradeoff: Tests cannot assert pointer inequality. They instead assert exact length, generation count, one live attempt, complete zeroization, retry bounds, and absence of escaped bytes.

whyNot.reason: B makes address inequality true by retaining up to seventeen failed allocations, contradicting the one-live-buffer bound without improving entropy safety.
C replaces distinct allocations with slices of one large arena and multiplies reserved memory, again changing a useful bound for no security gain.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A's exact-size fresh ownership lifetime. Borrow B's explicit proof that prior bytes remain zeroized until release, and C's generation-indexed tests, without retaining their extra storage.

harvest.use: Adopt as the runtime contract and primary proof.
Keep its zeroization evidence, but drop storage immediately instead of retaining it.
Use generation counters in the test-only provider seam, not a production arena.

decisions.title: Package key generation entropy failure
decisions.gist: Choose the exact fail-closed behavior when package-signing key generation cannot obtain operating-system entropy.
decisions.lesson:
Package key generation crosses two ratified laws. D-PKGSIGN1 requires `jet registry keygen` and automatic key creation on first publish. D-CRYPTO-RNG1 forbids key generation until its entropy failure has an exact command diagnostic, cleanup, exit, and no-artifact rule. D-CRYPTO-DIAG1 deliberately did not invent that command row.

Without a row, the helper exits silently and the caller currently misreports a generic helper-build error with cargo-install advice. That is neither safe product behavior nor an honest explanation. The command must either own a precise Jet diagnostic or remain unavailable.
decisions.explainer: This ballot owns only entropy failure for package-signing key creation through `jet registry keygen` and automatic first-publish keygen. It does not change Ed25519, key paths, overwrite protection E1248, signing policy, RandomError, runtime CryptoError, or other crypto commands. All options forbid fallback bytes and partial key files. A new diagnostic code is required for a command-specific row because E3001 is the unhandled Jet runtime-value boundary, while E0704 is a helper-build failure with unrelated recovery.
decisions.story: Mina publishes her first package on a supported host, but the operating system refuses the entropy request. Jet must not create a predictable signing key, leave half a keypair, modify the registry, or tell her that Cargo is missing. She needs one accurate recovery action.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet registry keygen
Error [E1275]: signing key generation needs cryptographic randomness
 What: Jet could not create the package-signing key
 Why: the operating system could not provide cryptographic randomness
 Fix: retry as a new operation on a supported host; no key files were created
decisions.detail: Under A, E1275 is class tool and exits 1. Terminal output is the exact four-line frame shown above, with normal color policy and no raw OS status, path, helper stderr, dependency name, generated Rust, or key bytes. Stdout is empty. `jet registry keygen` creates neither secret nor public file. Automatic keygen aborts publish before package upload, index mutation, signature publication, or key-file rename. Temporary files are absent or removed; secret buffers are volatile-zeroized before return. An existing valid key bypasses entropy and is never changed. JSON remains unavailable until a separate command-JSON owner ratifies its schema.

options.name: Add exact E1275 command row
options.detail: Recommended. Preserve explicit keygen and beginner auto-keygen. Launder provider failure into one command-owned E1275 frame, exit 1, publish nothing, remove temporary files, zeroize secret buffers, and allow only a new deliberate retry. The helper returns a closed internal status; only the Jet command renders copy.

options.name: Disable package key generation
options.detail: Keep `jet registry keygen` and first-publish auto-keygen unavailable until another future command-diagnostic design. Publishing with an existing valid key still works. This follows the strict block in D-CRYPTO-DIAG1 but suspends D-PKGSIGN1's beginner auto-keygen promise.

options.name: Project through E3001
options.detail: Treat helper entropy failure like an unhandled Jet runtime RandomError: emit E3001 and exit 70. This reuses an existing code but gives a first-party command the wrong error class and lifecycle, contrary to D-CRYPTO-DIAG1's command boundary.
options.code:
Error [E3001]: panic: package keygen: the operating system could not provide cryptographic randomness
// exit 70

comparisons.note: Key generation stops when secure randomness fails and does not substitute a deterministic key. Jet adds its own stable diagnostic and artifact cleanup contract.
E3001 owns an unhandled program error. A first-party package command instead needs a command-specific class, exit, cleanup, and recovery row.
comparisons.code: fn run() -> T ? CryptoError // unhandled value boundary, not CLI keygen

recommendation.why: A reconciles both ratified promises: beginners keep automatic signing-key setup, while entropy failure remains fail-closed, accurate, recoverable, and artifact-free.
recommendation.tradeoff: It allocates one new stable diagnostic code and requires terminal snapshots plus command cleanup tests. Runtime JSON remains intentionally unavailable.

whyNot.reason: B avoids a diagnostic row by removing the already-ratified beginner path and leaves first publish needlessly blocked.
C misclassifies a tool operation as a program panic and gives it the wrong exit and recovery contract.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A's exact E1275 projection. Keep B's rule that no command ships before its terminal lifecycle is tested, and C's reuse of the provider's redacted Display sentence only as the Why line, not as E3001.

harvest.use: Adopt the diagnostic, cleanup, exit, and retry contract.
Require snapshots and artifact tests before enabling the entropy-failure path.
Reuse only the redacted provider sentence inside E1275 Why.

decisions.title: Resolve the package-keygen diagnostic code collision
decisions.gist: D-CRYPTO-KEYGEN-DIAG1 selected E1275, but E1275 already belongs to the ratified Jetpack sandbox diagnostic. Choose a unique code without changing the keygen failure behavior just approved.
decisions.lesson:
A diagnostic code is a stable identity, not decoration. Tools, snapshots, documentation, and `jet explain` use it to mean exactly one failure. Two unrelated errors cannot share E1275.

E1275 already means that required build sandboxing is unavailable under D-JPK-NODAEMON1. The new keygen ballot accidentally reused it for entropy failure. Every word of the newly approved keygen lifecycle can remain unchanged if only its code moves to the next unassigned Jetpack slot.
decisions.explainer: The live diagnostics ledger assigns E1275 through E1291. E1292 is the next unassigned Jetpack code. This ballot changes only the code selected by D-CRYPTO-KEYGEN-DIAG1; its class tool, four-line copy, exit 1, redaction, zeroization, retry, and no-artifact rules remain exact.
decisions.story: Mina's editor receives E1275 after signing-key generation fails. Today E1275 tells tooling to explain sandbox policy, while the terminal says cryptographic randomness failed. A unique code keeps humans and machines on the same explanation.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet registry keygen
Error [E1292]: signing key generation needs cryptographic randomness
 What: Jet could not create the package-signing key
 Why: the operating system could not provide cryptographic randomness
 Fix: retry as a new operation on a supported host; no key files were created
decisions.detail: E1275 remains unchanged for sandbox-required/unavailable. Under A, every E1275 reference and test stays intact; the keygen implementation, diagnostics ledger, `jet explain`, snapshots, explicit keygen tests, and automatic-publish tests use E1292. No syntax, provider, error class, JSON schema, or cleanup behavior changes.

options.name: Move keygen to E1292
options.detail: Recommended. Keep E1275 stable for sandbox policy and assign the exact approved keygen entropy row to the next free Jetpack code, E1292.
options.code:
E1275 = sandbox required but unavailable
E1292 = package-signing key generation lacks OS entropy

options.name: Move sandbox off E1275
options.detail: Keep keygen on E1275 and renumber the older sandbox diagnostic. This changes an already-shipped code, its JSON output, snapshots, documentation, and automation solely to preserve the newer accidental assignment.
options.code:
E1275 = package keygen entropy failure
E1292 = sandbox required but unavailable

options.name: Share E1275
options.detail: Let both errors use E1275 and distinguish them by message text. `jet explain E1275`, machine consumers, and stable-code guarantees become ambiguous.
options.code: E1275 = sandbox failure OR keygen entropy failure // ambiguous

comparisons.note: Stable machine identities must not name unrelated failures. Reusing one identifier forces consumers to parse prose, defeating the identifier.

recommendation.why: A preserves the existing stable code and changes only the new, not-yet-implemented assignment. It is the smallest truthful reconciliation.
recommendation.tradeoff: The newly ratified ballot's example changes from E1275 to E1292; all other approved behavior remains identical.

whyNot.reason: B breaks existing sandbox diagnostics and consumers to protect a newer accidental collision.
C destroys one-code-one-meaning and makes `jet explain` and JSON consumers ambiguous.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A's unique E1292 assignment. Preserve B's concern for complete propagation by updating every new keygen fixture and durable document together; reject C's ambiguity entirely.

harvest.aspect: Preserve old code and allocate next free code
harvest.use: Adopt as the diagnostic identity law.
Apply only to the new keygen references, not the existing sandbox row.
Keep the implementation small, but retain unique identities.

decisions.title: Where the OCI image builder lives on the jet CLI
decisions.gist: The container-image builder and the jetos disk-image builder both want the word 'image'. Pick the spelling for each so they never collide.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's manifest has an `image.<name>:` block. It describes something you can build. Its `kind:` field says what kind.

`kind: .Oci` means a container image, the format Docker and Podman use. `kind: .Iso`, `.Qcow`, or `.Raw` means a bootable disk image for jetos, Jet's own operating system. Both kinds live under the same manifest word, `image`, but they build very different things. One is an app packaged to run on a server. The other is a whole installable operating system.

Today two separate commands build them. `jet image <name>` builds the container. `jet os image` builds the jetos disk.

A recent cleanup of Jet's command-line surface (card #497) grouped many long-tail commands under short group names, like `jet os` for jetos-related commands. Its rule listed `image` as one of the words that should move under `jet os`. Nobody checked that `jet os image` already means something else.

This ballot picks how to spell both commands. The goal: the two jobs stay distinct, and nobody types one command expecting one artifact and gets the other.
decisions.story: Priya packages a web service. She writes `image.api: { kind: .Oci, from: packages.api, expose: [8080] }` and runs `jet image api` to build a container she can push to a registry. Later she edits her home server's jetos config and runs `jet os image` to rebuild the bootable installer media after a hardware change. Two different jobs. Two different commands today. The #497 cleanup would silently merge one of those commands into a slot the other already owns.
decisions.inWild: docs/spec/spec.md already documents the split: ".Iso, .Qcow, .Raw, and from: system.<name> are jetos installer inputs handled by jet os image, not by jet image." That line was written before the #497 cleanup. The manifest schema already treats the two kinds as siblings under one `image.<name>:` block; only the CLI verb differs.

options.name: Stay flat: `jet image` for containers, `jet os image` for jetos
options.detail: The container builder keeps its current, already-shipped spelling, `jet image`, at the top level. jetos disk-image generation keeps its current spelling, `jet os image`. Neither command changes at all. The #497 cleanup's rule is corrected to drop `image` from its list of words that move under `jet os`. `push`, `bridge`, `services`, and `config` still move there, since those are genuinely jetos-domain commands.
options.code:
$ jet image api
building OCI image 'api'...
wrote oci-layout, index.json, blobs/sha256/3a9f21...

$ jet os image
building installer media for system.default...
wrote jetos installer media proof .jetpack/installer/2026-07-12-01/proof.json

options.name: Move the container builder into `jet os image`; rename the jetos command to `jet os media`
options.detail:
The container builder takes over the exact spelling `jet os image`. The jetos command that used to answer to that spelling is renamed `jet os media`. That word is not invented; the command's own output already says 'installer media' and 'image variant artifacts'.

Anyone with `jet os image` in a script or doc keeps typing the same words after this change, but now gets a different tool. The container builder wants a package name; the old jetos command wanted a host target. The caller sees an argument error, not a message pointing at the new spelling.
options.code:
$ jet os image api
building OCI image 'api'...
wrote oci-layout, index.json, blobs/sha256/3a9f21...

$ jet os image
error: 'image' expects a package name (e.g. jet os image api)
  hint: building jetos installer media? that command is now jet os media

$ jet os media
building installer media for system.default...
wrote jetos installer media proof .jetpack/installer/2026-07-12-01/proof.json

options.name: Group both under `jet os`, but give the container builder its own noun: `jet os oci`
options.detail: jetos disk-image generation keeps its current, unchanged spelling, `jet os image`. The container builder moves out of the top level and under `jet os`, spelled `jet os oci`. That word is not invented either; the manifest already spells the container kind `kind: .Oci`. The old flat `jet image` becomes a teaching error naming the new spelling, the same pattern #497 already uses for every other verb it moved into a group.
options.code:
$ jet os oci api
building OCI image 'api'...
wrote oci-layout, index.json, blobs/sha256/3a9f21...

$ jet image api
error: 'jet image' moved
  run: jet os oci api

$ jet os image
building installer media for system.default...
wrote jetos installer media proof .jetpack/installer/2026-07-12-01/proof.json

comparisons.note: A container-image builder and a disk/VM-image builder are never one subcommand, even though both make something people call an 'image'. Jet's manifest already draws that same line with `kind:`. The CLI should keep drawing it.
comparisons.code:
$ docker build -t api .
$ virt-builder fedora-38 -o disk.qcow2

recommendation.why: The container builder and jetos disk-image generation were never one job. The manifest already treats them as siblings distinguished by `kind:`, and the spec text already documents `jet image` plus `jet os image` as the correct, working pair. The #497 rule listed `image` next to real jetos-domain verbs by accident, not by design. Option A just corrects that oversight.
recommendation.tradeoff: The long-tail grouping cleanup keeps one exception: `image` stays flat while its neighbors in that same rule move under `jet os`. That is fine, because `image` was never a jetos-domain verb. It only landed on that list because of a shared English word, not a shared job.

whyNot.reason: Reusing `jet os image` for a different job than it already does is a silent meaning swap, not a rename. A caller who has run `jet os image` since it shipped gets routed to the wrong tool, with a confusing argument error instead of a message naming the new spelling.

Nests a build-artifact command, the same family as `jet build`, inside `jet os`, whose other members are all host-OS management verbs. That mismatch makes `jet os` harder to predict, for a rename that fixes nothing option A does not already fix for free.

hybrid.synthesis: Beginner and expert both get the status quo: `jet image <name>` for a container, `jet os image` for a bootable disk, exactly as already documented. The manifest's shared `image.<name>: { kind: … }` schema still expresses both artifact kinds from one declaration. Only the CLI entrypoint differs, matching the split the spec already describes. No new noun, no migration, no silent behavior change.

harvest.aspect: Zero migration, zero collision, already documented in spec.md.
harvest.use: This is the whole recommendation: correct the #497 rule text, change no code.

harvest.aspect: The jetos command's own output already uses the word 'media' for what it produces.
harvest.use: Not adopted here since option A needs no rename at all, but worth keeping as a candidate word if the jetos command is ever renamed for its own reasons.

harvest.aspect: 'oci' is already a manifest-level word (`kind: .Oci`), so it is a safe, non-invented noun.
harvest.use: Not adopted here since option A never needs a new noun, but confirms 'oci' as the right word if the container builder is ever grouped under a namespace in the future.
