decisions.title: Semantics of the seven hangar operational verbs
decisions.gist: What repair, copy, import, export, dump, restore, and sign actually do inside the hangar.
decisions.lesson: The hangar is a content-addressed, generational package store. Every realized package is an object named by its content digest; an object plus everything it references is a closure. These seven verbs are the store's integrity, portability, and trust surface. Words are ratified (D-CLI-STORE2=A). This ballot fixes their behavior. Every mutation is plan-before-apply with stable JSON, and every import is verified then quarantined before it counts (D-JPK-STORECLI1=D). The one open design question is whether serialization needs two concepts or one.
decisions.story: Maya runs an air-gapped CI box. On her networked laptop she realizes imaging@2.4.0 into the hangar. She must move that object and everything it references onto the offline box, prove nothing was tampered with, and make the box trust it. A week later a disk fault corrupts one object. She needs it whole again without rebuilding the world.
decisions.inWild: Maya's hangar holds `imaging-2.4.0-a91f` plus five references. `jet hangar verify` (already built) reports `imaging-2.4.0-a91f failed its content digest`. She has no network on the target box, so she must serialize the closure to a file, hand-carry it, and sign it so the offline box will register it. The ratified surface promises `export`, `import`, `dump`, `restore`, `copy`, `sign`, and `repair` for exactly this loop. Today each prints an honest `not yet built`.

options.name: Nix-faithful: one primitive per verb
options.detail: Each verb maps 1:1 to a nix-store operation. dump and restore serialize a single object as a raw stream, no closure and no signature. export and import carry the closure plus references plus signatures. copy is the live endpoint transfer. repair re-realizes. sign attaches a detached signature. Power users transfer Nix knowledge directly. Cost: dump-archive and export-archive are two serialization concepts a user must learn to tell apart.
options.code:
# laptop: serialize the imaging closure to a file, hand-carry it
$ jet hangar export imaging@2.4.0 --to imaging.closure
exported 6 objects (imaging + 5 references) -> imaging.closure (48 MB)

# air-gapped box: import verifies signatures, quarantines, then registers
$ jet hangar import imaging.closure
imported 6 objects into quarantine; 6/6 content digests OK
registered imaging-2.4.0-a91f into the hangar

# a single object, no closure, raw stream (nix-store --dump/--restore twin)
$ jet hangar dump imaging-2.4.0-a91f | ssh box jet hangar restore
restored 1 object (no references resolved)

# live store-to-store, no intermediate file
$ jet hangar copy imaging@2.4.0 --to ssh://box
copied 6 objects to ssh://box

# corruption: re-realize the broken object from its recipe
$ jet hangar repair imaging-2.4.0-a91f
imaging-2.4.0-a91f failed its digest; re-realized from recipe; OK

# trust: attach a detached signature
$ jet hangar sign imaging-2.4.0-a91f --key ci
signed imaging-2.4.0-a91f with key `ci`

# the friction: `dump` and `export` are two archive concepts.
# A user who reaches for `dump imaging@2.4.0` silently loses the closure.

options.name: Unified archive backbone: one format, seven ergonomic views
options.detail: One canonical, signed, self-describing `.hangar` archive. export writes it to a file, closure by default, with --no-deps for a leaf. import verifies and quarantines it. dump and restore are the stdin/stdout streaming twins that emit the same bytes. copy fuses export, transport, and import over an endpoint. repair verifies then re-realizes or re-fetches. sign (re)signs an object or archive. Beginners stop at export and import. Experts pipe dump and target copy --to ssh://. No verb invents a second serialization concept.
options.code:
# ONE archive format. export writes it, closure by default. Beginners stop here.
$ jet hangar export imaging@2.4.0 --to imaging.hangar
plan:  6 objects, signed by `ci`, 48 MB -> imaging.hangar
apply: wrote imaging.hangar

# a single object is the SAME format, just fewer objects
$ jet hangar export imaging@2.4.0 --no-deps --to leaf.hangar
plan:  1 object -> leaf.hangar
apply: wrote leaf.hangar

# import: same format, verified + quarantined before it counts
$ jet hangar import imaging.hangar
plan:  6 objects; signatures OK; 6/6 digests OK
apply: registered imaging-2.4.0-a91f (+5 refs)

# dump/restore = the same archive, streamed instead of filed (expert pipe)
$ jet hangar dump imaging@2.4.0 | ssh box jet hangar restore
apply: registered imaging-2.4.0-a91f (+5 refs)

# copy = export -> transport -> import, fused over an endpoint
$ jet hangar copy imaging@2.4.0 --to ssh://box
plan:  6 objects -> ssh://box (2 already present)
apply: transferred 4 objects; box verified 6/6

# repair = verify, then re-realize or re-fetch the broken object
$ jet hangar repair imaging-2.4.0-a91f
imaging-2.4.0-a91f failed its digest; re-realized from recipe; verified OK

# sign = (re)sign an object or an archive with a key
$ jet hangar sign imaging@2.4.0 --key ci
signed imaging-2.4.0-a91f with key `ci`

options.name: Acceptance-scoped: build the two workflows in use, defer the rest
options.detail: Implement only what jetos owner-parity needs today: repair, and the export/import closure archive. copy, dump, restore, and sign stay honest teaching errors that name the working path, until a ratified workflow demands them. The default surface stays small and nothing ships half-built. Cost: four ratified verb words sit dark, and a user reading the ratified surface meets gaps where the docs promised a verb.
options.code:
# what jetos parity needs today: repair + export/import (signed closure)
$ jet hangar export imaging@2.4.0 --to imaging.hangar
plan:  6 objects, signed by `ci` -> imaging.hangar
apply: wrote imaging.hangar

$ jet hangar import imaging.hangar
apply: registered imaging-2.4.0-a91f (+5 refs); 6/6 digests OK

$ jet hangar repair imaging-2.4.0-a91f
re-realized from recipe; verified OK

# the rest stay honest teaching errors until a real workflow needs them
$ jet hangar copy imaging@2.4.0 --to ssh://box
error: `jet hangar copy` is reserved but not built
  no ratified workflow needs store-to-store copy yet
  to move an object now: jet hangar export ... then import on the target

$ jet hangar dump imaging-2.4.0-a91f
error: `jet hangar dump` is reserved but not built
  for a single-object archive, use: jet hangar export --no-deps

comparisons.note: Nix splits single-path from closure serialization: --dump/--restore move one path as a raw NAR, while --export/--import carry the reference closure. Signing and repair are separate again. Option B unifies the two archive concepts; A preserves the split.
comparisons.code:
nix-store --export /nix/store/..-imaging | ssh box nix-store --import   # closure
nix-store --dump /nix/store/..-imaging  | ssh box nix-store --restore  # one path
nix store sign --key-file ci.key /nix/store/..-imaging
nix-store --verify --check-contents --repair

comparisons.note: guix archive folds single and closure export into one command with -r, and signing is mandatory: the target store refuses an unsigned import. This informs B's signed-by-default archive.
comparisons.code:
guix archive --generate-key
guix archive --export -r imaging | ssh box guix archive --import   # box rejects unsigned

comparisons.note: docker save/load is a flat layer tarball with no reference-closure model and content digests per layer. Signing is a separate trust subsystem. A hangar closure carries references Docker does not model.
comparisons.code:
docker save imaging:2.4.0 | ssh box docker load
docker trust sign imaging:2.4.0

comparisons.note: ostree is content-addressed like the hangar. fsck is the repair analog; commits are GPG-signed; pull-local moves refs between repos. Confirms repair = fsck + re-realize and sign = attach signature.
comparisons.code:
ostree fsck
ostree gpg-sign COMMIT KEYID
ostree pull-local /other/repo ref

recommendation.why: Option B. One signed, self-describing `.hangar` archive underlies all seven verbs. Beginners learn two words, export and import, and stop. Experts pipe dump, target copy --to an endpoint, and pass --no-deps for a leaf. Because dump and export emit identical bytes, there is exactly one way to mean serialize an object (I8), which kills the dump-versus-export confusion Nix carries. Every verb shares one verify, quarantine, and trust path, so integrity and signing behave the same everywhere. It keeps all ratified words and hollows nothing.
recommendation.tradeoff: All seven verbs stand on one archive format, so that format becomes a stability commitment. It needs a version field and a compatibility rule from day one, and repair and copy wait for the backbone to exist before they light up.

whyNot.reason: dump-archive and export-archive are two ways to serialize an object. That is a second way to mean the same job (I8 friction), and a user who reaches for dump silently loses the closure.
Leaves four ratified verbs dark as permanent teaching errors. The owner ratified the full surface; deferring most of it reads as a hollow default and a broken promise in the docs.

hybrid.synthesis: B is already the hybrid. The beginner surface is export and import, with closure and signing on by default and zero flags. The expert surface is the same mechanism reached differently. Dump and restore stream the identical archive over a pipe, copy fuses the round trip over an endpoint (D-JPK-STOREBACKEND1 adapters), and --no-deps narrows to a leaf. One archive format, one verify-and-quarantine gate, one signing model. The seven verbs are ergonomic entrypoints, never seven independent systems.

harvest.aspect: closure-by-default export and verified, quarantined import
harvest.use: kept as the default behavior of B's export and import

harvest.aspect: single signed .hangar archive behind all seven verbs
harvest.use: the shipped mechanism
implementation starts with the repair and export/import workflows jetos acceptance already needs

decisions.title: User-defined operators for structs and classes
decisions.gist: How users make `+ - * / == <` work on their own structs, like a `Vec2` or a `Money`.
decisions.lesson:
Operator overloading is powerful and easy to abuse. C++ repurposes `<<`, its bit-shift operator, to mean stream output in `cout << x`, a meaning unrelated to shifting bits. Readers then learn each library's private meaning for a symbol before they can read the code.

The guardrail Jet keeps under every option below: overload only existing symbols, never invent new ones, never let a user change precedence, and keep arithmetic symbols doing arithmetic. `v1 + v2` must read as addition, not a disguised side effect.
decisions.story:
Priya builds a physics demo. She has a `Vec2` struct and writes `pos = pos + velocity`, the obvious spelling. Today Jet rejects it, because `+` is defined only for built-in numbers and lane types.

She falls back to `pos = pos.add(velocity)`, then longer `.add(...).scale(...)` chains that bury the math. She wants the same `+` beginners already use on `Int` to work on her own type.

options.name: Operator hook traits
options.detail: Operators are trait sugar, the same family as `Index`, `Display`, and `Iterable`. You implement one trait per operator family on your type, and the compiler wires the symbol to the method. The beginner front-doors stay: `@Numeric` and `@Comparable` on distinct types, plus auto-derived `Equatable`, generate these same impls. One mechanism, several ergonomic entrypoints.

options.name: Direct operator functions
options.detail: Define the symbol itself as a function, the way C++ and Python spell it. `fn +(a: Vec2, b: Vec2) -> Vec2` reads tersely at the definition site. It adds a second definition plane beside traits: capability lives on `fn <symbol>`, not on a named trait, so generic code has nothing to require.

options.name: Named methods only
options.detail: Follow Go: no operator overloading for user types at all. Users write named methods like `pos.add(vel)` and `a.less_than(b)`. The teaching error for `v1 + v2` points straight at methods and the built-in hooks. Symbols stay reserved for built-in numbers and lane types.

comparisons.note: Operators are traits (`std::ops::Add`, `PartialOrd`), so a generic bound names the capability (`T: Add`). This is the model option A adopts, minus lifetimes.
comparisons.code:
impl Add for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn add(self, o: Vec2) -> Vec2 { /* ... */ } }
fn sum3<T: Add<Output = T>>(a: T, b: T, c: T) -> T { a + b + c }

comparisons.note: Operators are free functions or methods keyed by the symbol, which is option B's plane. No capability name, and `<<` shows how far a symbol's meaning can drift from its arithmetic origin.
comparisons.code:
Vec2 operator+(const Vec2& a, const Vec2& b) { return {a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y}; }
std::cout << v;   // same operator family, now stream output

comparisons.note: No overloading; named methods only, which is option C. Symbols stay honest, but numeric-heavy code turns into verbose method chains.
comparisons.code:
func (a Vec2) Add(b Vec2) Vec2 { return Vec2{a.X + b.X, a.Y + b.Y} }
v := a.Add(b).Scale(2)

comparisons.note: Dunder methods (`__add__`, `__lt__`) are per-class and dynamically dispatched, with no static bound a generic can require. Convenient, but the capability is invisible to a type checker.
comparisons.code:
class Vec2:
    def __add__(self, o): return Vec2(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y)

recommendation.why: Operators are already trait sugar in Jet: `Index` gives `x[i]`, `Display` gives `{x}`, and `Iterable` gives the `loop x in` header. Adding `Add`, `Comparable`, and `Equatable` to that family is the same mechanism, so there stays exactly one way to grant a type new syntax. The beginner bundles `@Numeric` and `@Comparable`, plus auto-derived equality, generate these exact impls, so magic and expert control share one spine (I8).
recommendation.tradeoff: You name the operator's trait (`impl Vec2.Add`) rather than write the bare symbol, so the definition site is a line longer than C++'s `fn +`. In exchange, generic code can bound on the capability (`<T: Add>`), and every operator reaches through the same door as `Index` and `Display`. Adopting this lifts the v1 non-goal on operator overloading and widens D-SIMD1 beyond built-in lane types.

whyNot.reason: A `fn +` plane duplicates the trait mechanism Jet already ships for `Index`, `Display`, and `Iterable`, giving two ways to grant syntax (I8). It also leaves generic bounds nothing to name, so `sum3<T>(a + b + c)` cannot state its requirement.

Named-only regresses beginner readability, priority #2: units and money math decay to `price.mul(qty).add(tax)`. It also contradicts shipped surface, since Jet already overloads operators on lane types and re-exposes them through `@Numeric` bundles, so a flat refusal is inconsistent rather than principled.

hybrid.synthesis:
Ship A as the one mechanism, then fold the other options' virtues into it. Beginner bundles (`@Numeric`, `@Comparable`) and auto-derived `Equatable` become front-doors that generate the same operator trait impls a beginner never has to write by hand.

Option B's brevity survives as short method names (`add`, `compare`) and inline `impl` inside the type body. Option C's restraint survives as the fence: overload only existing symbols, invent no operators, change no precedence, and keep named methods the advised path for mutating or side-effectful work.

harvest.aspect: Operators as trait impls in the existing hook-trait family.
harvest.use: The spine of the decision: one mechanism grants a user type every kind of new syntax, from `x[i]` to `x + y`.
Kept as short method names (`add`, `compare`) and inline `impl` in the type body, without adding a second definition plane.

harvest.aspect: Restraint: no new operators, no precedence changes, named methods for side effects.
harvest.use: Kept as the invariant fence around A and the advised path for mutating or side-effectful operations, where a symbol would mislead.

decisions.title: JWT/PASETO verify before the app graph
decisions.gist: Whether token verification ships as standalone functions now, or waits for the whole app graph.
decisions.lesson: A common, safe capability should not wait on unrelated infrastructure. Verifying a third-party token is useful long before Jet has an application graph.
decisions.story:
Priya runs an API gateway. A partner posts requests carrying a signed JWT, and she must reject any token whose signature, expiry, or audience is wrong before trusting the caller.

She does not want to stand up a full web app to do it. She wants one function that takes the token and the key and returns typed claims or a clear failure.

options.name: core.auth typed functions now
options.detail: Ship `core.auth` now with typed verify functions. `auth.verify_jwt(token, key)` returns `Result<Claims>` with expiry and audience already checked. When the app graph lands, `app.auth` calls these same functions, so there is one mechanism with two entrypoints.

options.name: Wait for the app graph (#438)
options.detail: Ship no standalone surface. Token verification exists only through `app.auth`, which rides the app graph. Until card #438 lands, naming the auth surface is a teaching stop that points to the pending card.
options.code:
use core.auth

fn handle(req: Request) -> Response {
  claims := auth.verify_jwt(req.bearer(), key: partner_key)?
  Response.ok(for: claims.subject)
}

# --- what Priya sees today under option B ---
#
#   $ jet build gateway.jet
#   Error [E0763]: token verification is not available yet
#     |-- gateway.jet:4
#     |   claims := auth.verify_jwt(req.bearer(), key: partner_key)?
#     |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ core.auth ships with the application graph
#     |
#     = why: auth is exposed only through app.auth, which is unbuilt (card #438)
#     = fix: track card #438; there is no standalone token API this release
#
# E0763 is a fresh code (0760-0762 used; 0763 free).

options.name: Put verify on core.crypto
options.detail: Home token verification in `core.crypto`, beside the primitives it uses. `crypto.verify_jwt(token, key)` returns `Result<Claims>`. The app graph, when built, calls into `core.crypto` for token work.

comparisons.note: The standard Go library parses and verifies tokens with a plain function call. It needs no web framework and no app-wide graph.
comparisons.code:
tok, err := jwt.Parse(raw, keyFunc)
if err != nil || !tok.Valid { http.Error(w, "bad token", 401); return }

comparisons.note: A standalone crate returns typed claims from one call, independent of any server. Validation (expiry, audience) is passed in.
comparisons.code:
let data = decode::<Claims>(&token, &key, &Validation::new(Algorithm::HS256))?;
let claims = data.claims;

comparisons.note: jose exposes token verify as a free async function, used the same way inside or outside a framework.
comparisons.code: const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, key, { audience: "gateway" })

recommendation.why: Verifying a token is a common, safe need that predates any app graph. Option A ships it now as typed functions, and app.auth later reuses the same functions, so there is one mechanism.
recommendation.tradeoff: A commits to the `core.auth` module name and its verify signatures before the app graph exercises them. That contract is worth fixing now, because the app graph will consume it unchanged.

whyNot.reason: B blocks a safe, ordinary task behind unrelated web infrastructure. A developer verifying a partner token gains nothing from waiting for the full app graph.
C files auth-level formats under crypto, breaking the teachable split where crypto moves bytes and auth handles identity. It also forks the auth story across two modules.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship `core.auth` verify functions now (A). Keep a card-pointing teaching stop (from B) for auth surface not yet built, and layer verify on `core.crypto` primitives (from C) so there is one primitive home.

harvest.aspect: Typed verify functions are usable without the app graph.
harvest.use: Ship as the standalone surface now.

harvest.aspect: A card-pointing stop teaches when a surface is unbuilt.
harvest.use: Reuse its teaching-error voice for any not-yet-built API.

harvest.aspect: Token verify is built on crypto primitives.
harvest.use: Have core.auth call core.crypto, keeping one primitive home.

decisions.title: Credential taint: attach grammar and leak sinks
decisions.gist: How a value gets marked as a credential, and which sinks reject it.
decisions.lesson: The ratified `.Credential` taint kind has no way to attach it and no leak sinks beyond the database. A password that reaches a log must fail to compile.
decisions.story:
Marco adds password login to his app. While chasing a bug, he logs the incoming form so he can see what the client sent.

The form holds the plaintext password. In plain languages that line silently writes the secret into log files that outlive the request. Jet should stop it at compile time.

options.name: Kinded taint: #Tainted(Credential) + credential sinks
options.detail: Attach a kind by naming it: `#Tainted(Credential) value`, generalizing the closed kind set D-TAINT1 already ratified. One lattice, one spread engine. The Credential kind adds log, print, and serialize as sinks, alongside the existing `Db`/`Exec`/`Net`.
options.code:
LoginForm := struct {
  email: String
  password: #Tainted(Credential) String   # kind named inline
}

fn debug_login(form: LoginForm) {
  print("login attempt: {form}")
}

# --- what Marco sees ---
#
#   $ jet build login.jet
#   Error [E0722]: a credential value reaches a logging sink
#     |-- login.jet:8
#     |   print("login attempt: {form}")
#     |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ form.password is #Tainted(Credential)
#     |
#     = why: credential taint may not reach print, log, or serialize sinks
#     = fix: log a non-secret field, or strip it with a #Sanitizer fn first
#
# E0722 sits beside E0721 (the existing Db/Exec/Net taint sink).

options.name: Distinct marker: #Credential
options.detail: Add a dedicated marker `#Credential value`, separate from `#Tainted`. It has its own spread and its own sinks. A value that is both personal data and a credential then carries two markers, and sanitizers split across two planes.
options.code:
LoginForm := struct {
  email: #Tainted(PII) String       # one plane
  password: #Credential String      # a second, parallel plane
}

#   $ jet build login.jet
#   Error [E0722]: a #Credential value reaches a logging sink
#     ... (same leak caught)
#
# but the two planes do not compose. A field that is BOTH personal data
# and a credential needs both markers stacked:
#
#   ssn: #Tainted(PII) #Credential String
#
# and #Sanitizer strips taint while #Credential needs its own stripper --
# two mechanisms for one job.

options.name: Type-driven: Secret<T> wrapper
options.detail: Wrap the value in a `Secret<T>` type from core, with no marker at all. Sinks reject `Secret<T>` in log, print, and serialize positions; `.expose()` is the audited unwrap. This mirrors Rust's `secrecy` crate, but stands beside the ratified `.Credential` kind rather than using it.
options.code:
LoginForm := struct {
  email: String
  password: Secret<String>   # the TYPE carries secrecy; no taint marker
}

fn debug_login(form: LoginForm) {
  print("login attempt: {form}")     # rejected: Secret<String> in a log
  print("email: {form.email}")       # fine
  store_hash(form.password.expose()) # audited unwrap at the one real use
}

#   $ jet build login.jet
#   Error [E0722]: Secret<String> cannot be formatted into a logging sink
#     |-- login.jet:7
#     |   print("login attempt: {form}")
#     |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ form.password is Secret<String>
#     |
#     = why: a Secret<T> has no Display/Serialize; only .expose() reads it
#     = fix: log a non-secret field, or call .expose() at a deliberate site
#
# NOTE: this leaves the ratified .Credential taint KIND unattachable --
# it would need amending D-TAINT1.

comparisons.note: The secrecy crate wraps secrets in a type with no Debug or Display. The only read path is expose_secret, a deliberate unwrap. This is option C.
The -T flag turns on runtime taint that spreads by dataflow and dies at sensitive sinks. A marker-plus-dataflow lattice is exactly option A, done at runtime.
comparisons.code: perl -T script.pl   # tainted data reaching exec/open/eval dies

comparisons.note: Ruby's bolt-on taint plane was removed in 3.0 as unenforceable at scale. A caution that a second, parallel plane (option B) rots.
comparisons.code: obj.taint   # removed in Ruby 3.0; the whole mechanism was dropped

recommendation.why: A adds only the two things the ratified decision left unspelled: a grammar to attach the kind, and the missing leak sinks. It stays one lattice and one spread engine.
recommendation.tradeoff: A means the Credential sink list (log, print, serialize) must be defined precisely, so ordinary formatting is not blocked everywhere. That precision is the point of the feature.

whyNot.reason: B forks taint into two mechanisms for one job, which I8 forbids. A field that is both personal data and a credential needs two markers, and the sanitizer story doubles.

C introduces a second way to mean secret beside the ratified `.Credential` kind, and would force amending D-TAINT1. Every read also needs `.expose()`, and it does not compose with existing taint spread.

hybrid.synthesis: Attach the kind and add the sinks in one lattice (A). Take the audited-unwrap idea from C as the `#Sanitizer` strip point, and heed Ruby's removed plane (B's shape) as the reason not to bolt on a second one.

harvest.aspect: One lattice attaches the kind and parameterizes sinks.
harvest.use: Ship as the mechanism.

harvest.aspect: A credential-specific diagnostic voice reads clearly.
harvest.use: Name credential explicitly in the E0722 sink error, even under A.

harvest.aspect: An audited .expose() unwrap marks the one deliberate use.
harvest.use: Model the #Sanitizer strip point on that audited-unwrap idea.

decisions.title: What is Jet's canonical email and SMTP surface?
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet constructs and sends secure, typed email for magic links, notifications, and expert SMTP workflows.
decisions.lesson:
Email has two separate jobs. A message describes recipients, subject, text, HTML, and attachments. A transport moves that message to a mail server. SMTP is the standard submission transport; applications normally use port 587 with STARTTLS or port 465 with TLS from connection start.

MIME represents Unicode text, HTML, and attachments. Correct generation prevents header injection, bounds sizes and lines, and encodes content safely. Server acceptance is not inbox delivery: a relay can later bounce or filter a message. SMTP also has an ambiguous failure boundary: a connection can disappear after acceptance but before Jet sees the reply, so automatic retry can duplicate mail.

DKIM signs final message bytes, while SPF and DMARC are domain DNS policy. Jet already owns scheduler-aware sockets, TLS, tasks, deadlines, DNS, encoding, files, and crypto. This decision chooses one typed message model, one honest result/error law, safe beginner defaults, and explicit expert transport policy.
decisions.story: Mara adds passwordless login to a small service. She wants one clear call that sends a magic link securely. Later her team adds HTML branding, DKIM signing, a private relay, cancellation deadlines, and delivery audits. Those needs should extend the same Message and Mailer values instead of replacing a beginner-only sender.
decisions.detail: Acceptance: register core.email and real source-level types; hostile address/header/MIME/Bcc/bounds tests; scripted SMTP greeting/EHLO/STARTTLS/AUTH/MAIL/RCPT/DATA/reply/QUIT tests; verified TLS/downgrade/credential-order/plaintext tests; scheduler park/deadline/cancel/drop proofs; exact Cancelled/Timeout/Transient/Rejected/DeliveryUnknown boundaries with no auto-retry; DKIM published vectors; D-AUTH1 uses injected Mailer; UI diagnostics and local-relay golden; docs cover environment defaults, expert overrides, limits, recipient policy, cancellation, and acceptance meaning; no external dependency, hidden thread-per-send, raw transport error, or credential leak. Implementation order: propagate ratification to durable specs; register Core types/signatures in sema; add failing source and hostile tests; implement one bounded serializer; implement one SMTP state machine over core.net/core.tls; map every state to EmailError/SendReport; add DKIM over final bytes; wire D-AUTH1; run targeted sema/codegen/Core/SMTP/TLS/task/UI/golden gates, then parent full suite.

options.name: Native core.email over Jet runtime
options.detail: Jet owns typed messages, MIME, SMTP submission, DKIM, reports, and errors. smtp_from_env supplies safe beginner configuration; smtp(config) exposes the same Mailer with expert policy. No external dependency or FFI exception.
options.technical: Types: Address, Message, Attachment, Envelope, Mailer, SmtpConfig, SmtpSecurity, SmtpAuth, DkimConfig, SendReport, RecipientReport, EmailError. Default submission is port 587 with verified STARTTLS required; port 465 TLS is explicit. STARTTLS never falls back, AUTH never precedes verified TLS, remote plaintext requires explicit insecure opt-in and forbids password auth. EHLO capabilities govern AUTH, SIZE, SMTPUTF8, and 8BITMIME. Credentials use existing taint and never appear in debug/errors. MIME uses CRLF, safe folding, Unicode encodings, unpredictable boundaries, Bcc envelope-only handling, bounded attachment streaming, and dot-stuffing. The default RequireAll policy aborts before DATA on any RCPT rejection; DeliverAccepted is explicit. SendReport means relay acceptance, not delivery. EmailError distinguishes configuration, DNS, connect, TLS, auth, protocol, rejection, transient, timeout, cancellation, and DeliveryUnknown. No hidden retry. send parks through existing task-aware net/TLS and inherits earliest context deadline. Concurrency uses tasks.spawn; no send_async duplicate. Optional DKIM signs final bytes. SPF/DMARC remain documented DNS duties. Implementation is std-only Core runtime composition with no compiler dependency.
options.code:
use core.email as email
use core.tasks as tasks

config := email.SmtpConfig.{
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 465,
    security: .Tls,
    auth: .Password(username: "mailer", password: smtp_password),
    recipient_policy: .RequireAll,
    limits: email.Limits.safe(),
}
mailer := email.smtp(config)?
job := tasks.spawn(take(mailer, message) () => mailer.send(message))
report := job.join()?

options.name: Message model, provider-only delivery
options.detail: Jet standardizes Message, SendReport, and EmailError, but provider packages send through HTTP APIs. This gains managed analytics but makes D-AUTH1 depend on a vendor package/token and cannot serve private SMTP relays.
options.technical: core.email owns message and result types only. Each provider maps proprietary acceptance, webhooks, and retry behavior into them. No built-in SMTP client ships.
options.code:
use core.email as email
use postmark.email as postmark

message := email.message(from: email.address("login@example.com")?, to: [email.address(user.email)?], subject: "Sign in", text: "Open {link}")?
report := postmark.client(token).send(message)?

options.name: External SMTP bridge
options.detail: Jet exposes A's API but delegates SMTP/MIME to an approved Rust library behind a Core bridge.
options.technical: Approve a new stdlib external dependency outside compiler seams. Jet must still own public types, diagnostics, task/deadline mapping, credential redaction, and acceptance law; raw dependency errors never escape.
options.code:
use core.email as email
mailer := email.smtp_from_env()?
report := mailer.send(message)?

comparisons.note: Python separates EmailMessage construction from smtplib transport. Jet keeps that useful split while adding typed addresses, safe defaults, task cancellation, and honest delivery states.
Nodemailer offers one approachable transport object and rich message options. Jet can preserve that shape without dynamic maps, callback errors, or silent fallback.
comparisons.code: await transporter.sendMail({ to: user, subject: "Sign in", text: link })

comparisons.note: Rust mail libraries provide typed builders and SMTP transports. Jet keeps those strengths behind a smaller surface aligned with Jet tasks, errors, taint, and diagnostics.

recommendation.why: A completes D-AUTH1 with one provider-neutral transport built from Jet's existing audited runtime. Beginners get secure submission; experts retain explicit SMTP security, limits, signing, envelope, and recipient policy.

whyNot.reason: A vendor package and token become mandatory, while private relays, local test servers, and provider-neutral deployments remain unsupported.
It adds an external trust and release boundary although Jet already owns the required sockets, TLS, scheduler, encoding, DNS, files, and crypto primitives.

recommendation.tradeoff: Native SMTP cannot promise provider analytics or inbox placement. Jet reports relay acceptance honestly; provider packages may later reuse the same Message and SendReport types.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep A as the single Core mechanism. Harvest B's transport-neutral message/report types and C's hostile conformance knowledge without requiring a provider or dependency.

harvest.use: Built-in transport and beginner default.
Future packages consume the same Message and return the same SendReport.
Harvest hostile cases into Jet tests without importing dependency/error surfaces.

decisions.title: What exact structured IOError tree should every byte stream use?
decisions.gist: Choose the public IOError variants and shared context fields that let files, TCP, Unix sockets, TLS, and codecs implement one nominal Reader/Writer contract without flattening failures into strings.
decisions.lesson:
A byte-stream trait can unify operations only if its error type preserves the facts callers need. The variant answers what kind of failure happened, such as timeout or permission denial. Context answers where and during which operation it happened. An optional operating-system code and cause preserve audit detail without making host-specific text part of program logic.

Clean EOF is not an error: Reader.read returns an empty byte list only after the peer or file reaches end-of-stream. Invalid limits, cancellation, timeout, closed handles, and transport failures must remain distinguishable errors. If adapters collapse NetError, file errors, and TLS errors into Other(message), beginner code can still print the text, but expert code cannot reliably retry, cancel, classify, or audit it.

D-NETIO-CONTRACT2 already ratified one core.io.Reader/Writer contract and the semantic facts IOError must carry. It did not ratify exact constructors or field names. This ballot fixes that public surface before more adapters are wired.
decisions.story: Mara writes one copy function that accepts any Reader and Writer. It works for a file locally, then production reads through TLS over TCP. Beginner code uses ? unchanged. Her service policy retries TimedOut, stops immediately on Cancelled, reports PermissionDenied with a path, and marks Closed as a lifecycle bug. The same match must work across every adapter without parsing messages.
decisions.detail: Acceptance: one public core.io.IOError tree serves Reader/Writer adapters for files, TCP, Unix, TLS, and codecs; exact constructors and fields enter Syntax.rs if user-typeable; read(0) is InvalidInput and empty success means clean EOF only; native errors map losslessly into stable variants/context; beginner Display text remains concise; experts can match kind, operation, resource, OS code, and cause without parsing text; cancellation and timeout never become Other; diagnostics/examples/reference docs and hostile AOT/default-dev tests cover every mapping; obsolete flat adapters are removed rather than retained as a second path.

options.name: Closed variants plus shared IOContext
options.detail: IOError has stable semantic variants and every variant carries the same IOContext record. Beginner code uses ?; expert code matches a variant and inspects one predictable context shape.
options.technical: Public tree: InvalidInput(IOContext), NotFound(IOContext), PermissionDenied(IOContext), TimedOut(IOContext), Cancelled(IOContext), Closed(IOContext), and Other(IOContext). IOContext fields are operation: IOOperation, resource: String?, os_code: Int?, and cause: String?. IOOperation is a closed enum for Read, Write, Flush, Connect, Accept, Close, Resolve, and Codec; adapters select the closest canonical operation. resource contains a path, address, or codec identity when known. os_code is audit data, never portable control flow. cause preserves owned source detail and never contains secrets. Display renders variant + operation + resource, then cause. Existing NotFound(path), PermissionDenied(path), and Other(message) migrate to the context-bearing form; no compatibility alias remains in current-law mode.

options.name: Variants with per-kind fields
options.detail: Keep stable variants, but give each constructor only fields relevant to that kind. Matches are shorter for common cases, while generic logging must normalize several shapes.
options.technical: Examples: InvalidInput { operation, reason }, NotFound { operation, path }, PermissionDenied { operation, path, os_code }, TimedOut { operation, resource, os_code, cause }, Cancelled { operation, cause }, Closed { operation, resource }, Other { operation, resource, os_code, cause }. Every adapter still maps to a typed variant, but adding shared audit data later may change several constructors.

options.name: Keep the three-variant tree
options.detail: Retain NotFound(path), PermissionDenied(path), and Other(message). Network, TLS, cancellation, timeout, closed, and invalid-input failures remain formatted inside Other.
options.technical: No new public constructors ship. Adapter implementations preserve human-readable text but typed programs must parse messages or inspect native errors before conversion. Generic Reader/Writer consumers cannot distinguish retry, cancellation, timeout, or lifecycle policy.

comparisons.note: Go wraps operation, network, source, destination, and cause in net.OpError, then supports errors.Is for timeout and cancellation. A keeps the useful shared context while using a closed Jet enum instead of interface probing.
Rust io::Error exposes a stable ErrorKind plus an optional OS code and source. A makes the kind a Jet variant and the remaining audit facts one typed context.
Python uses an OSError hierarchy with errno and filename fields. A keeps typed classification and resource context without exception subclass ambiguity.

recommendation.why: A provides one semantic mechanism for beginners and experts. ? stays ceremony-free, while every stream adapter preserves the same typed classification and audit context. Shared context also keeps formatter, debugger, report, and policy code uniform.

whyNot.reason: Per-variant records repeat the same operation/resource/cause law and force generic tooling to normalize several shapes. Future shared audit facts would touch every constructor.
It contradicts the already-ratified structured contract: cancellation, timeout, invalid input, and closed lifecycle become unmatchable strings after nominal conversion.

recommendation.tradeoff: A exposes a small IOContext value even for simple path errors. That value is the canonical place for cross-adapter facts and avoids a second native-error channel.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A as the single public tree. Harvest B's concise matching through enum-pattern ergonomics and keep C's short Display text, without flattening stored facts.

harvest.use: Canonical storage and adapter mapping.
Pattern examples bind only fields callers need.
Display remains short while typed context stays available.

decisions.title: What exact SMTP configuration, send, report, and trust surface should Jet expose?
decisions.gist: Fix the constructible types and method signatures needed to implement D-EMAIL1 without inventing SMTP spellings in code.
decisions.lesson:
D-EMAIL1 already chose one native Mailer, secure STARTTLS or TLS-from-connect, honest relay-acceptance reports, no hidden retry, and task-aware cancellation. Implementation still needs exact public shapes. A configuration must say where to connect, how TLS starts, how credentials are supplied, how partial recipient rejection is handled, and which certificate authorities are trusted.

Certificate trust and encryption are separate. A custom CA is useful for private relays and local tests, but it must extend trusted roots while preserving hostname verification. A trust-all switch would make encryption unauthenticated and must not exist. Deadlines and cancellation already belong to Jet's ambient task context; duplicating timeout fields in SMTP config would create two competing authorities.

SMTP envelope recipients are separate from visible headers. Bcc must reach RCPT TO but never MIME headers. Relay acceptance is also not inbox delivery, so SendReport must describe server acceptance and rejection without claiming delivery. A disconnect after DATA may be DeliveryUnknown: retrying automatically could send a duplicate.
decisions.story: Mara starts with smtp_from_env and mailer.send(message). Her production team later uses a private relay with a company CA, requires every recipient to be accepted before DATA, and cancels through a request context. The same Mailer must expose those controls without a second expert transport or an insecure test mode.
decisions.inWild:
config := email.SmtpConfig.{
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    security: .StartTls,
    auth: .Password(username: "mailer", password: smtp_password),
    recipient_policy: .RequireAll,
    trust: .System,
    limits: email.Limits.safe(),
}
mailer := email.smtp(config)?
report := mailer.send(message)?
print("relay accepted {report.accepted.len()} recipients")
decisions.detail: Acceptance: every public type, variant, field, constructor, and method below is registered with decision adjacency; smtp_from_env and smtp(config) create the same Mailer mechanism; STARTTLS never downgrades and password auth never occurs before verified TLS; custom CA input extends roots and retains hostname verification; no trust-all option exists; Message owns the default envelope and expert envelope replacement preserves Bcc/header separation; Mailer.send has one signature and inherits the earliest ambient task deadline/cancellation; reports distinguish accepted/rejected recipients and relay acceptance without claiming delivery; EmailError has stable typed variants including DeliveryUnknown; no automatic retry; hostile real-socket/TLS tests cover reply bounds, capability parsing, downgrade, auth order, partial recipients, DATA ambiguity, cancellation, and drop.

options.name: Closed records plus one send method
options.detail: Use constructible records and closed enums for expert policy, while smtp_from_env and message defaults keep beginner use short. Mailer.send(message) is the only send mechanism.
options.technical: SmtpConfig fields: host:String, port:Int, security:SmtpSecurity(.StartTls|.Tls), auth:SmtpAuth(.None|.Password{username:String,password:Secret<String>}), recipient_policy:RecipientPolicy(.RequireAll|.DeliverAccepted), trust:TlsTrust(.System|.SystemPlusCa{pem:[U8]}), limits:Limits. Custom CA never disables hostname verification. Limits is a constructible record for reply-line/reply-count/capability/recipient/message/auth-challenge bounds and Limits.safe() supplies defaults. Message contains its default Envelope. Envelope fields are from:Address and recipients:[Address]; email.envelope validates it; message.with_envelope(envelope) is the expert override and still cannot add headers. Mailer uses a write receiver and `send(message: Message) -> SendReport ? EmailError`; ambient #Context is the sole deadline/cancellation authority. SendReport fields: server:String, accepted:[RecipientReport], rejected:[RecipientReport], response_code:Int, response:String, accepted_at:String. RecipientReport fields: address:Address, accepted:Bool, code:Int, message:String. EmailError variants: Configuration, Dns, Connect, Tls, Auth, Protocol, Rejected, Transient, TimedOut, Cancelled, DeliveryUnknown; each carries operation:String, server:String?, code:Int?, and reason:String. smtp_from_env maps environment into the same SmtpConfig and rejects missing/unsafe values.
options.code:
mailer := email.smtp_from_env()?
report := mailer.send(message)?

custom := message.with_envelope(email.envelope(from, audit_recipients)?)?
report := email.smtp(config)?.send(custom)?

options.name: Fluent builders
options.detail: Keep config and message internals opaque; expose chained with_host, with_tls, with_auth, with_policy, with_ca, and with_envelope methods before send.
options.technical: Every policy becomes a method call returning a new opaque value. Mailer.send remains singular and ambient context still owns cancellation. This avoids public record fields but creates a larger method vocabulary and makes configuration serialization/audit less direct.
options.code:
mailer := email.smtp_builder("smtp.example.com")
    .start_tls()
    .password(username, smtp_password)
    .require_all()
    .system_plus_ca(company_ca)?
    .build()?
report := mailer.send(message)?

options.name: Environment-only Mailer
options.detail: Expose only smtp_from_env and mailer.send(message). Configuration, trust, envelope, and report policy remain opaque environment conventions.
options.technical: Beginners get the shortest path, but private CA roots, explicit recipient policy, reproducible tests, audited configuration, and programmatic multi-relay use cannot be expressed through typed Jet values.
options.code:
mailer := email.smtp_from_env()?
report := mailer.send(message)?

comparisons.note: Rust SMTP libraries commonly use typed transport builders and TLS parameter objects. A keeps typed policy while using one inspectable record and Jet ambient cancellation.
Go exposes tls.Config with RootCAs and ServerName, but net/smtp leaves protocol policy low-level. A preserves verified root extension and hostname checks behind a smaller safe enum.
Nodemailer uses a dynamic transport object and sendMail. A keeps the approachable one-transporter/one-send shape with closed typed fields and explicit acceptance states.

recommendation.why: A supplies the missing expert controls while preserving one beginner path and one send mechanism. Records are auditable and serializable; closed enums prevent downgrade/trust ambiguity; ambient context avoids a second timeout model.

whyNot.reason: It multiplies configuration methods for fields that form one coherent value, making policy discovery, diffing, and audit less direct.
It denies explicit private-CA trust, envelope control, recipient policy, reproducible fixtures, and multi-relay configuration to expert users.

recommendation.tradeoff: A exposes several small records and enums. They are the one canonical typed policy surface and replace environment-string conventions rather than adding a parallel mechanism.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A as the canonical mechanism. Keep C's smtp_from_env as beginner sugar that constructs A, and harvest B's discoverability through docs/completion rather than duplicate builder methods.

harvest.use: Canonical configuration, envelope, reports, errors, and trust.
Completion and examples explain each record field and enum variant.
smtp_from_env constructs the same SmtpConfig and Mailer.

decisions.title: How should SMTP limits, password secrets, and custom certificate trust become exact?
decisions.gist: Complete the missing SMTP configuration law without inventing field names, weakening certificate checks, or creating a second secret mechanism.
decisions.lesson:
An SMTP client reads lines and message data from a server. Every read needs a limit, because a hostile server can send endless lines or an enormous authentication challenge. A Limits value makes those memory and work ceilings visible and testable. Limits.safe() supplies ordinary defaults.

A password must not behave like a normal String. Jet's Secret value prevents ordinary display and debug output. The open question is whether email uses that existing value, makes Secret generic, or adds a narrower password type.

Transport Layer Security checks two things: encryption and server identity. A private certificate authority can extend trusted roots for a company relay. It must never disable hostname verification. SystemPlusCa therefore means system roots plus supplied certificates, not trust every certificate.
decisions.story: Mara uses the safe defaults for a public relay. Her operations team later adds a company certificate authority and lowers reply bounds for a locked-down relay. Passwords must remain redacted in both setups.
decisions.inWild:
limits := email.Limits.{
    max_reply_line_bytes: 512,
    max_reply_lines: 100,
    max_capabilities: 100,
    max_recipients: 100,
    max_message_bytes: 33554432,
    max_auth_challenge_bytes: 4096,
}
config := email.SmtpConfig.{
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    security: .StartTls,
    auth: .Password(username: "mailer", password: smtp_password),
    recipient_policy: .RequireAll,
    trust: .SystemPlusCa(pem: company_ca),
    limits: limits,
}

options.name: Existing Secret, exact limits
options.detail: Keep Jet's existing non-generic Secret for SMTP passwords. Ratify six explicit limit fields and a verified system-plus-CA trust bridge. Beginners still use Limits.safe() and smtp_from_env().
options.technical: Limits fields and safe defaults are max_reply_line_bytes=512, max_reply_lines=100, max_capabilities=100, max_recipients=100, max_message_bytes=33554432, and max_auth_challenge_bytes=4096. Valid ranges are 64..65536, 1..1000, 1..1000, 1..10000, 1..1073741824, and 1..65536. Validation follows field order and returns EmailError.Configuration on the first failure. SmtpAuth.Password stores password:Secret. SystemPlusCa parses PEM certificates, appends them to system roots, and retains DNS-name verification. Empty, malformed, or certificate-free PEM is rejected before SMTP credentials can be sent.
options.code:
password := Secret.from_text(env.get("SMTP_PASSWORD")?)
config := email.SmtpConfig.{
    host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587, security: .StartTls,
    auth: .Password(username: "mailer", password: password),
    recipient_policy: .RequireAll, trust: .System,
    limits: email.Limits.safe(),
}

options.name: Generic Secret payload
options.detail: Make Secret generic and use Secret<String> for SMTP passwords. Limits and certificate trust stay identical to A. Other secret APIs must choose their payload types too.
options.technical: The six Limits fields, defaults, ranges, validation order, and SystemPlusCa law are identical to A. Secret<T> becomes the canonical secret wrapper. Existing bare Secret uses require a ratified default parameter or migration to Secret<[U8]>. Debug, display, clone, serialization, reflection, and error behavior remain redacted for every T.
options.code:
password: Secret<String> := Secret.from_text(env.get("SMTP_PASSWORD")?)
auth := email.SmtpAuth.Password(username: "mailer", password: password)

options.name: Dedicated EmailPassword
options.detail: Add a purpose-specific EmailPassword value for SMTP authentication. Limits and certificate trust stay identical to A. Callers must convert an existing Secret into this narrower value.
options.technical: The six Limits fields, defaults, ranges, validation order, and SystemPlusCa law are identical to A. EmailPassword is move-only, redacted, and non-serializable. Conversion consumes Secret. No plain String constructor exists outside smtp_from_env, which performs the same protected conversion internally.
options.code:
password := email.EmailPassword.from_secret(^smtp_password)
auth := email.SmtpAuth.Password(username: "mailer", password: password)

comparisons.note: Go extends a RootCAs pool and still verifies ServerName. Jet's SystemPlusCa keeps that identity check while hiding certificate-pool mechanics.
Rust secrecy wrappers redact values, while TLS clients use explicit root stores. A keeps both properties behind Jet's smaller existing types.

recommendation.why: A completes the ratified SMTP policy through Jet's existing secret mechanism. It gives beginners fixed safe defaults and experts explicit, bounded, hostname-verified control.

whyNot.reason: Payload generics do not strengthen redaction or SMTP safety. They change every existing secret API and create type choices where one protected byte value already works.
A second protected password type duplicates Secret's semantic job and adds conversion ceremony without a stronger safety boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: Secret does not encode a String payload in its type. SMTP interprets its protected bytes as UTF-8 only when forming authentication data, with invalid bytes rejected as configuration.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A as the one mechanism. Keep B's payload validation at the SMTP boundary and C's purpose-specific handling inside SmtpAuth, without adding public wrapper types.

harvest.use: Store SMTP passwords as Secret and keep safe defaults short.
Validate protected bytes as UTF-8 when SMTP AUTH needs text.
Keep password extraction private to SmtpAuth and transport internals.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: I still have absolutely no clue what this means. Give me a user story with example code so I can learn what you mean
questions.answer: Ratified A (2026-06-20). Not a language feature — a naming clash inside our own spec docs. Two ratified decisions both coined "Layer 2": S26 (derive ladder: built-in derives) and S60 (capability tier: compile-time pure eval + data embedding). A keeps both numbers and adds one cross-reference sentence on S60 so the next reader can tell them apart. No code, no rename. Compile-time embedding work files under S60.

questions.text: I am leaning B but want to understand the practical tradeoofs of going with B & C respectively
questions.answer: Ratified B (2026-06-20). B (stdlib Guard value: scope.guard(() => {…})) delivers ~95% of C's value — cleanup on every exit path including the ? early return — for zero new syntax and zero ratification, running on existing Drop + lambda machinery, and keeps Jet's one-cleanup-story (RAII) intact. C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?
questions.answer: Bloat is bounded by published-API surface × support window, NOT codebase size, via four bounds: (1) only `#PublishedSchema` types accrue migrations — internal types never do; (2) migrations live in `migrations/`, are build-tier, and cost zero at runtime; (3) you keep migrations only back to your declared support floor; (4) `jet schema squash` collapses old chains into a fresh baseline snapshot. So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: Please reform the ballot using a2 & c beta (#context) as the baseline. Give me grammar options to pick from using those two choices. That is what I want to pick but need to ensure I like the syntax/grammar
questions.answer: Reformed and now RATIFIED. A2+Cβ fixed as the baseline; the grammar pick resolved to G2 — `#context(field: value) { … }`, reusing Jet's single `name: value` spelling (S61/S29), with `=` staying reassign-only. No single-field shorthand; bundle-spread deferred. Shipped as the c74 Smart Context feature.

questions.text: Option D but I dont want to defer the full implementation if avoidable. We are close to epoch 3 anyway, so what should we do to get this working? Propose a new approach in this decision.
questions.answer: Proposed Option D+ so nothing is deferred: an interpreter seam now (Phase 1) plus a Cranelift JIT this Epoch-3 (Phase 2, tiered — interpreter tier-0, Cranelift tier-1). I6 still holds because Cranelift is runtime-side, never in Source/. This needs your approval of the runtime-side Cranelift dependency (same posture as the regex dep). Recommendation: D+. Decision still open pending your call on the dep.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: I think the $ is fine for me, but what about people trying to use the language globally? Is having such a commonly needed symbol an issue? What if people dont have that symbol? How likely is that? Is it a reasonable concern or not a big deal
questions.answer: Not a blocker. `$` is plain ASCII and universal on physical keyboards; Jet already left the ISO-646-invariant subset behind by depending on `# @ { } [ ]`, so `$` adds nothing new. Programmers type `$` constantly (shell/PHP/JS) and no mainstream language uses it as a binding operator, so no conflicting habit. Answered in the D-BIND2 card; rec stands at A (`$=`); decision stays open for your pick.

questions.text: Please update this card so it isnt called "raw mode" AND we will have a separate library for TUI. This gives experts control but also provides batteries included TUI development features out of the box. Please update this question accordingly & give me alternatives to "raw mode"
questions.answer: Reformed the D-TERM1 card: dropped 'raw mode' (naming menu, rec `live { }`; alts direct_input/live_keys/keys/interactive/immediate/cockpit/takeover); confirmed a SEPARATE batteries-included `core.tui` library on top (old Option D is the library, not core), so experts get the low-level primitive and beginners get widgets out of the box; the card now decides only the primitive name + surface (A scoped block rec / B handle / C free fns).

questions.text: Break this into multiple cards, I cant choose multiple on one card
questions.answer: Split the old mega-card into three separate Focus Mode decisions: D-MIGRATE2A for migration operation vocabulary (`add`/`remove`/`change`/reorder), D-MIGRATE2B for where type-change converters come from (inline `via`, named `impl`, or both), and D-MIGRATE2C for `jet schema` CLI verbs (`status`, `squash --before`, and whether CI needs a separate `check`). c73 now links to all three IDs.

questions.text: I dont understand the downside. Please explain more precisely why we shouldn't just allow all core calls.
questions.answer: Updated D-CTCORE1 with the precise downside: allowing all Core at comptime turns pure compile-time evaluation into running a second runtime during compilation. That harms reproducibility, allows ambient side effects during builds (fs/env/process/net/secrets), forces the comptime interpreter to duplicate runtime behavior, complicates supply-chain policy, and creates machine-dependent compile failures. The recommendation stays B: deterministic pure whitelist now; explicit build-time IO/sandboxed recipe tier later.

questions.text: Please update the options to have a large number of sigils that include the = operator and are only two characters long. I want to see a wide array of options that may be more physically ergonomic & logical as an immutable operator before finalizing such a fundamental change
questions.answer: Expanded D-BIND2 with a broad two-character `=` candidate menu: `$=`, `::`, `::`, `!=`, `?=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `~=`, `.=` , `<=`, `>=`, `:=`, `=:`, `==`, `=>`, and `=<`. The shortlist is `$=`, `::`, `~=`, and `=:`; the card still recommends `$=` because it is unused, two characters, contains `=`, and is visually far from mutable `:=`.

questions.text: I like the three @, #, $ prefixes. Clean up the rest of the card to just have these options, then give a thorough analysis of logic, psychology, & the tradeoffs associated with each option
questions.answer: Updated D-BIND2 to only compare `::`, `::`, and `$=`. The card now focuses on what each prefix teaches: `::` reads anchored/address-like, `::` reads marked/metadata-like, and `$=` reads value-centric without borrowing meaning from another Jet sigil family. Recommendation remains `$=` because it keeps `=` in the binding family, stays visually far from `:=`, and does not overload Jet's existing `@` or `#` semantics.

questions.text: Break this into multiple questions, I cant choose multiple answers to one question
questions.answer: Done — the single card was split into four standalone, single-answer cards under board card c78: D-SOA2A (keyword name, rec `columnar`), D-SOA2B (whole-struct vs partial, rec A), D-SOA2C (reserve per-container spelling, rec A), D-SOA2D (serialization interaction, rec A). Each now takes one pick.

questions.text: I still have no idea what this looks like in practice between the two. I dont understand the difference. In general I want to keep the surface smaller & allow flags for experts to specify the behavior they want but out of the box it should be magic. Please update the ballot accordingly
questions.answer: Done — the card was reformed around the steer (small surface, magic default, expert flags) and now shows the actual terminal session under each option for both a script and a server: A = one verb `jet dev` that auto-detects (rerun a run-to-completion program, hot-swap a resident one) with `--restart`/`--swap`/`--watch=off` overrides; B = two verbs where the wrong one silently full-restarts a server. Rec flipped to A; Q2 (dev↔release output-diff = release blocker) kept as a hard rule. (Since submitted as D-DEVMODE1=A.)

questions.text: For generics, we use <T> -> can we use that?
questions.answer: Two things were colliding on the brackets. `[Particle]` is Jet's *list type* ("a list of Particle"), NOT a generic parameter — generics stay `<T>` and are untouched by this card. The old gist's `columnar [T]` just meant "the keyword in front of a list type," where T was the element. So the real question is the *spelling* of the per-container form, and yes — a generic-style `Columnar<Particle>` is now a real option (B) alongside the prefix keyword `columnar [Particle]` (A). The difference: A reads as a storage modifier on the same list type (no new type, same API, just a layout hint), while B (`<T>`-style) makes layout part of the type identity — `Columnar<Particle>` becomes a distinct container needing conversions and its own impls/trait bounds, like `Map<K,V>`. Recommendation stays A: a layout is how a value is *stored*, not a type parameter, and the prefix keyword keeps one word (`columnar`) across both the struct attribute and the per-use form. `<T>`-style is available as B if you'd rather layout live in the type system. Card reformed with the Owner Q answer, the third option, and an updated tradeoff table.

questions.text: This seems broken, there are no options to choose from
questions.answer: Real bug, now fixed. The card's nine candidate keywords were written as a code block plus a table, not as `- **Option X — …**` bullets, and Tower only builds selectable choices from those bullets — so the card rendered with nothing to pick. Reformed the card into nine proper options A–I, one per keyword (A `soa`, B `lane`, C `columnar`, D `striped`, E `slipstream`, F `parallel`, G `split`, H `fieldwise`, I `wingspan`), each with its own example; the comparison table is kept as Tradeoffs. Recommendation is C (`columnar`) — self-defining from the column-store picture, strong prior art (Arrow/Parquet), no collision with concurrency vocabulary. The card is now pickable.

questions.text: How is this handled in Jai & Odin?
questions.answer: Answered in the D-CAP10 card. Odin: no implicit overloading; explicit overload GROUPS only (proc{a,b}). Jai: has overloading but dispatches on argument TYPE. Neither treats capability/mutability as an overload axis, so process(Data)/process(~Data) has no prior-art equivalent. Reinforces Option A; Odin's explicit-group model is the escape hatch if grouping is ever wanted.

questions.text: How is this handled in odin & jai?
questions.answer: Answered in the D-CAP9 card. Odin: ^T ptr type, &x address-of (prefix), p^ deref (POSTFIX). Jai: *T ptr type, *x address-of (prefix, = the doc's raw-of), deref moved from prefix <

questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.
